title: Al-An'am
label: Plain-English commentary
intro:
Al-Anʿām means "The Cattle". It is a long Makkan surah, 165 verses, and it spends the whole of that length on one subject: the oneness of Allah, argued out at length against people who readily agreed that Allah created the heavens and the earth and then shared their worship with something that cannot create anything. The app's translation gives its first words: "All praise is for Allah Who created the heavens and the earth and made darkness and light." From that opening the surah moves through creation, through the signs the Meccans demanded and refused, through the fate of earlier nations, through the story of Ibrāhīm (Abraham) and his argument with his people, through the law about what may be eaten, and on to the Day when everyone will learn whose outcome is the abode. Abū Isḥāq al-Asfarāʾī said that this surah contains all the principles of the oneness of Allah and all its details as well.

### When and how it was revealed

ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās held that the surah came down in Makkah, and Aṭ-Ṭabarānī recorded his fuller statement: all of it was sent down in Makkah at night, accompanied by seventy thousand angels whose voices rose in glorifying Allah. The same report about the seventy thousand angels reached As-Suddi from Murrah, from ʿAbdullāh. ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās also described this as one of the surah's distinctions: all of it, except for some verses, came down in a single descent in Makkah, with the company of seventy thousand angels following it and reciting Allah's name. Mujāhid, al-Kalbī, Qatādah and other early authorities said very much the same. Al-Awfiyy, ʿIkrimah and ʿAṭāʾ likewise transmit from Ibn ʿAbbās the ruling that the surah is Makkan.

### Why praise comes first

The surah opens with Allah praising and glorifying Himself, for making the heavens and the earth a dwelling place for His servants, and for making darkness and light so that night and day serve them. Saying it first is itself a lesson. It teaches the servants how to praise, as though He had told them: say, all praise belongs to Allah.

The opening is not there because praise is needed. Whether anyone praises Him or not, Allah is, in His own perfection, the Praiseworthy One by Himself. What the sentence does is straighten the reader's perspective, and it does so by naming a proof in the same breath. All praise belongs to Allah, and the very next words point to what He has made. A Being who holds power and wisdom of that size is plainly the One who deserves praise, and the worship that follows from praise belongs to Him alone.

### What the wording of verse 1 is doing

Some of the surah's argument sits in the grammar of its first line.

Darkness is put in the plural, while light is put in the singular. One reason given is that light is the more honored of the two. A second is more pointed: light stands for the correct way and the straight path, and that is one thing, while the layers of darkness stand for the paths of error, and those run into the thousands. The Qur'an elsewhere sets a singular and a plural together in the same way, as in "To the right and to the lefts" (16:48). Near the end of this surah the same thought appears as a command: "And verily, this is my straight path, so follow it, and follow no (other) ways, for they will separate you away from His way" (6:153).

The heavens are named in the plural and the earth in the single, although another verse states that the earth is seven, like the heavens (65:12). Māzhari suggested that the wording marks the difference the seven heavens have from one another in form and in attributes, while the seven earths resemble each other, so they are counted as one.

The verbs differ as well. The heavens and the earth are said to be created, while darkness and light are said to be made. The hint is that darkness and light are not independent things standing on their own the way the heavens and the earth do. They are accidents and attributes, which need something else to be there. And darkness is mentioned before light, since darkness is the base state of this world, while light belongs to particular causes. When those causes are present there is light, and when they are absent there is darkness.

### The beliefs the opening came to end

Having the oneness of Allah and its plain proof stated in one line is also a warning. It is aimed at people who do not believe in it simply, and at those who say they believe it and have lost its reality.

The first group named are the Magians, who hold two creators, Yazdan and Ahriman, one the maker of good and the other the maker of evil, and identify the two with light and darkness. Against them the verse says that Allah created the heavens and the earth and made darkness and light. Both belong to Him, and neither is a rival.

Others are named for the same reason. The polytheists of India take gods beyond counting as partners in Allah's divinity. The Arya Samajists accept oneness, yet treat spirit and matter as things with no beginning, standing outside Allah's power and creation, which leaves the reality of oneness behind. The Christians profess one God and then take ʿĪsā (Jesus) and his blessed mother into divinity with Him, and prop the whole up with the Unity in Trinity, an idea that has to be accepted without being reasoned. The idolaters of Arabia went further than all of them in handing out godhood. In their judgment any rock on a hill was good enough to be the object of worship for the whole of mankind. The human being, whom Allah made the noblest of His creation and for whom the universe was made to work, sank to lying prostrate before sun, moon, stars, fire, water, trees, stones and crawling insects, expecting them to provide for him and untie his problems. Once the verse has said that Allah is the Creator of the heavens and the earth and the Maker of darkness and light, every one of those positions collapses. If He is the sole Creator and Maker of everything, giving Him partners is not a difference of opinion. It makes no sense.

### The argument the surah keeps making

The surah's way of proving oneness is to look at how the world is run and to ask what it takes. The system governing heaven and earth is coordinated and single, and the task is enormous. The universe is unimaginably great in its vastness, in its wisdom and in the fact that it means something. The earth turns in space around the bright sphere of the sun with flawless regulation, and light and darkness, day and night, come into being because it does. None of that is within human comprehension.

Two conclusions follow. A being who organises a universe to perfection has no gap in his work that a partner would have to fill. And a Lord whose whole creation runs as one system is one Lord. The order itself is the proof. The greatness involved also rules out the other half of the idea: Allah does not need an assistant, either in creating or in managing what He has created.

### What the surah covers

The opening three verses state the claim, and verses 4 to 11 show the Meccans treating Allah's signs with indifference, rejecting the truth once it arrived, and mocking it, with the ruin of earlier and stronger nations held up as the answer to the question of what that ends in. Verses 12 to 21 establish what Allah owns, what He has forbidden, who His witness is, and what happens to people who invent lies about Him. Verses 22 to 32 drag the partners into the open on the Day of Judgement, describe the spiritual blindness of those who turn away, and measure this life against the next.

Verses 33 to 39 console the Prophet ﷺ against rejection, set the limit on what anyone can do for a person who has decided not to listen, and point to the animals and birds as communities like theirs. Verses 40 to 55 trace the pattern of nations taken by degrees while their own devices answer for them, and then turn to the believers whom the Meccan leaders wanted pushed out of the Prophet's ﷺ company, with the ranks each of them holds. Verses 56 to 62 close the door on the demand to be given the unseen, set the Prophet's ﷺ ignorance of it against Allah's complete knowledge, and use sleep and death as signs of His power over souls. Verses 63 to 73 answer the question of who rescues people when the distress of sea and land arrives, warn against sitting with those who mock revelation, and contrast the dead who cannot hear with the blind who cannot be led out.

Verses 74 to 90 give Ibrāhīm's argument with his father and his people, his reading of the stars, the moon and the sun, his fearlessness, the rank Allah gave him, and the line of prophets he leads, ending with the guidance of all of them as one guidance. Verses 91 to 103 refute the claim that Allah never sent a human being as a messenger and the attribution of sons to Him, and set the Qur'an up as a blessed confirmation that leaves people without an excuse. Verses 104 to 113 deal with clear insights refused, with the ban on insulting what others worship, with the demand that angels or the whole of the unseen be produced, and with the way devils among humans and jinn decorate doubt for one another.

Verses 114 to 127 state that Allah's words are perfect in truthfulness and justice, warn against the majority who mislead away from His path, and lay out the rule for what may be eaten, with the command not to follow steps of satan and the reminder that Allah knows what people conceal and reveal. Verses 128 to 141 gather jinn and humankind to account, give everyone ranks by their deeds, and then expose the dishonest arithmetic by which the pagans set aside portions of their crops and cattle for Allah and for their idols, and killed their children out of fear of poverty. Verses 142 to 150 sort out the eight head of livestock, name the only things actually forbidden, list what was additionally closed to the Jews, and answer the argument that Allah could have destroyed the idolaters had He willed to.

Verses 151 to 158 gather the ten commands Allah gave, hand the reader back to the Torah as a completed guidance, present this Book as blessed, and warn what it is like when the signs of your Lord arrive and belief avails a person nothing. Verses 159 to 165 end the surah by walking away from people who split their religion into sects, promising the good a tenfold reward and the bad its like, and settling the question of who gets what: prayer, sacrifice, living and dying are for Allah, Lord of the worlds, with no partner, and each person carries their own burden, made a steward on earth and tested in what has been given.

### In short

- Al-Anʿām is a Makkan surah of 165 verses, reported to have come down at night in a single descent, accompanied by seventy thousand angels glorifying Allah.
- Its subject is the oneness of Allah, and Abū Isḥāq al-Asfarāʾī said it carries both its principles and its details.
- It opens with praise, and the creation of the heavens, the earth, the darkness and the light is offered as the proof that praise belongs to Allah alone.
- Its plural "darknesses" against its single "light" marks one straight path against many paths of error, and its choice of "made" for darkness and light marks them as attributes rather than independent powers.
- The surah argues from the ordered running of the universe, and it aims at every position that hands a share of divinity to something created, including the worship of stones and insects.

1.text:
The surah begins with praise and ends its first sentence with an accusation. "All praise is for Allah Who created the heavens and the earth and made darkness and light." One claim, one proof, and then a contrast: in the face of what He has made, "the disbelievers set up equals to their Lord". Nothing is argued at length here. The making of the heavens, the earth, the darkness and the light is put forward as something anyone can see, and the worship given to anything else is shown as a mistake so plain that no evidence is needed to expose it.

The whole surah is built on this line. It is a surah about the oneness of Allah, and it opens the way a house is inspected, at the foundation.

### Phrase by phrase

**"All praise is for Allah"** is al-ḥamdulillāh. Abū Isḥāq al-Asfraʾīnī said that a surah which begins this way is going to be about the oneness of Allah, in its principles and in its details, and the opening is what tells you so. On one reading of the phrase, what belongs to Allah is gratitude and divinity together: people thank Him, and they worship Him, and neither of those two is owed to anyone else. Only the One who made the heavens and the earth out of nothing is described with perfection, praised with noble qualities, and loved. He made the night and the day, and they follow one another without a gap. The night carries darkness and the day carries light, and each of them is a benefit.

Allah opens by lauding Himself. He praises Himself with a laudation that has no beginning, and reports His own self-sufficient brilliance and His single, unshared elevation. This is the praise of a tremendous Lord and a wise maker of things. He exists by His own existence, He is beyond compare by His own attributes, He is vast by His own greatness. His rank never ends, His brilliance stands on its own, His existence is one, His being needs nothing, His face is majestic, His power is complete. Glory be to Him. He is the One, the All-Subjugating (39:4), the high, the overwhelming, the great, the transcendent. One of the great figures of the religion, and a leader of the Ṭarīqah, the path of spiritual training, said in effect: who is worthy of praise except the One whose power made all this. His answer: who is fit to be praised for purity, or named for greatness, except the One who created heaven and earth, made day and night, set the heaven up like a roof, laid the earth out like a cradle, readied the day for people to earn a living, and made the night a time of rest?

**"Who created the heavens and the earth"** singles out those two from all the rest of creation, because for anyone who looks they are the largest thing in sight. The heavens and the earth are everything a person can point at, and both of them were made from nothing. On a reading transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās, the two days of creating the heavens were Sunday and Monday, and the two days given to the earth were Tuesday and Wednesday.

**"and made darkness and light"** means every darkness and every light. Ẓulmah is the Arabic for one patch of darkness, and nūr is light. Darkness is put in the plural and light in the singular, for two reasons that both carry weight. The first is that light is the more honored of the two. The second is that darkness has many causes, and each of them is a separate thing, while light reaches us by one road. That very unevenness is counted among the proofs that Allah is one. Some said that darkness and light here stand for faith and disbelief, and that the plainer sense is night and day. The unevenness was also read the other way round, as instruction: light means the correct way and the straight path, and there is one of those, while the layers of darkness mean the roads of error, and those run into the thousands. That is how it was drawn out in al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ.

**"Yet the disbelievers set up equals to their Lord"** is the turn in the sentence. Despite the proof, some of Allah's servants disbelieve, and hand partners and rivals to the Lord who nurtured them. The Meccan idolaters ascribe idols as equals to Him. Some of them claimed a wife for Allah, and some a son, and He is made far above, and removed from, anything they say about Him.

### Is this a statement or an act of worship?

Grammar gives the opening three possible jobs. It may be news, a plain statement that praise does in fact belong to Allah, so that whoever hears it believes it. It may be an act of worship, Allah teaching His servants how to extol Him, as though He were saying: say, all praise is for Allah. Or it may be both at once, and that is the likeliest of the three. The surah's first words would then be doing two things in one breath: telling you what is true about Allah, and showing you what to say about Him.

### Why heaven and earth, and not the rest?

The verse could have listed everything. It names two things and then two more. The heavens and the earth were chosen because they are the most awesome created thing available to an observer, and because a person who agrees that Allah made those two has already conceded the argument. Everything anyone worships instead of Him sits inside one of them.

The same two appear again as an inner picture. On that reading the heaven means the heaven of recognition, which is the hearts of people who come to know Allah, and the earth means the earth of service, which is the souls of people who worship. Allah decorated the visible heaven with the shape of the stars, hung the sun and the moon in it, and made it a place for the people of the earth to look at. He decorated the other heaven in the same way, with the sun of knowledge, the moon of pure oneness and the stars of thoughts, and made it a place for the people of the heaven above to look at. When devils try to overhear, they are driven off from the high heaven by stones thrown at them, and the Exalted Lord said of that: "We have made them stonings for the satans" (67:5). In the same way, whenever satan tries to pour unease into someone, a flash lights up in the heart of the faithful servant from his heaven of recognition and burns the attempt off. That is what the verse about the mindful means when it says that a visit from satan touches them and at once they see things (7:201). And on the flat of the earth He spread seven seas, and in them are use and livelihood for His creatures.

### In short

- The surah opens with a claim and a proof: all praise, and with it all thanks and all worship, belongs to Allah, and what He made is the evidence.
- He praises Himself first to teach His servants how to praise, and because praise is owed to Him whether anyone offers it or not.
- Darkness is plural and light is singular because darkness has many causes and light comes by one road, and because light is the more honored. That is itself counted as proof of Allah's oneness.
- The heavens and the earth are named because they are the largest thing in sight, and because whatever anyone worships besides Allah stands inside them.
- Setting up equals to Allah is the odd thing in the verse, not a competing argument: people who claimed a wife or a son for Him were claiming it against evidence every observer can see.

2.text:
The surah now turns from the big universe to the small one. "He is the One Who created you from clay, then appointed a term ˹for your death˺ and another known only to Him ˹for your resurrection˺—yet you continue to doubt." Three things are claimed about you: you were made, your life has an end written on it, and there is a second end, fixed with Allah, that nobody else has been told. The verse then expresses astonishment that anyone doubts after that.

### Phrase by phrase

**"He is the One Who created you from clay"** speaks to the whole of mankind at once, and its first meaning is their father. Allah created Adam from clay and then gave him life. Mankind began from him, multiplied, and spread east and west. The route from clay to a person runs through ordinary food, which comes from the damp of the earth, and from food comes the sperm, and from the sperm the human body is made. So "created you from clay" is not a poetic way of talking. It describes a chain that is still running.

A report about that clay goes further. Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī said he heard the Prophet ﷺ say that Allah created Adam from a handful taken out of the whole earth, mixing its ingredients together, and that is why Adam's children come out different from one another in colour, in shape, in character and in habit. One is black, another white, another red. One is hard, another soft, one good-natured, another ill-tempered. This was transmitted with a good chain.

**"then appointed a term ˹for your death˺"** is, on the reading Saʿīd ibn Jubayr gave from Ibn ʿAbbās, the Hereafter, and the verse mentions it first as the term already decreed. Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid took it the other way round, and this is the reading many prefer: the appointed term is the span of this earthly life, and the other term, fixed with Allah, is the term of a person's life up to his death. That second sense fits the verse that comes later in this surah, where Allah takes the souls at night and knows what people did by day, so that an appointed term may be fulfilled (6:60). Much the same was relayed from As-Suddi and ʿAtiyyah, from Muqātil ibn Ḥayyan, from Zayd ibn Aslam and ad-Daḥḥāk, and from Qatādah, al-Ḥasan, ʿIkrimah and Mujāhid, among others.

Whichever way the two terms are assigned, one is a personal end and the other is a collective one. A person's own end is death, and it has a fixed term that he has reached whenever he reaches it. Nobody has been given the knowledge of when that is, though the angels know, and in a way people know it too, since the dying of Adam's children all around them, everywhere and all the time, is common experience. The other end is the end of the whole world, the Qiyamah, the day of Doom, when all mankind and every created thing that serves them come to their close together. That term stands fixed with Allah, and its full knowledge has not been given to any angel or any human being.

**"and another known only to Him"** means exactly that: none but He knows when it will happen. The Qur'an says of the Hour that its knowledge belongs to his Lord alone, and that none can reveal it at its time but He (7:187), and again, when people ask when it will land: you have nothing to say about it, and its end rests with your Lord (79:42-44).

**"yet you continue to doubt"** is addressed to the people of Makkah. As-Suddi took the doubt to be doubt about the coming of the Last Hour. They are uncertain about the Resurrection although they know who began their creation, and One who can begin can certainly bring back. He created this world and fixed a term for its ending. He made living things whose span runs out at death. And the other term is the one after which there is no death and nothing wears away.

### Why your own body proves the Hereafter

The argument in these two verses is a ladder. The first verse showed a big universe made by Allah, and the second says that you are a small universe made the same way. Start from the beginning of a person and follow through to his end, through birth, living and death, across all the internal distances a body contains, and the oneness of Allah turns out to be a fact as plain as anything you can check.

Then comes the doubt, and the doubt is answered out of the same body. This world has a limited age. Life in it cannot be free of grief, pleasantness arrives with unpleasantness attached, and good cannot be separated from evil or evil from good. Given that, a person finds it hard to picture an eternal world that is free of grief altogether, the world the Qur'an describes when it speaks of toil being stripped away (35:34). If the Next World is made out of some other stuff, then it is beyond anyone's reach to imagine. If it is made out of the stuff of this world, then this world looks too poor to produce a world of total perfection.

But the person asking the question is his own answer. A human body is built entirely out of earth's elements, and it has properties that no earth has anywhere. It hears, it speaks, it thinks, it does astonishing things, and the dirt it was made from does none of those. Something that is not earth at all has come out of earth, and everyday experience confirms it. If a living, active person can rise out of clay, and if sweet-smelling flowers and heavy fruit can come out of the same ground, then a world more perfect than this one is not too much to ask from it. So there is no room for the doubt, and using a person's own death as the evidence for the end of the whole world system is the most natural and most logical thing in the world. The verse ends in wonder that anyone keeps doubting a Qiyamah proved like that.

### Why the proof does not land

If the reasoning is that clear, why does it leave people unmoved? Because every one of these proofs arrives behind a curtain of causes. When a sign reaches someone's attention he credits it to the cause he can name and lets the sign itself go unnoticed. He is not inclined to accept it, and instead of answering the call he says that if it really came from Allah, then Allah and His angels would have to be visible to the naked eye. That demand is empty. When Allah and His angels do appear in their glory, the time for preaching the truth and declaring Allah's greatness will be over. It will be the time for settling accounts.

### Clay and spirit

There is an older reading of "from clay" that takes the verse apart at its seams. Adam was two things, clay and spirit. His clay belonged to the world of creation, and his spirit to the world of command. What belongs to creation is this: Allah kneaded Adam's clay in His own hand. What belongs to command is this: "I have blown into him of My spirit" (15:29). And the two verses about him match the two halves of him. "Allah chose Adam" (3:33) belongs to the beauty of the command, while "Adam disobeyed" (20:121) belongs to the drag of the clay.

In him there was a rose garden and a bed of mud at once, and the mud was where the roses grew. Every rose, though, has its thorn. A rose like Ibrāhīm (Abraham) came with a thorn like the rebellious Nimrod. A rose like Mūsā (Moses) came with thorns like Pharaoh and Hāmān. A rose like ʿĪsā (Jesus) came with thorns like the Jews who wronged him. A rose like Muḥammad the Arab came with a thorn like Abū Jahl, and no luck in it. No one's mind has flown far enough to reach the branch of Adam's good fortune, and no one's insight has taken in the brightness of the sun of his clarity.

When Adam was at rest in the highest gardens, he assumed that tent of safety would stay pitched for him forever. Then he was addressed, from the side of the All-Compeller and the court of the Most High: "What, one brought up in ornaments and unable to argue clearly?" That is the question the Qur'an puts in the mouth of the deniers (43:18). And the rebuke that goes with it runs like this. Allah said: I want to make a real man out of you, and you have settled for colour and scent, like a bride contented with dress. How long will you sit still and hope for adornment? Set your aim on the road and walk like a man. Take your hands off the neck of your wife, because your hands are needed for gripping the crocodile of passion. Be the drinking companion of the lion of the Sharīʿah. Withdraw from the qualities you were made of, and travel with discipline for feet and blame for boots, out into the wide country of having nothing. Sit down on a dust heap, be happy with one piece of bread, torn clothes and a ruin, and then you will be a man. Throw your life away, walk the road, stand straight, and be a man, and you will be kept alive once your skirt is emptied of all this rubble.

### In short

- "From clay" is literal: Adam was made of clay, mankind came from him, and every person is still built out of food that grows out of damp earth.
- The two terms are a person's death and the end of the world, and the order of the two was disputed. Either way, one is known to the angels and to experience, and the other to Allah alone.
- Your own body is the answer to the doubt about the Resurrection. Earth, by itself, cannot hear, speak or think, and it produced something that does all three.
- Doubt survives the evidence because evidence arrives through causes, and through a demand that Allah appear visibly, which would end the time for being invited in the first place.
- The verse is read as astonishment: the people who doubt it are the people of Makkah, who had watched the Prophet ﷺ grow up among them.

3.text:
The third verse closes the argument the first two opened. "He is the Only True God in the heavens and the earth. He knows whatever you conceal and whatever you reveal, and knows whatever you do." After the big universe and the small one, one Being is left standing, worshipped in both of them, and knowing everything done in either. What follows in the surah, from the demands for signs to the weighing of secret motives, grows from those last three clauses.

### Phrase by phrase

**"He is the Only True God in the heavens and the earth"** is read by Ibn ʿAbbās as the consequential outcome of the first two verses. Because He made all that, He alone deserves worship and obedience in the heavens and on the earth. He is the God of the dwellers of heaven and the God of all the dwellers of the earth. He is the One called Allah throughout them all, and He is the One they single out: the inhabitants of the heavens and of the earth believe in His divinity, they name Him Allah, and they ask Him in fear and in hope. Those who disbelieve among jinn and among humankind are the exception. The Qur'an says elsewhere, in the sense the same words carry: "He is the God of those in heaven and those on earth" (43:84), and that He knows every affair, the public and the private.

**"He knows whatever you conceal and whatever you reveal"** covers what you keep inside your chest and what you say out loud to one another, the intention, the statement, and everything you make public as much as everything you hide. Nothing of it is harder for Him than anything else.

**"and knows whatever you do"** is what you earn, every good deed and every bad one. And He will judge you by them.

### Does "in the heavens" mean He is inside them?

These words have been read as a map of how He relates to things, not a place where He is. He is in the heaven by His essence, and everywhere by His knowledge. He is with the spirit by His company and with the soul by His nearness. The soul comes to nothing in Him, and where the spirit disappears He is what is left of it. He is found where people find, and known where people know. Reports about Him do not spoil the ultimate reality, and the reality does not cancel the reports. Say "He established Himself on the Throne" (7:54), because He is upon the Throne in a sitting that befits Him. Recite "He is with you wherever you are" (57:4), because He is with you. He does not occupy a place because He needs one. He displays places out of mercy. He built the Throne for those who are seeking Him, not for those who already know Him. And if someone who knows Him drew one breath without Him, he would have tied the belt of unbelief back on.

The same voice turns the verse into a prayer: you are my tongue's boast in both worlds and my spirit's joy in the seeing that comes tomorrow. Remake what occupies me, with Yourself. I have no spirit left to scatter in front of the finding of You, and no tongue equal to acknowledging your favours. Whoever sees You is hidden inside the seeing, and whoever looks for You is not on the earth and not in the heaven.

### In short

- The verse moves from creator to God: because He made the heavens, the earth, darkness and light, He alone is worshipped in all of them.
- Its knowledge covers hidden intention, spoken word and earned deed, and the three are the ground of the judgement that the surah keeps announcing.
- Only disbelieving jinn and human beings are outside that worship, and they are outside it by choice, not because He is unknown to them.
- The phrases "in the heavens" and "on the Throne" are read alongside "He is with you wherever you are", and explained as nearness and knowledge, not location.

4.text:
Verse 4 states a fact about these people rather than an argument. "Whenever a sign comes to them from their Lord, they turn away from it." The word for sign, āyah, covers a miracle, a proof and a verse of the Qur'an, and the verse is a complaint: it is not that the evidence is weak, it is that the people shown it keep turning their faces aside. The chronically heedless human race is being described here, and the fault is its obstinacy against what is true.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Whenever a sign comes to them from their Lord"** means the people of Makkah. The signs are Allah's proofs of His own oneness and of the truth of His noble Messengers, verses sent down in the Qur'an, clear demonstrations, and miracles of the kind that cannot be explained away.

**"they turn away from it"** is the whole of their answer. They do not consider these signs and they do not trouble themselves about them. Whatever is shown them for their guidance, they swing their face away from it and pay it not the least attention. The idolaters ignore a proof or a miracle from their Lord as though it had not arrived. The clear demonstrations of Allah's oneness, and the miracles that prove His messengers truthful, came to them, and after that they still turned aside. They have taken to a way of their own, and that way runs away from evidence.

### What signs were they refusing?

The signs meant here are the kind the Qur'an reports for this Prophet ﷺ and this people. The eclipse of the sun was one, the splitting of the moon was one, and the stars were among them. Each one came, and each one was met with unbelief. A sign that arrives does not oblige anyone to think, and this verse is a description of people who have decided in advance not to, before the next verse reports what that decision ends in.

### In short

- The verse is a complaint, not an invitation to produce more evidence: the people described have signs and refuse to look at them.
- Āyah here means sign, miracle, proof and revealed verse together.
- Turning away is an act of the will. The verse does not say they could not see, it says they could not be bothered.
- Their stubbornness is described as a habit of their own, which is why the punishment in the next verse is presented as something that will meet them on level ground.

5.text:
""They have indeed rejected the truth when it came to them, so they will soon face the consequences of their ridicule"." Verse 4 said they turned away. Verse 5 says what that amounted to, denial of the truth once it was in front of them, and what it will amount to, being told the news of what they are laughing at now. The middle of the sentence is a warning and a hard threat at once: they will find out that what they denied was true, and they will taste how their own conduct ended.

### Phrase by phrase

**"They have indeed rejected the truth when it came to them"** turns on one word, al-Ḥaqq, the Truth, and that word is left open here to two things: the Qur'an, and the blessed person of the noble Prophet ﷺ. Both came to them, and both were denied, and the two belong together, since the Book arrived in the company of the man who brought it. It was the people of Makkah who denied it, denying the Qur'an and the sign at the same time. They had turned away from clear proofs and demonstrations, and then they went on to something plainer still and denied it.

**"so they will soon face the consequences of their ridicule"** is a threat of punishment. Right now these people are careless about their own fate. They mock the miracles and the commandments of Allah that the Prophet ﷺ brought, and they mock the message that there is a Qiyamah and a Hereafter. Soon the news of that ridicule will come to them, and it will come as the punishment for it. The realities they laughed at will be standing in front of their eyes. There will be a Qiyamah, and there will be a Reckoning in which everyone answers for faith and for deed, and everyone is given the reward or the punishment that matches what was done. Believing and admitting it at that point will not serve them, because that day is not a day for doing anything. It is the day of being paid back.

### The sign they could have checked

The strongest reason for calling this a rejection of the truth is that the truth arrived in a form these people had already inspected for forty years. He lived his whole life among these Arab tribes. They watched him grow through boyhood into a young man, and through his youth into later life. They also knew perfectly well that no human teacher had taught him, to the point that he could not write his own name by himself, and all of Arabia knew him by the title unlettered and unschooled. In forty years he showed no marked interest in poetry, which was the distinction of that age, and no aptitude for formal learning. Then, at the end of his fortieth year, there was a sudden change, and an overnight flowering of what nobody could have expected. His tongue became a spring of insights, realities, knowledge and arts that disarmed the best minds in the world. He challenged every eloquent master of words in Arabia to produce the like of what he had brought, and at the very least one verse like a verse of the Qur'an. Those same opponents were ready to give up life, wealth, honour, children and family, at any moment, to defeat him. On a challenge that would have cost them nothing but effort, they had no courage at all.

So the bare fact that this man was there, and that this Qur'an was with him, was a sign of unanswerable authenticity. Add to it the thousands of miracles and open proofs that came about through him, and no sane person can say that they were invented, and the size of the refusal becomes clear. They denied all of it, and that is what the verse records.

### Three days when the news arrived

The material connects the consequences promised here to days the audience could identify: the day of Badr, the day of Uḥud, and the day of the Confederates. The news of what they mocked came to them on those days, in the form of punishment, and long before the Reckoning they were still refusing to take seriously. This surah was revealed in Makkah, and the sense of the promise is not that the threat is cancelled by an escape period. It is a God-sent piece of luck, and the sense is: act now, for it is by faith alone that a person succeeds in this world and in the world that lasts.

### In short

- The truth they rejected was the Qur'an and the Prophet ﷺ himself, and both came to them in a town where he had lived his whole life under their eyes.
- Forty years of an untaught man and then a sudden flowering of speech no one could answer is presented as a proof in its own right.
- The threat is that the mocked realities will one day be plainly in front of them, at a Reckoning that will be a day of payment rather than a day of action.
- Some of that news landed in this world, on the days of Badr, Uḥud and the Confederates.
- The delay is a mercy with a deadline in it, and the verse reads as an appeal to use the time still left.

6.text:
Verse 6 changes the evidence from a prophet in their own town to the ruins around them. "Have they not seen how many ˹disbelieving˺ peoples We destroyed before them? We had made them more established in the land than you. We sent down abundant rain for them and made rivers flow at their feet. Then We destroyed them for their sins and replaced them with other peoples." The nations in question were not present for anyone to look at, so the seeing meant here is the seeing of the mind: to ponder, to travel and to read what is left. History is offered as a document, and the verse is an appeal to a reader of documents

### Phrase by phrase

**"Have they not seen how many ˹disbelieving˺ peoples We destroyed before them?"** asks the people of Makkah whether they were not informed, in this Qur'an, and whether they had not heard of it in their trading journeys to Syria and elsewhere. In Arabic the word behind "how many" here is a statement rather than a question, and its sense is simply: many. A generation, qarn, means a body of people living together in one period, and it is also used for a long stretch of time, put at anything between ten and one hundred years. The events and the reports point to one hundred. The Prophet ﷺ told ʿAbdullāh ibn Busr al-Maʿzinīyy that he would live for one qarn, and when he prayed for a certain child that he live a whole qarn, the boy lived exactly a hundred years. Most scholars take the well-known hadith, the one still recited in the khuṭbah of Jumuʿah all over the world, to mean precisely this: a qarn is a hundred years.

**"We had made them more established in the land than you"** says that Allah gave them sovereignty, room and time in it, more than He has given the people of Makkah. They had more of everything: more wealth, more children, more buildings, wider provision, greater riches and more soldiers. Their place in the land was fixed through strength and plenty. The address shifts here, out of the third person into the second, and that shift is the point of the sentence: whoever is being spoken about is being compared with whoever is being spoken to.

**"We sent down abundant rain for them and made rivers flow at their feet"** is rain let loose in torrents, one after another, whenever they needed it, and rivers running under their homes, their fields, their plantations and their trees, with the springs full. That abundance was itself a form of being let go on.

**"Then We destroyed them for their sins"** for the errors and mistakes they committed, and above all for denying the prophets and going against Allah. **"and replaced them with other peoples"** means He raised up after them a different generation, and on one reading a better one, so that He could test them in their turn. Some of those replaced the old sins with the same sins and were destroyed the way their ancestors had been.

### What history is for

A large part of the Qur'an is made of historical accounts that are meant to be read for wisdom, and events of the past are documents full of warning. A wise man used to say that the world is the best book and time is the best teacher. That is why the Qur'an keeps taking the essence of history out and using it as something that warns and advises. It does not do what the usual story-telling does, where the event is the point and the end. It sets part of a narrative where the subject and the moment of its message need it, and it tells another part of the same story somewhere else, on another occasion, for another purpose. A report is not an end in itself. What matters is the outcome of what happened and the practical thing it asks of you, so a person takes what his own aim requires, moves ahead, and looks at his circumstances in that light, learning the lesson that matters from what went before and correcting himself.

Speaking generally, people have refused to give world history any serious part in running their lives. They use it as an intellectual pastime, something that helps them sleep or fills spare time. So this verse puts the question to them twice, as if to say: have they not seen, and do they not know Allah's way of destroying communities that did wrong?

### What that spectacle says about power

The last clause is not a footnote about replacement. It says that Allah's power was not simply the power to wipe out nations of strength and authority in a single flash. It was there, on the ashes of their destruction, making other peoples rise and fill the same places, as though nothing had happened there and no one were missing from the scene. That is an observable thing, in its own way, in every period. Thousands die every day and no vacuum is left anywhere, and we never stop to notice that the people who belonged to a place no longer belong to it.

One who stood on the plain of ʿArafat, with something like a million men and women spread around him, was struck by a thought. Seventy or eighty years before that day, not one person in that entire assembly had existed. And on that same plain, seventy or eighty years earlier, roughly that many human beings had stood, and today there is no trace of any of them. Apply the same picture to any gathering you have ever been in. Think about its past and its future, and see what you are left with: somebody telling you to wake up to what is finally true of everything. Praised be Allah, the best of creators.

### Why this is aimed at Makkah

The point of the comparison is that the people of Makkah did not have the strength of the people of ʿĀd and of Thamūd, the legendary nations, and they did not have the wealth of the people of Syria and Yaman, and yet the nations who had both were finished. So the lesson these generations teach is worse for the people of Makkah than it was for them, and the verse spells out why. Those old nations perished and became a tale and a story, and the new ones were tested and destroyed for doing what their predecessors had done. Beware of the same end, for you are not dearer to Allah than those nations were, and the Messenger you are defying is dearer to Allah than the messengers they defied. That makes you more likely to be punished, and only Allah's mercy and kindness keeps it off.

### In short

- Seeing the fate of past nations means pondering them, since nobody alive could watch them fall, and what they have to go on is travelling and memory.
- A qarn is a people of one period, and in the reports about it a hundred years, which is how most scholars take the hadith read in the Friday sermon.
- Those nations were given more land, wealth, children, buildings, provision and soldiers than the Meccans, and none of it stood against punishment for their sins.
- New peoples were raised on the site of the destroyed ones, which shows that Allah's power is as much replacement as destruction, and that is what makes history a warning instead of a mystery.
- Qur'anic history is not story for its own sake. Its purpose is the outcome of the event and the correction it asks of the person reading it.

7.text:
This verse takes the demand for a sign and pushes it to the length it would have to go to. "Had We sent down to you ˹O Prophet˺ a revelation in writing and they were to touch it with their own hands, the disbelievers would still have said, “This is nothing but pure magic!”" A book from the sky is not enough. It has to be written down, they have to hold it, and even then it will be called sorcery. The verse is not describing a lack of evidence. It is describing malice, and it says that the people making the demand would not stop at anything they were given, because they were never going to follow it.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Had We sent down to you a revelation in writing"** means a Scripture inscribed on parchment, brought down in one piece. On the plainest sense, this is the Qur'an itself coming down as a finished written document, which is what ʿAbdullāh ibn Umayyah al-Makhzūmī and his friends had asked for, with Gabriel bringing it down in a single bulk.

**"and they were to touch it with their own hands"** is stronger than merely seeing it, because touching removes doubt more effectively than looking. They would hold it and read it, and be eye-witnesses of its coming down, with no room to claim sleight of hand, a trick of the eye, or enchantment.

**"the disbelievers would still have said"** identifies them here as ʿAbdullāh ibn Umayyah al-Makhzūmī and the people of Makkah. **"This is nothing but pure magic"** is what they would say, and the comment on it is blunt: a clear lie. Their answer to the evidence would be stubbornness and denial. They would say: what you have brought is obvious sorcery, and we will never believe in it.

### The man who made the demand

The verse came down against a particular scene. ʿAbdullāh ibn Abī Umaiyyah put a hostile condition in front of the Prophet ﷺ. He said he could not bring himself to believe until he saw the man climb all the way into the heavens and come back down with a book brought from there, in front of their eyes, with his own name in it, ordering him to testify to his prophethood. And after asking all that he added that even this would not impress him, since he was not a likely convert in any case. Fate has strange turns: that same man later accepted Islam, and accepted it with such seriousness and quality that he became a victorious fighter in its cause, and he was given his wish in another way, receiving martyrdom, shahādah, at the battle of Ṭāʾif.

Al-Kalbī gives the demand another shape. The idolaters of Makkah said: by Allah, we will not believe, O Muhammad, until you bring us a book from Allah, with four angels alongside it, their testimony confirming that it comes from Him and that you are His Messenger. Verses of this kind were revealed in answer.

The same stubbornness appears elsewhere in the Qur'an, where it is described in the same impossible terms. If a gate from the heaven were opened for them and they kept climbing up through it, they would say their eyes had been dazzled and that they were a people bewitched (15:14-15). And if they saw a piece of the heaven fall down, they would say it was only clouds piled up together (52:44).

### What the consolation is for

These demands and the mocking, insulting talk that came with them were aimed at a man who was gentler toward his own people than their own parents ever were to them. What such coarse manners do to a heart like that is beyond measuring. It can only be sensed by someone consumed with the good of his people the way this Prophet ﷺ was. So Allah comforts him, by showing that the demands were not put forward to be answered. The people making them were not the kind who follow a sign when it arrives. The saying comes from malice and hostility, not from an open question, and that is why no amount of evidence changes it.

There is also a general rule in this verse about how a person goes astray. In this world he has complete freedom to reject the Truth, and he even gets the chance to build fine justifications for wrong thoughts, words and deeds. If the one who brings God's word looks like an ordinary man, he is explained away as a born leader whose grip on a crowd has nothing to do with righteousness or with truth. If a complete book came down from the sky, the reason given is that it is mere magic. People devoted to externals cannot recognise the Messenger of God from the weight of his message. He appears to them as a man who suddenly emerged and started claiming very high standing, they assess him on appearances, find him small there, and deny him.

### In short

- A written book from heaven, handled and read, would not have moved them, which is the verse's proof that the problem is disposition and not evidence.
- Touching was set above seeing because contact is the stronger remover of doubt.
- The demand is tied to ʿAbdullāh ibn Umaiyyah al-Makhzūmī, who later became a fervent Muslim and was martyred at Ṭāʾif.
- Al-Kalbī reports the demand in a form that asks for a book escorted by four angels testifying to it.
- The verse consoles the Prophet ﷺ: such demands are not asked in order to be met.

8.text:
""They say, “Why has no ˹visible˺ angel come with him?” Had We sent down an angel, the matter would have certainly been settled ˹at once˺, and they would have never been given more time ˹to repent˺"." The demand now is for a second speaker, an angel to back the Prophet ﷺ up. The answer is that an angel does not come down to argue. An angel comes down to end the argument, and ending it that way is the destruction of the people who asked.

### Phrase by phrase

**"They say"** is again ʿAbdullāh ibn Abī Umaiyyah al-Makhzūmī, and this verse also came down out of an episode involving him. He came to the Prophet ﷺ in the company of an-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith and Nawfal ibn Khālid, and their condition was belief only on condition that he go and bring a book from the heavens, with four angels as its escort, its witnesses attesting that Allah alone sent it and that Muhammad is His Messenger.

**"Why has no angel come with him?"** means: send someone down to confirm his truthfulness. ʿAbdullāh ibn Umayyah is the one named as asking for this, and what he wants is an angel who will testify for what the Prophet ﷺ is saying, speaking to them and bear witness that he is a messenger, conveying the message with a warning alongside.

**"Had We sent down an angel, the matter would have certainly been settled"** means the judgement would be executed. The angel comes down to take their souls and to punish them, and it is also said that if an angel came down he would destroy the whole of them. **"and they would have never been given more time"** means no delay, no further respite for repentance, and no chance to offer an excuse.

### The law behind the answer

The divine rule runs like this: when a people ask their prophet to produce a miracle of their own choosing, and the miracle is then worked by Allah's will and power, and they still hold back from faith, they are destroyed by a general punishment that takes all of them. These people of Makkah were not asking with good intentions, which would at least have left some hope that they might accept. So the fact that the demanded miracle is not produced is real good fortune for them. Without the delay they would be nowhere.

This is Allah's way with those who came before: a nation was destroyed when it disbelieved after its request had been granted. The Qur'an states the rule in other places, in the sense given here. "We send not the angels down except with the truth, and in that case they would have no respite" (15:8). And on the day they see the angels, there will be no good news at all that day for the criminals (25:22).

### In short

- The demand for an angel is a demand for a witness who testifies rather than argues.
- An angel sent down to settle a claim ends the case at once, and ending it that way means punishment.
- Not producing the requested sign is mercy: it keeps the respite open, and the respite is the only room in which faith is possible.
- The answer appeals to a known pattern in earlier nations, and to verses that state it, 15:8 and 25:22.

9.text:
"And if We had sent an angel, We would have certainly made it ˹assume the form of˺ a man—leaving them more confused than they already are." The verse closes the loophole. Their complaint was that a human messenger carries no weight. If the messenger were an angel, he would have to appear as a man to be dealt with at all, and the same objection would be back on the table, with the added confusion of a being that is not a man and looks like one.

### Phrase by phrase

**"And if We had sent an angel"** covers two cases: an angel sent along with the human Messenger, and an angel sent as a messenger to mankind in his place.

**"We would have certainly made it a man"** means He would have sent him in the shape of a human being, so that people would be able to look at him, speak with him and take teaching from him. Ibn ʿAbbās, as ad-Daḥḥāk reported from him, said that if an angel were sent to them he would come in the form of a man, because they would not be able to bear the sight of an angel because of the light. No human being is capable of seeing an angel as he is.

**"leaving them more confused than they already are"** means confusing them over the confusion they already have. Al-Walībī transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās the shorter form of it: We would throw doubts back on them. They are already confusing the matter for themselves when they say of a man of flesh and blood that he is nothing but a mortal like the rest of you. Making the sender a man in outward form would obscure his real nature for them, exactly as they now obscure the qualities and the description of Muhammad.

### Why a human messenger, then

An angel can come down in one of two ways. He comes as he actually is, in his own form and state of being, and then no human being can stand before that real awesomeness. The likelier result is death at a sight never imagined. Or he comes in human shape and form, which is how Jibrīl al-Amīn, Gabriel the Trusty, came to the Holy Prophet ﷺ more than once in the shape of a man. In that second case the objector has the very same objection available against the angel as he has against you, because he will take him to be nothing but human. Asking for an angel is therefore a demand that cancels itself.

Sending every kind of creation a messenger from among their own kind is counted here as a mercy from Allah to His creation. A messenger of their own sort can call his people to Allah, and they can talk to him, ask him questions and benefit from him. That favour is stated elsewhere in the Qur'an: "Allah conferred a great favour on the believers when He sent among them a Messenger from among themselves, reciting His verses and purifying them" (3:164). And the rule behind it is stated as an answer to the demand: if there were angels on the earth, walking about in peace and security, We would have sent down to them from the heaven an angel as a Messenger (17:95).

### In short

- An angel sent to people would have to be a man in form, or they could neither look at him nor learn from him.
- Their objection would then repeat itself, and their confusion would be doubled rather than solved.
- The sight of an angel as he really is is beyond human capacity, and the likelier answer to it is death rather than belief.
- The demand is thus self-defeating, and a human messenger from among their own kind is the mercy that makes teaching possible.

10.text:
"˹Other˺ messengers had already been ridiculed before you ˹O Prophet˺, but those who mocked them were overtaken by what they used to ridicule." After three verses of argument about signs, this verse turns to the Prophet ﷺ himself. It is a comfort, and it comes with a warning attached for the people mocking him. He is not the first to be laughed at, and the laughers have a record: what they mocked arrived and closed around them.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Messengers had already been ridiculed before you"** means their own people ridiculed them, as this people is ridiculing you now. The denial of him by his people is set in a line of denials that went before.

**"but those who mocked them were overtaken"** means the punishment they denied and laughed at when it was announced to them surrounded them and befell them. It is said of those of them who mocked, meaning the disbelievers, that the consequence of their mockery is what reached them.

### Why the task is hard

Conveying the Word of God in this world is a complicated business, and the reason given is that Allah has decreed that the Truth be wrapped in doubt, so that a person finds reasons for rejecting it next to arguments for accepting it. The real test is whether he can tear that veil of doubt down and lift himself to certainty: abandoning doubt in every disguise, and holding firmly to the truth that comes from above. To believe without seeing is what the test is. Once reality is put in front of the eyes, agreeing with it is worth nothing.

The same page explains why mockery keeps happening. Man denies an obvious truth, and when he gets power he puts others down, and one person makes another the victim of his tyranny. It is fair to ask whether that means he has absolute power here, and whether there is nobody to stop his hand. Is there a contradiction in Allah's rule, since He seems to have filled the human world with oppression and injustice and the rest of creation with mercy and meaning? The answer is no. The Lord of heaven and earth is also the Lord of the creature that works by day and rests by night. As His grace is given to the universe without stint, so it is given to human beings. The difference is one of timing. For everything else that grace is visible in full from the first day, and for people it will be shown in full on the Day of Judgement.

### The other half of the comfort

The verse does more than say that others suffered the same. It promises the Messenger ﷺ and the believers with him Allah's victory and a good ending, in this life and in the Hereafter. Its point is that his duty is to convey Allah's commands. Once he is satisfied that he has conveyed them, his heart can rest. Whether the message moves anyone or not is not part of his job as Allah's Messenger, and that worry should not be allowed into his heart. The earlier prophets faced the same heart-breaking treatment from their people and did not give up hope.

### In short

- Ridicule is not evidence against the message. It is the standard treatment of messengers, and the verse names it as such.
- What the mockers denied came and encompassed them, which is the warning inside the comfort.
- The Truth is deliberately veiled in doubt, so that certainty has to be earned by believing without seeing.
- The Prophet's ﷺ duty ends with delivery, and the outcome is not his to carry.

11.text:
"Say, “Travel throughout the land and see the fate of the deniers.”" The passage that began with a demand for a miracle ends by sending the demanders on a journey. No sign needs to be produced for them. They are told to look at what is already there, in the landscape, and to notice where denial ended.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Say"** addresses the Prophet ﷺ, and what he is told to say is an instruction to the people of Makkah.

**"Travel throughout the land"** means travel on earth, in the trading routes and the places where earlier nations lived. **"and see the fate of the deniers"** means: reflect on what the end was for those who denied Allah and His messengers, how they were destroyed by chastisement. They were in a position of strength and power when Allah's punishment fell on them.

### Looking instead of asking

They had demanded a written book and an escort of angels. They are sent instead to think about their own case, and to consider the afflictions Allah struck the earlier nations with for defying and denying His messengers. Torment, affliction and punishment came to those nations in this life, and the painful torment of the Hereafter is with them, while Allah saved His Messengers and the servants who believed. The hope in the command is small but real: perhaps they will take heed. Travel is here an instrument of thought, and the verse treats the ruins and the reports of the past as evidence already in circulation, which needs only to be read honestly.

### In short

- The command to travel converts the demand for a new sign into a duty to inspect an old one.
- The fate in view is not only destruction in this world. It includes the torment of the next, and the salvation of the messengers and the believers.
- Strength and power were no protection for the nations destroyed, which is the exact contrast the people of Makkah needed.
- Reflection is offered as the last courtesy before the judgement the previous verses described.

12.text:
The passage about demanded signs has ended, and the opening of what follows puts the demanders a question instead of answering them. "Ask ˹them, O Prophet˺, 'To whom belongs everything in the heavens and the earth?' Say, 'To Allah!' He has taken upon Himself to be Merciful. He will certainly gather ˹all of˺ you together for the Day of Judgment—about which there is no doubt. But those who have ruined themselves will never believe." Two things are established by this order to ask: ownership, which they already conceded, and mercy, which Allah has written for Himself, and the second is what makes the first a hope rather than a threat.

The reason for answering the question instead of waiting is that the reply was already agreed. The disbelievers of Makkah were soaked in shirk, the association of partners with Allah, and in idolatry, yet they did not deny that Allah Almighty was the Master of the heavens and the earth and of everything in them. Allah states here that He is the King and the Owner of both and of all they contain. If they answer, well. If they do not, the questioner answers for them, because no other reply is available, and there is nothing else that could be said.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Ask ˹them, O Prophet˺, 'To whom belongs everything in the heavens and the earth?'"** is addressed to Muḥammad ﷺ, and what he is to ask about is dominion: who owns the created beings in the heavens and the earth, and whatever lies between them.

**"Say, 'To Allah!'"** Their total control belongs to Allah. He is the Owner of the creation of the heavens and the earth.

**"He has taken upon Himself to be Merciful"** means He wrote mercy on His own noble Self, decreed it as something He binds Himself to, and made mercy His own choice rather than something owed to Him. It is recorded in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs, from Abū Hurayrah, that the Prophet ﷺ said:

> "When Allah created creation, He wrote in a Book which He has with Him above the Throne: My mercy overcomes My anger."

The same wording appears in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, in a narration from Abū Hurairah, as al-Qurṭubī cites it: when Allah made His creation, He made Himself a written promise, and what is written in it is that His mercy stays in front of His wrath. On one reading this mercy is specified for the community of Muḥammad and consists in the punishment being deferred. He establishes mercy upon Himself out of grace for His servants, and so does not rush to punish them. This is not a neutral piece of information. It is a gentle summons: come, and the invitation is being made by the One who has already committed Himself.

**"He will certainly gather ˹all of˺ you together for the Day of Judgment"** is an oath taken by Allah's own honored Self that He will assemble His servants. The Day of Resurrection will certainly occur, and about it there is no doubt, no uncertainty at all. It is the day of an appointed meeting at a known time (56:50). Allah's believing servants have no doubt in this fact, while those who deny it and refuse it are left in confusion and disorder. The verb "gather" opened a question of its own about the particle meaning "towards" in the phrase "He will surely gather you towards a day of doom". Al-Qurṭubī reports two answers. It may be used in the sense of "take in full" or "bring to a finish", so that Allah gathers everyone, first and last, on the day of Qiyamah. Or it may mean gathering into the graves, so that human beings are kept being collected into their resting places until the Day of Qiyamah, when they are raised back to life.

**"But those who have ruined themselves will never believe"** gives the reason some do not believe in the Return and therefore do not fear what that Day will do to them. They are the ones who destroy themselves on the Day of Resurrection, who forfeit their own souls by exposing them to the chastisement, and who bring them to the point of ruin by their disbelief. The loss of the universal mercy named earlier in verse 12 comes from their own deeds, because they did not take the road that leads to mercy, which is the road of belief and faith. And they will not believe, and so will not rescue their souls from that loss.

### Why they are told to ask

The wording of the second half of the sentence has been read as a single thought with its two parts reversed: "those who have forfeited their souls" is the subject, "they do not believe" is the predicate. The promise of mercy and the threat of the gathering stand in one verse on purpose. Allah swore by Himself that He will assemble everyone to requite them for their deeds, and the same verse says that His mercy was written before that Reckoning, so that a person who hears the warning also hears what the warning is for.

### The inner reading

There is a way of hearing this verse that leaves no room for the question at all. Ask them: does anyone at all dwell in the house? Does the rightful due of anything that exists carry any weight with the Real? If they cannot answer, that silence is a healing for them. So say: Allah in His lordship is enough. Allah, and nothing else, and the rest is nonsense. It does not belong to anyone to give to Him, nor to Him to receive from anyone. All is from Him to Him. A world full of things and full of people, and He overturns all of it in a single breath, and a hundred eyes would not be enough for me to look at that work.

Before He began making what comes into being, and before He originated anything that is generated, mercy was minted in the treasury of the Unseen, and it became the hard cash of what His servants do and are. He had already said: "Surely I am Allah. There is no god but Me" (20:14). His mercy comes before His anger. On the Day of Mustering the Messenger will call out in the bazaar of the resurrection: here is a handful of the disobedient. Let me be told to dress them in the shirt of Your mercy, since You said: "We sent thee only as a mercy to the worlds" (21:107). It is the day of the bazaar for these beggars, and I was catching them with the lasso of the invitation and making them many promises. Do not put Muḥammad to shame in this gathering of the crowds, and make Your promise of generosity real, since You Yourself said: "O My servants who have been immoderate against yourselves, despair not of Allah's mercy" (39:53).

And the call of generosity comes back from the court of majesty: the affair of your community lies between three things. They are either people of faith, or people who have come to know, or people who disobeyed. If they believed and hoped for Paradise, then here is My Paradise. If they disobeyed and hoped for My forgiveness, then here is My mercy and My forgiveness.

### In short

- Ownership of the heavens and the earth was already conceded by the people of Makkah, which is why Allah answers the question He tells the Prophet ﷺ to ask.
- Mercy is something Allah wrote for Himself before the Reckoning, and it is stated here as a summons rather than a doctrine.
- The gathering for the Day of Judgement is sworn to by Allah Himself, and only those who deny it are thrown into confusion by it.
- Ruining oneself means failing to take the road that brings mercy, and so not believing in the Return.

13.text:
"To Him belongs whatever exists in the day and night. And He is the All-Hearing, All-Knowing." Verse 12 claimed ownership of everything in the heavens and the earth. This verse claims the two halves of time and the ears and the knowledge that go with them. Whatever exists in the night and whatever exists in the day is His, all of it under His authority, His power and His will, and there is no deity worth worshipping except Him.

### Phrase by phrase

**"To Him belongs whatever exists in the day and night"** uses a word, sukūn, that is at the center of the sentence's meaning. It can mean being still, settled, at rest, and then the sense is that Allah owns everything present in the night and in the day. It can also carry stillness and movement together, everything that tarries and everything that moves, and only rest is named because movement, which is its opposite, was obvious enough to go unstated. All that inhabits night and day is His: He is their Lord, their Creator and their Possessor. Whatever lies hidden in the night and whatever goes about openly in the day are His servants and His creation, all of them under His domination and control.

**"And He is the All-Hearing, All-Knowing"** means He hears what His servants say and knows what they do, what they keep and what they hide. He is the Hearer of what is said and the Knower of what is done, and He will judge by them.

### What they had said, and what it is worth

The hearing is particular. It came about, on one account, because of what people said to Muḥammad ﷺ: give up our religion and come back to ours, and we will make you rich, marry you, give you standing, and make you king over us. Allah's answer sets His ownership of night and day against that offer. He is the Hearer of what they say, and the Knower of the punishment they are heading into, and of the provision every created being lives on. Kingship, wealth and a wife are exactly the kind of thing that belongs to Someone else.

### Night, day, and the angel holding both

The same verse has been read as a picture of time itself. Night, on this account, is a darkness spread over the world at large, and day is a brightness reaching the whole of it. Neither night nor day existed before the world was made, or before light and darkness were made. And in the Garden there is no sun, yet the whole of it is day, because brightness in general is already there. Whatever stands nearer to Allah has the fuller light and the brighter glow.

ʿAbdallāh ibn Masʿūd said: there is no day and no night with your Lord. He lights the heavens with the radiance of His own face. And the traditions mention that the Lord of the Worlds created an angel of tremendous size and put the night in one of his fists and the day in the other. Whenever he closes one fist and opens the other, that is the day taking charge. Whenever he closes that one and opens this one, that is the night taking charge. On the strength of that image, the allusion runs: the disk of the sun sits in the angel's fist, but the hearts of My friends were never handed to anyone else. The angel has no share and no power over the hearts of the friends of Allah. The disk of the sun rests in the angel's fist, while the hearts of those who love are held in the fist of the King, and majestic and high is He. Al-Muṣṭafā said that the hearts of the servants lie between two fingers of the Most Merciful.

### In short

- Ownership extends over time as well as space: what rests and what moves, in night and in day, is all His.
- Sukūn means rest, and it can be taken to cover rest and movement together, with the stillness named because the movement needs no naming.
- Hearing and knowing are here an answer to a specific bargain offered to the Prophet ﷺ, and a warning that nothing said is unheard.
- The inner reading takes day and night as created things held in an angel's fists, with human hearts outside that arrangement and inside Allah's hand.

14.text:
Two orders are given here, and both are spoken by one mouth. The Prophet ﷺ is told to say: "Will I take any guardian other than Allah, the Originator of the heavens and the earth?" And then: "I have been commanded to be the first to submit and not be one of the polytheists." The question is rhetorical and it is personal, and it is addressed to the idolaters of Makkah who worship their idols alongside Allah. Allah told His servant and Messenger Muḥammad ﷺ, sent with pure tawḥīd and the straight religion, to call people to Allah's straight path, and this is how he is told to answer a demand that he find a patron somewhere else. He will not take a guardian except Allah, with no partners, and he says so out loud.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Will I take any guardian other than Allah"** asks whether it makes sense for him to hold to anyone besides Him as a lord to worship, a protector from whom help is sought. It was said of this Prophet ﷺ: after Allah honoured him with His own friendship, should he take another as a friend? After the brightness of Allah's care fell on him, should his eyes go to anyone else in either of the two worlds?

**"the Originator of the heavens and the earth"** is the One who made them without any precedent, with no creator before Him, the Originator who brought earth and heaven into being. He is the one who arranges the world and its people, and He knows the outward and the hidden.

**"Who provides for all and is not in need of provision"** means He gives sustenance to His creatures without needing them. Some read it: He feeds but does not eat, meaning that Allah does not eat. He does not take a daily portion, He assigns a daily portion to His servants. Generosity is His own attribute, so He feeds. What is owed to Him by right is everlastingness, so He is not fed. None of His servants provides for Him. He has no need of them, and they have every need of Him.

That is also why He does not need anyone's worship at all: "I did not create jinn and humans except to worship Me" (51:56).

**"Say, 'I have been commanded to be the first to submit'"** means: my Lord ordered me to be the first of this ummah, this community, to surrender to Him as a Muslim, to be humble and to accept. It is also said that the meaning is the first among the people of his own time to worship sincerely and to declare Allah's oneness. **"and not be one of the polytheists"** is the same order from the other side: do not be one of those who associate partners with Him, do not join the idolaters and their religion. And do not let anyone order you to worship other than Allah. The Qur'an puts that answer elsewhere in his mouth: "Say: Do you order me to worship other than Allah, you fools?" (39:64).

### A prayer after eating

That He feeds and is not fed was drawn out of a meal. Abū Hurayrah narrated that a man from al-Anṣār, from the district of Qubāʾ, invited the Prophet ﷺ to food, and we went along with him. When the Prophet ﷺ had eaten and washed his hands, he said:

> "All praise is due to Allah, who feeds and is never fed. He bestowed bounty on us. He guided us and fed us and gave us drink and covered our nakedness. For every favour He has given us, all praise is due to Allah, a praise that must not be left aside. My Lord, we affirm that we can never thank You enough, or appreciate You enough, or be free of need of You. All thanks and praise are due to Allah, who fed us food and gave us drink and covered our nakedness and guided us after misguidance and gave us sight after blindness and honoured us above many of His creatures. All praise is due to Allah, Lord of everything that exists."

### Why his heart could not ask for anyone else

He was given such standing at the front of what is accepted that Allah at times puts up with his disdain. "By your life!" (15:72) is the oath the Qur'an uses where this rank is in view. At other times it is the grip of created qualities that polishes the mirror of his heart, out of care for him: "Did We not expand for you your breast?" (94:1). And at other times the recorder of the register that has no beginning and no end hands the acceptance and the refusal of the creatures over to his threshold: "Whatever the Messenger gives you, take it, and whatever he forbids you, leave it" (59:7). With that much good fortune, rank, care and kindness, how could his heart go asking for somebody else, or look toward this world or the next? About this world he said plainly: what have I to do with it? About the next world the verse says of his eye that "the sight did not swerve, nor did it overreach" (53:17). Neither this world nor the next, then, but the seeing of the Patron.

### What a will is for

A human being has a will of his own, and that is why his worship has to be given freely. Those who will not use that will properly have no share in God's bounties, since they have not done what they were made for. Nothing has power here, because power belongs to God alone. Everyone depends on Him and He depends on nothing. Whatever a person's arrogance leans on has no value in this universe, and on the Day when God takes the direct control of everything into His own hands and His scale of justice is working, the ones who come forward are the ones who admitted the reality and surrendered. The rest are the losers.

### In short

- "Originator" means He made the heavens and the earth with no precedent and no predecessor, so nothing else can be the first place to go for protection.
- "He feeds and is not fed" states that He sustains creation without needing it, and one reading takes it to mean plainly that Allah does not eat.
- The Prophet ﷺ is told to be the first to submit in this ummah and never to join the polytheists, and that is an order, not a personal preference.
- The verse is explained out of a shared meal, in a prayer that thanks Allah for feeding, guiding, covering and honouring.
