They hold the duty of giving water to the pilgrims at the Hajj. They are the keepers of the Kaʿbah and its keys are in their hands. If prophethood is theirs as well, what is left for the rest of Quraysh? A third version comes through Abū Maysarah: the Prophet ﷺ passed by Abū Jahl and his companions, and they said to him: by Allah, we do not call you a liar, we count you truthful, and what we deny is what you have brought. Yet another report names the man this verse was about as al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAmir, spelled al-Ḥarth in other copies, a man of the line of ʿAbd Manaf ibn Quṣayy who used to deny the Prophet in public and then said at home: Muḥammad is not one of those who lie.

### Why honesty was not enough to accept

The people of Makkah who had not believed still admitted that he was a righteous man. But calling a man truthful is a way of glorifying him, and that was the honour they would not hand over. As long as he was a man of their own level they had a kind of satisfaction. To accept that Allah's own discourse came from his lips was to raise him above themselves, and few things are harder for a proud man to say yes to. God does not appear in this world in His own shape. He appears before people in the shape of arguments, signs and symbols. So to refuse an argument for the truth, or to shut one's eyes at a sign pointing to it, is to refuse God and to look away from His face. But it was never part of His plan to appear with compelling miracles. Where the call arrived with no room to refuse it, the freedom that makes the test a test would be over. So whoever carries this message should not be crushed by having only the weight of argument to offer and no power to compel. The effort is a trial of his patience and of his hearers at once. Can they see a glimpse of Allah's representative in a man like themselves, and bow before an argument that has no army behind it? For whoever has life in him the whole universe is full of signs. Whoever has put out his own sensitivity will take a lesson from nothing except the terror of Doomsday.

### In short

- The verse begins by telling the Prophet ﷺ that his grief over them is known to Allah.
- Their quarrel was not with his honesty but with the signs of Allah, and three separate reports record them calling him truthful.
- The chiefs listened to the Qur'an at night for three nights and kept returning despite their oaths.
- Abū Jahl's own answer names the real obstacle: tribal rivalry with Banū ʿAbd Manāf and Banū Quṣayy.
- Belief asked for in a world of arguments and unforced signs is worth what it is, because compulsion would end the test.

34.text:
"Indeed, messengers before you were rejected but patiently endured rejection and persecution until Our help came to them." This verse sets the experience of one messenger inside the experience of many. What he is living through is not evidence that he has been abandoned. It is the road every one of them was sent along.

### Phrase by phrase

**"messengers before you were rejected"** means their own people denied them, as this people is denying him now. **"but patiently endured rejection and persecution"** tells how they carried it: patience under the denial of their people and under the harm they were given, and the patience was kept up while the calling went on, not after it stopped. **"until Our help came to them"** is the help that arrived through the destruction of their peoples, victory in this world, and the good end that was theirs after the denial and the hurt. **"And Allah's promise ˹to help˺ is never broken"** refers to His decision that victory in this life and the next belongs to His believing servants. **"And you have already received some of the narratives of these messengers"** means the news of them has reached him, how they were denied, how they were patient, and how they came out on top, and in that there is a good example and something for the heart to settle on.

### The promise that cannot be changed

The sentence about Allah's words being beyond alteration is a ruling and not only encouragement. Other verses carry the same content. "And verily, Our Word has gone forth of old for Our servants, the messengers, that they shall be made triumphant, and that Our hosts shall be the victors" (37:171-173). And: "Allah has decreed: it is I and My messengers who shall be victorious. Allah is All-Powerful, Almighty" (58:21). Read the two together and the shape of the verse here is clear. The help is written, so patience has something to wait for, and the delay is not a defeat.

### Why the consolation is put in the past tense

The verse speaks of messengers already gone, and that is how it does its work. Do not think that this kind of denial is something new, only aimed at what you have brought. No one can hold back the help Allah has written and promised to His messengers, and the destruction of their enemies was that help. So the instruction buried in the report is simply: be patient until the victorious help reaches you, the way it reached them.

### In short

- The verse comforts the Prophet ﷺ by putting his case inside the case of earlier messengers.
- Their patience covered both denial and physical harm, and it ran to the end.
- Help came to them in this world through the ruin of their people, and victory in the hereafter followed it.
- "Allah's promise is never broken" is about His settled decision that His messengers come out on top.
- The narratives that had reached him were there to steady his heart and to give an example.

35.text:
"If you find their denial unbearable, then build—if you can—a tunnel through the earth or stairs to the sky to bring them a ˹more compelling˺ sign." The verse meets a grief that has run out of options with a command nobody can carry out, and that is the whole method of it.

### Phrase by phrase

**"If you find their denial unbearable"** is addressed to the Messenger of Allah, whose concern for his people made their turning away hard to bear. **"then build—if you can—a tunnel through the earth"** means: dig an underground passage and go down into it. **"or stairs to the sky"** means a ladder, or any way that lets you climb up. The purpose is stated plainly. Bring them a sign, a proof of the kind they are asking for, or a better one than what has already been given them. **"to bring them a ˹more compelling˺ sign"** adds nothing to the burden except this, that it cannot be done. The meaning of the command is: you will not be able to do it, so be patient until Allah gives His judgment.

### What Ibn ʿAbbās drew from it

ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah reported this from Ibn ʿAbbās: if you can find a tunnel and bring them a sign through it, then do it. Or climb a ladder into the sky and bring them a better sign than the one I have already given them, and then do that too. Qatādah, As-Suddi and others gave it the same drift. Then comes the sentence that closes the matter: had Allah willed, He could have brought them all together on true guidance. Ibn ʿAbbās explained the background: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was eager for everyone to believe and to follow him. Allah told him that only those whose happiness has been written for them in the first Dhikr will believe. Had your Lord willed, the words say elsewhere, everyone on earth would have believed, all of them at once.

### The two things the verse forbids

It forbids the demand for a sign as the price of patience, and it forbids ignorance about how guidance actually happens. On the first, the tunnel and the stair are a way of saying that the messenger is not the one who produces proofs. On the second, the sentence "so do not be one of those ignorant of this fact" means: do not be among the foolish about My decree concerning their disbelief, and do not lose yourself in regret over it. Guidance, when it comes, is the declaration of Allah's oneness, and hearts are not turned by an increase in visible evidence. Had Allah willed to gather them all on guidance He would have done it. He did not, because of His wisdom, and the verse expects the Prophet ﷺ to rest in that.

### In short

- The answer to unbearable grief is a command to do the impossible, which cancels the grief's demand rather than the messenger's patience.
- Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatādah and As-Suddi all took the tunnel and the stair as a rebuke, not as a possibility.
- Allah could have gathered them all on guidance, and the reason He did not belongs to His wisdom.
- Only those whose happiness was written in the first Dhikr will believe.
- The verse ends by forbidding ignorance of this, because ignorance of it turns into sorrow that accomplishes nothing.

36.text:
"Only the attentive will respond ˹to your call˺." After the tunnel and the stair, this verse narrows the matter down to the one condition that makes a response possible, which is attention, and then it names the people who do not have it.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Only the attentive will respond"** means those who hear in a way that lets them understand and take heed. Those who listen to the speech, take it in and act on it are the ones who answer the call. The ones who only let it pass over them answer nothing. **"As for the dead, Allah will raise them up"** speaks of the disbelievers, whose hearts are dead, and they are compared to corpses as a way of holding them cheap and showing how little a dead heart can respond to anything. The raising is after death, and it is real rather than figurative. **"then to Him they will ˹all˺ be returned"** places the return in the gathering, where each of them is repaid for what he did. A further reading takes "the dead" to mean the dead of Badr, of Uḥud and of the battle of the Confederates.

### Attention is the whole difference

This is why the message is addressed to the living. It is so that it may warn whoever is alive, and so that the charge may stand against the disbelievers (36:70). The verse just before had said that Allah could have gathered them all on guidance. This one says what guidance needs in order to land, and it is not a stronger sign but a listener who is attentive. A person who has extinguished that attention cannot be reached by argument, and he will not be reached by a miracle either. What is left for him is the raising, the return, and the repayment. The dead of heart are called worthless here, and the sharpest part of the picture is that they are not even asked to respond, because the demand to respond only makes sense to something alive.

### In short

- Response is limited to those who hear so as to understand and take heed.
- Deniers of the message are called dead, because a dead heart cannot answer a call.
- Allah will raise them after death and they will be returned to Him for repayment.
- One reading attaches "the dead" to the dead of Badr, Uḥud and the battle of the Confederates.
- The verse explains why the warning is aimed at the living, in the words of 36:70.

37.text:
"They ask, 'Why has no ˹other˺ sign been sent down to him from his Lord?'" The demand is for a sign of their own choosing, and the answer refuses the terms of it without denying the power behind it.

### Phrase by phrase

**"They ask"** means the disbelievers of Makkah, and the material names them: al-Ḥarth ibn ʿAmir and his people, Abū Jahl ibn Hishām, al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra, and Umayyah and Ubayy the two sons of Khalf. **"Why has no ˹other˺ sign been sent down to him from his Lord?"** is the question of people who want a miracle they have designed, something to prove his prophethood: a sign like the she-camel of Sālih, or the staff of Moses, or the Table sent down to Jesus. They also said: "We shall not believe in you, until you cause a spring to gush forth from the ground for us" (17:90). **"Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ 'Allah certainly has the power to send down a sign'"** is the answer, and the verb can be read in two forms, either of them saying that He is able to send down the very sign they have asked for. **"though most of them do not know"** is the reason the request is not granted. They have no knowledge that a sign is sent down by Allah's wisdom and not on demand.

### Why the sign is withheld

Allah is able to send a sign, and He decided out of His wisdom to hold it back. If a sign of their liking were sent and they still refused to believe, their punishment would be brought forward, the way it came to the nations before them. Two other verses say exactly this. "And nothing stops Us from sending the signs except that the people of old denied them. And We sent the she-camel to Thamud as a clear sign, but they wronged her. And We send the signs only to warn, and to make people afraid of destruction" (17:59). And: "If We willed, We could send down to them from the heaven a sign, to which they would bend their necks in humility" (26:4). A sign sent at the demand of stubborn people, and then denied, is not a mercy. It turns belief into recognizing what is standing in front of you, and it ends the test at the same moment it ends the excuses. The delay of acceptance in these verses is a stalling tactic, and the demand for a sign is part of the stalling, not a step toward faith.

### In short

- The demand was for a sign chosen by the demanders, in the style of the she-camel, the staff or the Table.
- The answer concedes the power and refuses the schedule: Allah is able to send down a sign.
- Most of them do not know that signs come down by wisdom, so their asking cannot set the terms.
- A granted sign that is then denied would hasten destruction, as 17:59 explains about Thamud.
- 26:4 states the other half: a compulsion sign would leave them with necks bent, not with hearts convinced.

38.text:
"All living beings roaming the earth and winged birds soaring in the sky are communities like yourselves." The verse answers the demand for a sign by pointing at what is already moving around them, and it says that these creatures are not a background to the story but a people of their own.

### Phrase by phrase

**"All living beings roaming the earth"** means every animal that creeps or moves on the earth, and **"winged birds soaring in the sky"** means every creature that flies through the air between earth and heaven with its wings. **"are communities like yourselves"** was explained in more than one way. Mujāhid took it as various species that carry distinct names. Qatādah said: birds are an ummah, human beings are an ummah, and the jinn are an ummah, the word used for a community that is a distinct creation with its own name. As-Suddi took it as creations and species, and another reading adds that they are servants like you, resembling you in eating, in reproduction and in understanding one another, and that this resemblance is itself a sign. **"We have left nothing out of the Record"** means the Preserved Tablet, the Lawḥ Maḥfūẓ, in which nothing has been left unwritten, and it also means that everything needed has been spelled out in the Qur'an. **"Then to their Lord they will be gathered all together"** is the Day of Judgment, when the beasts and the birds are assembled along with everyone else, and each is recompensed for what it deserves.

### What the Record contains

Knowledge of all of them sits with Allah, and He forgets none of His creatures, nor their provision, nor their affairs, whether they live on land or in the sea. "And there is no creature moving on earth but its provision is due from Allah, and He knows its dwelling place and its deposit, all of it in a Clear Book" (11:6). And: "And so many a moving creature carries not its own provision. Allah provides for it and for you, and He is the All-Hearer, the All-Knower" (29:60). In these records there is written the name of every creature, its number, its movements and its stillness. O children of Adam, the likeness the verse draws between you and the animals is in how creation is ordained for them, together with sustenance and affairs, exactly as it is ordained for you.

### Gathered, settled and turned to dust

On "then to their Lord they will be gathered", Ibn ʿAbbās said that death gathers them. Others said the Day of Resurrection gathers them, and the verse that says it plainly is: "And when the wild beasts are gathered together" (81:5). ʿAbdur-Razzaq recorded from Abū Hurayrah that all creatures will be assembled on that Day, the beasts, the birds and the rest, and Allah's justice will be so exact that the sheep without horns takes retribution from the sheep with horns. Then He will command them: be dust. At that moment the disbeliever says what the Qur'an reports: "Woe to me, would that I were dust!" (78:40). The same account reaches the Prophet ﷺ in the hadith about the Trumpet. A second chain runs from Abū Hurairah, and Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and al-Baihaqī transmit it that on the Day of Qiyāmah the rights of every holder of a right are vindicated, to the point that a hornless goat is vindicated against the horned one, which is also how Al-Baghāwī reports it. The point of all that is not that animals are accountable.

### Why the animals are a sign

The verse is also read as an answer to the people who wanted a miracle of their own choosing. Only human beings and jinn are given a law to keep, and reward and punishment do not run over creatures that were never addressed. The retaliation is Allah's regard for equity, and it tells you how serious the rights of His creation are, since even the non-obligated are not let off. What God requires of these living creatures is the same as what He requires of you. His writ runs over animals as instinct and over human beings as Islamic law, and the birds and the beasts carry it out to the letter while a man is not ready to accept it. Their world is also a lesson in another way: they are out for food and do not persecute one another for it, their needs are met without selfishness, and when one of them bothers another there is no settled hostility. Tasks are done among them without anyone claiming credit. The animals are the world of nature, and the question the verse leaves with you is what justification there is for a person to choose a way other than the one every creature of Allah is already walking on the path of.

### In short

- Every animal and every bird is a community of the same kind as us, with its creation, provision and affairs ordained.
- Nothing has been left out of the Preserved Tablet, and 11:6 and 29:60 spell out what that includes.
- Gathering to Allah is stated both as death and as the Day of Resurrection, with 81:5 as its proof.
- The hornless sheep takes its right from the horned one and then all of them are ordered to become dust, which is when the disbeliever wishes he were dust (78:40).
- Animals fulfill God's writ by instinct and human beings by Islamic law, which is why the demand for a new sign misses the point.

39.text:
"Those who deny Our signs are ˹wilfully˺ deaf and dumb—lost in darkness." The verse leaves the animals and returns to the people who asked for a sign, and it ends by describing what is wrong with the asking.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Those who deny Our signs"** are described by what they have become rather than by what they lack. **"deaf"** means deaf of heart, and it is also taken to mean that they act as if they cannot hear the truth. **"and dumb"** means they pretend to be mute where the truth and guidance are concerned. **"lost in darkness"** means they are holding fast to disbelief, and the sense of the three together is that they are in a darkness in which they cannot see, unable to take in what is said and unable to say what is right. Their case is like that of a deaf-mute who can neither hear nor speak and is blinded by darkness on top of it, and the question the verse implies is obvious: how can such a person be put on the path, or change the state he is in?

### The darkness spelled out

Elsewhere the same condition is drawn as a picture. "Their parable is that of a man who kindled a fire, and when it lit up everything around him, Allah took their light away and left them in darkness, so they cannot see. They are deaf, dumb and blind, and they do not turn back" (2:17-18). And: "Or like darkness in a vast deep sea, overwhelmed by a great wave, with a great wave above it, and dark clouds above that, darkness one above another. When a man stretches out his hand he can hardly see it. And for whoever Allah has not appointed light, there is no light" (24:40). Those two passages explain the ordering here. The loss is not a shortage of evidence. It is a condition in which evidence cannot arrive, and so it is described as a chain of coverings over a covering.

### Who is guided and who is left

"Allah leaves whoever He wills to stray and guides whoever He wills to the Straight Way" is read in more than one way, and none of them makes the sentence arbitrary. One reading takes it as: He lets whoever He wills die in disbelief, and whoever He wills He lets die on the straight path He is pleased with. Another takes it as: He abandons whoever He wills, and He gives guidance, success and firmness to whoever He wills. The straight way is a road without crookedness, and it is Islam. The point that runs through all of it is that Allah does with His creatures what He wills, and the guidance being asked about is not produced by a stronger sign but by light being appointed. Whoever has none is left with none, and whoever is given it is given a path he can walk.

### In short

- Deniers of the signs are called deaf, dumb and in darkness, which describes a state rather than a lack of proof.
- Their likeness is the deaf-mute who cannot speak and is blinded besides, so the path cannot be found from inside that condition.
- 2:17-18 and 24:40 give the same picture as a fire taken away and as darkness layered over a deep sea.
- Leaving someone to stray and guiding someone else is Allah's will at work, and neither reading makes it unfair.
- The straight path is a road with no crookedness, and guidance in this verse means light being appointed to a person.

40.text:
"Ask ˹them, O Prophet˺, 'Imagine if you were overwhelmed by Allah's torment or the Hour—would you call upon any other than Allah ˹for help˺?'" The verse puts a hypothetical question, and the answer to it is already known. It is not a question about what these people say they believe in calm weather. It is about what they will do when there is no calm left.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Ask ˹them, O Prophet˺"** is addressed to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and the words "imagine if you were overwhelmed" mean: tell them to look at themselves and consider what they are saying. **"if you were overwhelmed by Allah's torment"** is about this world, and one reading points to what actually happened, the way things went on the Day of Badr, on Uḥud and at the battle of the Confederates. **"or the Hour"** is the torment of the Day of Judgment, and it also covers the Hour that comes suddenly, with no warning they can prepare for. **"would you call upon any other than Allah ˹for help˺?"** asks whether they would then cry out to anyone besides Him to lift the punishment off them. **"˹Answer me˺ if your claims are true"** is the challenge: say that these idols are His partners and that they can bring benefit or push harm away, and then call on them if it is so. The point Allah is making about His creatures is that He does with them whatever He wills, and no one can resist what He has decided. He has no partner, and He accepts the supplication of whomever He wills.

### Why the question cannot be dodged

The answer was given long before it was asked. It is a fact about them rather than a claim about the message. In that kind of hour they will not call on anyone but Allah, because they know that none except Him can remove an affliction. Another verse states the same reaction at sea: when harm touches you on the water, those you used to call upon besides Him vanish from you, and He alone is left (17:67). A person in necessity forgets his idols and his false deities, and calls on the One he had put aside. History testifies to it, since a man who relied on other beings, or who did not even believe that God exists, starts invoking His name at the crucial moment. When the outward veils are lifted and a person dismisses what he had been entertaining, nothing is left in his mouth but the name of Allah. That is nature's own witness that Allah exists and that the authority is His alone.

One reading presses the same question from inside it: if harm touches you, whom do you want to remove it, and if an affair turns against you, from whom do you hope for gentleness? The child of Adam is pitiable, for he does not know the worth of that gentleness and does not recognize the danger of that exaltedness. The verse is at once a manifestation of Allah's majesty, exaltedness and independence of His servants, and a preparation for His gentleness, bounty and mercy. Hear it as though from Him: if in My lordship I were to assault these creatures out of justice, who would hold the assault back and come to their aid? If I were to raise the banner of the resurrection suddenly out of the ambush of the unseen, where would these servants flee, whose hand would they take hold of, whom would they call? Then generosity answers on their behalf, and the verse goes on to tell them that He is the one they will call on.

### The test is the uncovered moment

What the Qur'an asks for is not this kind of admission. Recognition at the point of helplessness is compulsory, and a compulsory confession is not what the attestation of Allah and His Messenger was meant to be. Every animal except man leads a realistic life by instinct, without being argued into it. In the human world the thing that does the work instinct does for animals is fear of Allah, taqwa, held on while everything is still going well. The verse is there to show them the shape of their own behavior under pressure, and then to ask why they will not give that behavior now, when the test is still open.

### In short

- The verse asks the people of Makkah to imagine the torment or the Hour arriving and answer honestly whom they would call on.
- One reading connects it to Badr, Uḥud and the battle of the Confederates, another to the Day of Judgment.
- Their own known reaction is that they would call on no one but Allah, since only He can remove an affliction, as 17:67 says about the sea.
- One reading takes the question as a display of majesty that opens the door to mercy.
- Compelled recognition at the point of helplessness is not faith, because faith is meant to be given before the compulsion arrives.

41.text:
"No! He is the only One you would call." The answer to the question is spoken for them, because it has been spoken many times already by their own behavior in distress. The verse then adds what follows from it, and what they will do with the partners they had appointed.

### Phrase by phrase

**"No! He is the only One you would call"** means that in a time of tribulation they call on Him and on no one else, and they will not summon anyone besides Allah to lift the torment. **"And if He willed, He could remove the affliction that made you invoke Him"** puts the relief entirely in His hands. He removes what you ask Him to remove, such as suffering, if He wills to remove it. He is the One worthy of that and able to do it. **"Only then will you forget whatever you associate with Him ˹in worship˺"** means that you leave the idols, abandon them and stop calling on them. You neglect them, in other words, and do not address them at all, because you know in that hour that they can bring no benefit and cause no harm.

### What the forgetting proves

The verse turns their own instinct against the arrangement they had built. The partners were appointed as problem-solvers and granters of wishes, and the devotion to them was supposed to start working exactly in the hour of trial. That is precisely the hour in which they are dropped. So when will the devotion work, if the moment it was needed is the moment it is forgotten? The affliction itself is not what is being denied here, since Allah could take it away if He willed, and the removal is not produced by the intensity of the crying out but by His will.

A Sufi commentary gives the answer a voice of its own, in which Allah says: you will call on Me, you will know Me, and you will ask Me to take the trial off you. I am the powerful one, the bounteous one, the friend whose doing and whose wanting are alike beautiful. Then the reports of David are brought in. In them the Lord says: ask the dwellers on earth why they will not be My friends, when I am worthy of friendship. I am generous without stinginess, knowing without ignorance, patient without weakness, and there is no change in My attributes and no turning back from bounty. In the beginningless I wrote mercy toward them against Myself, burned the incense of love, and lit up their hearts with the light of recognition. Those who turn away, He says, would die of yearning and cut every tie for love, if they knew how long He waits for them and how He longs to set their disobedience aside. He gives blessings and they thank someone else for them, He wards off the trial and they credit someone else with it, their shelter is His presence and they take shelter elsewhere. Let them go, let them flee, and in the end they will come back. You too have a brightness from Me, and you will wander and then arrive. He is the friend of whoever befriends Him, and the companion of whoever takes Him as companion.

The state of the servants answers that with a line of thanksgiving. Love for Your essence is the belief of Your friends, and remembering Your description, Lord, takes the grief of the grieving away. The cash a servant holds in hand is the treasure-house of His bounty, so the hopeful go on stitching their purses of hope.

### In short

- The verse answers its own question: in distress they call on Allah alone.
- The removal of the affliction depends on His will, not on the strength of the call.
- At that moment the partners are forgotten, because a dying heart knows they can do nothing.
- The question the verse leaves open is when a devotion that fails in the hour of need was ever going to succeed.
- One Sufi reading hears in it an address about friendship, waiting and returning, drawn out of the reports of David.

42.text:
"Indeed, We have sent messengers before you ˹O Prophet˺ to other people who We put through suffering and adversity ˹for their denial˺, so perhaps they would be humbled." This verse widens the argument from one city to the whole history of prophethood, and it explains what suffering is for. Allah did not send punishment on any people all at once. What came first was admonition, and admonition is a call to come back. The question put in 6:41 had already been answered for them, and this verse shows that the same method has run through every nation.

### Phrase by phrase

**"We have sent messengers before you to other people"** is sent to this people exactly as it was sent to those peoples, and their answer was to deny the messengers and turn away from what they brought. **"who We put through suffering"** means being seized with extreme poverty, the loss of wealth and diminished provision, and with loss of health, illness, disease and pain. **"and adversity"** is tribulation, fear of one another, hardship and hunger. **"so perhaps they would be humbled"** states the aim: that they would believe, submit, grow humble, and call on Allah with humbleness, and that they would pray for the punishment to be lifted.

### The second test

A community that fails the first test is not simply abandoned to it. They were tried with hardship and suffering to see whether it would turn them to Allah, and when they failed and became more absorbed in disobedience instead, they were given a different kind of trial. The doors of worldly comfort were opened for them, and they were given everything they wanted in the material world, so that through these blessings they might come to know their Benefactor. Instead they were so lost in the labyrinth of luxury that they forgot the message and the teachings of Allah and His Messenger. Having traded their souls for the glitter of passing comforts, they failed at both tests, and the case against them stood proved. Then the punishment came suddenly and consumed them.

That is also the answer to an excuse that appears in every age. There are always people who disobey Allah and His Prophet ﷺ openly and keep prospering in wealth, property, influence, recognition and power. They say that the prophet's word is a delusion. Weighing the whole world against their own short experience and taking the two sides of the argument at once, they are pushed to that conclusion by their own excuse-seeking, and by Satan. So the fate of the nations before them is quoted back at them, a punishment that came from the sky and from under the earth, and by means that reduced whole peoples to ashes. The people of Nūḥ were drowned in a flood that did not stop at the mountain tops. The people of ʿĀd were destroyed by a wind that lasted eight days and left no survivor. The people of Thamud were killed by a terrifying sound. The whole habitation of the people of Lūṭ was turned upside down. What is left of it lies in the west of Jordan as a low, lifeless body of water, which is why it is called the Dead Sea and the Sea of Lūṭ.

### Punishment, sample and showroom

Allah makes hardship do two jobs at once. Outwardly it looks like punishment, and the word for being seized here is the word for punishment. But its point is to shake heedlessness off, and in that sense it is mercy, since everyone turns to Allah naturally when he is in distress. The same is said of this world's terrors elsewhere: We will make them taste the nearer punishment instead of the greater one, so that they may come back (32:21).

What is settled here is a question about this world, which is no abode of reward. Where, then, is the point of hardship and ease in a place where good and bad seem weighed on one scale and the evil often fare better than the good? The answer is that the hereafter is the place of recompense, the Day of Judgment, Yawm al-Jazāʾ, and that some hardships here are a sample of punishment while some comforts are a sample of reward. Nobody is won over to a thing, or warned off an approaching danger, except by a model he can see. Some people of insight went further: every comfort in this world points to the comforts of Paradise, so that a person learns to long for them, and every sorrow points to the punishment of the hereafter, so that he prepares to keep clear of it. On that reading the whole world is a showroom of the hereafter. Prosperity and poverty, happiness and sorrow are then not reward and punishment in the real sense. They are a way of bringing creation back to the Creator it had grown alienated from.

### The smaller doom

There is also a reading of the word "Hour" that brings it closer. Besides the commonly acknowledged Qiyāmah, the Hour here can mean the smaller doom, al-Qiyāmatuṣ-Ṣughrā. It stands established for every single person the moment he dies, because for whoever dies his doom begins right then. A preliminary sample of the final reckoning meets the deceased in his grave and in the state of barzakh, the interval between death and resurrection. The taste of what is coming begins to show itself from this side. That is why the warnings in these verses work on two clocks at once: a nation can be destroyed in one stroke, and a person can be overtaken the moment his life ends. Kufr and shirk are refuted in this passage by the same questions that affirm tawḥīd, and the disbelievers of Makkah are asked who would deliver them when the calamity arrives. At such a time even the greatest mushrik forgets all about his idols and the objects of worship he had appointed, and calls on none but Allah, the One, the All-Powerful.

### The closing of all roads

In a reading of this verse that follows the inward sense, Ibn ʿAṭāʾ said of the seizing with misery and hardship: He cut off from them every road so that they would come back to Us, and He shut all their ways so that they turned away from the realm of being altogether and busied themselves only with His companionship, putting love for Him in their hearts. Ibn ʿAṭāʾ took as his illustration the story of Majnūn. The man was seen going around the Kaʿbah out of touch with himself, the sea of passion throwing waves in his chest, his hands lifted: "O Allah, increase me in love for Laylā." May Allah increase the passion for Laylā in his heart and multiply her trial a thousand times. His father, the prince of that time, said to him: many people have risen against you, so leave for a few days, and perhaps they will forget you and this madness for Laylā will lessen. Majnūn went away, came back on the third day and said: excuse me, passion for Laylā has closed every road to me, and the only road left is the road to her street. Everyone has a niche he prays toward, and each one's hope leans on it, but the niche of Sanāʾī is your street.

### In short

- The verse generalizes the Prophet's experience: messengers before him were sent to peoples who were then tried.
- The trial has two forms, poverty and sickness first, and then every kind of comfort, and a people can fail both.
- Life's events are messages sent to wake a person up, and hardship aimed at humility is mercy in method.
- The destructions of Nūḥ's, ʿĀd's, Thamud's and Lūṭ's peoples are listed as evidence that the pattern is old.
- Ibn ʿAṭāʾ reads the closing of roads as a mercy that leaves the heart one road only, and illustrates it with Majnūn and Laylā.

43.text:
"Why did they not humble themselves when We made them suffer?" The verse is an asking-that-marks-a-fact, and the fact it marks is the strangest part of the story. The proof that a person can be shown what he needs and still not use it.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Why did they not humble themselves when We made them suffer?"** means: why did they not believe and abase themselves before Us when We tested them with disaster? The thing that required humility was standing right in front of them. **"Instead, their hearts were hardened"** says that they did not become soft or humble, and their hearts dried up and would not yield to faith. **"and Satan made their misdeeds appealing to them"** is the other half of the explanation. Shayṭān made fair-seeming what they used to do: the shirk, the defiance and the rebellion. They went on doing them because they had been made to look good, and they kept saying that nothing was wrong. Their disbelief was dressed up as something creditable, so they persisted and took no lesson from what had happened to them.

### What a hardened heart is

The condition named here is not a shortage of information. A person faced with the truth who refuses it is not left alone with his refusal. Allah gives him jolts, a monetary loss or a physical trouble, so that he reviews his way of life and his thinking turns around. Events of this kind are messages rather than happenings, and their whole purpose is to wake a person out of the sleep of forgetfulness. What he does instead is to console himself: these are ordinary ups and downs, and everyone has them. That is how Satan all too often pulls a mind away from the possibility of divine displeasure. He supplies plausible justifications, and says the kind of thing that leaves a man negligent about his duties. When this is repeated, the heart loses its sensitivity to what is true and what is false, to right and wrong, and the conscience ends blunted. The hardening in this verse is that end, and it came to these people after the test had already been made as clear as a test can be made.

A further layer sits in another reading: what the devil made to seem fair to them was the ordinary shape of life itself, the way hardship alternates with ease and comfort, so that nothing in it looks like a message and nothing looks like a warning. If that is their case, then the verse's question carries both reproach and surprise. The one thing they had been given, a heart that reacts, had been spent.

### The mercy that was still available

The counterfactual is drawn out plainly. Had they humbled themselves and begged Allah to lift the calamity off them, mercy would have followed. That is what "so perhaps they would be humbled" in 6:42 was pointing at. The door was not shut when the suffering arrived. What they did not do was to ask, and asking is what humility looks like when it is real.

### In short

- The question is reproach, not inquiry: nothing stopped them from humbling themselves except themselves.
- Hardened means dry, unyielding and past softness, and it followed the test rather than replacing it.
- Satan's work here is described as making a person's own deeds look fair, so he keeps on doing them.
- Conscience is dulled by repetition, and a heart that keeps explaining events away ends unable to read them.
- Had they asked when the calamity came, mercy was the answer waiting.

44.text:
"When they became oblivious to warnings, We showered them with everything they desired." This is the verse people fear, because it says that relief can be the beginning of the end. The gates of good things are opened, and the opening is not approval.

### Phrase by phrase

**"When they became oblivious to warnings"** means they forgot what they had been reminded of and neglected it. They ignored the admonition given through hardship, and turned their backs on what they had been commanded with in the Scripture. **"We showered them with everything they desired"** is read as: We opened the gates of all things to them. Provision, vegetation, the fertility of the land and comfort came in from whichever side they wanted, and the stated purpose is to draw them on by degrees. **"But just as they became prideful of what they were given"** catches them in the middle of their enjoyment of wealth, children and provision, rejoicing wantonly in what they had been handed. **"We seized them by surprise, then they instantly fell into despair"** is the sudden taking, and the despair is being confounded, cut off from any hope of good. We seek refuge with Allah from such an end.

### What the affluence is not

This verse warns everyone not to be deceived by affluence. Do not see wealth and comfort pouring out on a person or a group and conclude too fast that these are the people on the correct path, or that their life is a model of success. Among them there may be someone picked out to be seized with a sudden and terrible punishment, and a hadith names that state as being lured on to destruction. When you see blessings and wealth raining on a man while he is deep in sin and disobedience, know that he is being drawn on, and that his affluence is a sign he will be taken in punishment. Aḥmad records it through ʿUqbah ibn ʿĀmir.

Ibn Jarīr reports another wording of the same rule through ʿUbādah ibn al-Ṣāmit. When Allah wills that a nation survive and increase, He creates in them two qualities: moderation in everything they do, and modesty and chastity, which means abstinence from what is not right. And when He wills a nation to come to ruin, the doors of breach of faith are opened for them, so they seem successful in the world in spite of their treachery and their wrongdoing.

### Al-Ḥasan al-Basrī on the same verse

Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī said that whoever is given provision and thinks Allah is not testing him with it has no wisdom. Whoever has little and thinks Allah will not provide for him has no wisdom either. He then recited this verse. He also swore by the Lord of the Kaʿbah that Allah had deceived these people: He gave them what they wanted, and then He punished them for it. Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded that statement of his. On the same reading, the prosperity after poverty and the health after sickness are not a change of mind about them, and they are not a reward for their pride in it either. They are the completion of the second test, and once it is failed the case is closed.

### In short

- The verse describes abundance as a form of trial rather than as evidence of favor.
- Forgetting the warning is what precedes the opening of the gates of everything good.
- The rejoicing is cut short from the middle, which is what makes the seizure sudden.
- Affluence over an unrepentant sinner is named in a hadith as luring on to destruction, and the doors of breach of faith are its sign.
- Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī took both ends of provision as tests, and swore by the Lord of the Kaʿbah that giving people what they want can be how they are deceived.

45.text:
"So the wrongdoers were utterly uprooted." The sentence closes the account of the nations that were tried twice and failed twice. Nothing of them is left standing, and the verse finishes with praise.

### Phrase by phrase

**"So the wrongdoers were utterly uprooted"** means that the roots of the people who did wrong were cut off, the last remnant of them exterminated through punishment when the help of Allah came to His messengers. Those who ascribed partners to Allah were wiped out, and the phrase for uprooting leaves no survivor behind to remember them. **"And all praise is for Allah—Lord of all worlds"** is said in gratitude for that. Say: praise and thanks be to Allah, for giving victory to the messengers and destroying the disbelievers, for annihilating the enemies and helping the friends. It is praise because He is the Lord of all that exists.

### Why praise closes the passage

One note on this verse brings out the turn. When mass punishment came, the wrongdoers were uprooted to the last man, and immediately after that comes: praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds. The hint is that whenever the wrongdoers and the unjust are visited by punishment or calamity, that is a blessing for the whole world, and a blessing the people should be grateful for. The passage that began by comforting a grieving prophet ends by telling him that the outcome is settled and that the right to have one's greatness praised in this world belongs to one Being alone. A person who ignores divine truth is disrespecting the one whose world this is, and setting up his own greatness under a sky already filled with the majesty of Allah.

### In short

- Uprooting means the last remnant of a wrongdoing people being cut off, and it came as help to the messengers.
- The praise at the end is gratitude for victory given and for enemies removed.
- Allah is named Lord of all worlds, which is why the outcome belongs to Him and not to the strongest party.
- The destruction of the unjust is presented as a mercy to the rest of the world, and so as a thing to be thankful for.

46.text:
"Ask ˹them, O Prophet˺, 'Imagine if Allah were to take away your hearing or sight, or seal your hearts—who else other than Allah could restore it?'" The argument is put as an imagination exercise, and it starts from the one thing nobody disputes: these senses are there, and nobody put them there.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Ask ˹them, O Prophet˺"** means: say this to the people of Makkah, to these idolaters who deny what you have brought. **"Imagine if Allah were to take away your hearing or sight"** is a question about something He has already given. He would leave you unable to hear any admonition or guidance, and unable to see the truth. **"or seal your hearts"** means that nothing would reach you from either. The hearts would no longer take in the truth or understand anything. **"who else other than Allah could restore it?"** asks who besides Allah could hand back what He has taken. The gods meant here are their idols, the very beings they count as partners. **"See ˹O Prophet˺ how We vary the signs, yet they still turn away"** is the comment on it. Look at how the proofs are set out in more than one way and made plain and clear. After all that they still turn aside from the truth, and keep others from following it.

### The senses are evidence, not property

The two senses named here are also named elsewhere as gifts: it is He who created you and endowed you with hearing and sight (67:23). And: "Say: it is He who produces hearing and sight" (10:31). Another verse adds the third piece and the power over it: know that Allah comes in between a person and his heart, and that He withholds the use of a sense from whom He wills (8:24). A further reading takes the verse as a description of what is already happening rather than as a threat of physical loss. On it, the disbelievers are not allowed to benefit from their hearing and sight in religious matters at all. On that reading the sealing has begun, and the question only names what they have already brought on themselves. The signs, explained in this variety, testify to the oneness of Allah in lordship, and to the falseness of everything worshipped besides Him.

### The worse deprivation

Ears, eyes and a heart are given so that a person will hear the signs, see them and accept them through rational argument. What a man is meant to do with these capacities is decided by the One who gave them. If he does not use them for the purpose they were made for, he runs the risk of being judged incapable, with the capacities themselves snatched away. A person left deaf, blind and unable to reason is helpless enough in this world. That is the picture the verse puts in front of them. But a greater helplessness than that exists, and this is the point of the exercise. It is to have ears and be deaf to the truth. It is to have eyes and be blind to it, and to carry a heart in one's chest that cannot understand it. That deprivation is worse than the first, because it leaves a man debased and worthless where it matters. No shortcoming is more heinous than that.

### In short

- The verse asks the people of Makkah to name anyone but Allah who could restore hearing, sight and understanding once He has taken them.
- Their idols are the gods meant in the question, and they cannot give back what they never had.
- 67:23, 10:31 and 8:24 are quoted to show that these senses are produced and withheld by Allah alone.
- On one reading the sealing is not threatened but already in force, since no religious benefit reaches them through these senses.
- The real loss is not blindness but having the equipment and refusing to use it.

47.text:
"Ask, 'Imagine if Allah's punishment were to overwhelm you with or without warning—who would be destroyed other than the wrongdoers?'" The people of Makkah are now asked to say where the punishment would land if it came at all. The answer takes the fear out of one side of it and puts it back, heavier, on the other.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Imagine if Allah's punishment were to overwhelm you"** means it strikes while you are unaware and have no news of it, or comes in the middle of the night. **"with or without warning"** is the second half of the pair: openly, in the daylight, before your eyes, in public. **"who would be destroyed other than the wrongdoers?"** is answered by the verse itself: no one but the evildoing and unbelieving folk would perish. The torment falls on people who have done wrong against themselves by shirk. The people who worship Allah alone, without partners, are saved from it, and they have no fear and no sorrow. Another reading takes the wrongdoers here to be the idolaters specifically. The other half of that safety is spelled out later in this surah, in the words about those who believe and do not confuse their belief with wrongdoing, that is, with shirk (6:82).

### The dare that misreads the situation

A man who is warned about the result of denying the truth and still answers insolently is a man who has been well placed in the world. He has concluded that he need not fear the scourge of Allah, and he imagines himself exempt from divine retribution. The more daring among them put the challenge into words. They say to the messenger of God that if he is truthful, Allah should let His wrath fall on them, and they will watch it arrive. They do not understand that when Allah vents His anger, it lands on them and on nobody else. The verse before asked whether anyone could give their senses back. This one asks whether anyone can stand in the way of a punishment, and both questions have the same answer.

### In short

- The verse asks them to say whom the punishment would reach, with warning or without it.
- Its answer is that none perish except the wrongdoing people, and the idols cannot change that.
- Those who worship Allah alone are saved, and so have nothing to fear and nothing to grieve over.
- The insolent demand to be shown the punishment at once only proves that they think themselves exempt.
- Another verse in this surah names the other half of the same quality: belief that has not been confused with wrongdoing or shirk (6:82).

48.text:
"We have sent messengers only as deliverers of good news and as warners." The verse states the job description, and with it the limits of what a messenger is for. He is not sent to compel, and the two halves of his work belong together.

### Phrase by phrase

**"We have sent messengers only as deliverers of good news"** means they bring glad tidings to Allah's servants, good news of Paradise for whoever believes, and they command whatever is good and righteous. **"and as warners"** is the other half: they warn whoever disbelieves of Allah's anger and of every kind of torment, with news of the Fire. **"Whoever believes and does good"** is the one who believes in his heart with what the messengers were sent with, trusts in them and in the Scriptures, and puts his deeds right by following them, setting straight what is between himself and his Lord. **"there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve"** says that nothing will befall them on the Day of Judgment when fear falls on the people of Hell, and that they will not grieve over the pleasures of this world they missed when the people of Hell grieve.

### Why the pair cannot be split

The preacher of Allah's word appears in the world as a bearer of good news and as a warner at once, and the test runs on exactly that. A person is asked to recognize the truth when it arrives in the language of admonition and reform himself accordingly. If he refuses to recognize it and makes magic feats and charms a condition for accepting it, he proves nothing except his own moral blindness. For people with that blindness nothing is left but ruin and destruction in this world of Allah. The good news and the warning are one message, delight that never ends on one side and severe punishment on the other.

### What they leave behind

The promise has a second edge, about the past rather than the future. Whoever believes and does right has no fear of what is ahead, and no grief over what he left behind in this world, because Allah is the Wali, the Protector, over whatever they leave. The protection covers what was given up, which is how the verse answers the complaint that a believer loses out. He does not, and the One who guards what he left is no distant party.

### In short

- The verse limits the messenger's work to two things: good news for the obedient and warning for the disobedient.
- Belief here is belief in the heart, matched by deeds put right through following the messengers.
- No fear reaches these people about what is ahead of them, and no grief about what they missed.
- Allah is their Wali and Protector over what they leave behind, which is what closes the complaint of loss.
- A demand for feats of magic as a condition of belief turns the warner's work into proof of the demander's blindness.

49.text:
"But those who deny Our signs will be afflicted with punishment for their rebelliousness." The other half of the pair is put in one line, and the line is about why the punishment falls.

### Phrase by phrase

**"But those who deny Our signs"** are the people who deny the Qur'an and deny the messenger it came through. **"will be afflicted with punishment"** is the torment falling on them, and **"for their rebelliousness"** names the reason: they were wicked and went against obedience. The punishment strikes because they disbelieved the message the messengers brought, defied Allah's commands, did what He prohibited and crossed the limits He had set. Had they not gone against Him, had they carried out His instructions and stayed away from what He prohibited, the punishment would not have touched them at all.

### In short

- Denying the signs is described as rebellion, which is a refusal that knows what it is refusing.
- The torment is caused by their own conduct, not by the warning that announced it.
- The counterfactual is stated plainly: obedience and keeping away from what is prohibited would have kept the punishment off them.
- The verse is the second half of the job description in 6:48, and it belongs to it.

50.text:
"Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ 'I do not say to you that I possess Allah's treasuries or know the unseen, nor do I claim to be an angel. I only follow what is revealed to me.'" The verse is the answer to a demand, and the answer consists of four denials and one claim.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Say, ˹O Prophet,˺"** is addressed to Muhammad ﷺ and, through him, to the people of Makkah. It came down about Abū Jahl, al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith, ʿUyaynah and their companions. Then, it is said, it came down about the clients of the tribe as well. **"I do not say to you that I possess Allah's treasuries"** means that he does not own the treasures of Allah or hold any power over them. He does not have the keys of provision, vegetation, fruit, rain or punishment. **"or know the unseen"** denies knowledge of what is hidden from him and has not been revealed to him. The knowledge of the unseen sits with Allah, and he only knows what Allah conveys to him of it. **"nor do I claim to be an angel"** means he does not say that he is one of the angels from heaven. He is a human being to whom Allah sends revelation, and that revelation is the honor He gave him and the favor He singled him out with. **"I only follow what is revealed to me"** is the one positive claim in the verse. Its sense is: I say and do only what I am commanded with in the Qur'an, and I never disobey the revelation in the least. **"Say, 'Are those blind ˹to the truth˺ equal to those who can see?'"** asks whether the misled man and the man who is guided and follows the truth are the same. It asks whether the disbeliever and the believer are equal in deeds of obedience and in reward. **"Will you not then reflect?"** asks them to think about the comparisons the Qur'an sets out. Another verse puts the same contrast in these words: "Is the one who knows that what has been revealed to you from your Lord is the truth like the one who is blind? Only people of understanding pay heed" (13:19).

### The demands behind the answer

The disbelievers of Makkah put three demands to the Prophet ﷺ on different occasions. Bring us the treasures of the whole world by the power of miracle, if you really are Allah's messenger. Tell us what is going to happen to us, good and bad, so that we can take hold of it or keep clear of it in advance. And explain how a human being like us, born of a mother and a father, who eats, drinks and walks about in the streets and markets as we do, can suddenly become a messenger of Allah. If he were an angel, whose make and qualities are worthier than ours, they said, they would have accepted him. This verse answers all three at once, by refusing the terms of every one of them.

### What the denials are for

The denials are not modesty for its own sake. They define the office. Nothing in the claim to prophethood requires that a messenger own the treasures of Allah, or know everything in the domain of the unseen, or be a being with attributes other than human. What his office is, is to follow the revelation sent to him, to act on it himself, and to invite others to it. The denials remove the picture the demanders were working with. On it, a true prophet would have to be a supplier of wealth, a foreteller and a superhuman being all at once. Once the office is described correctly, only the closing question is left: is the man who sees the same as the man who has eyes and will not use them?

### In short

- The verse denies four things and keeps one: he is not the owner of Allah's treasures, not the knower of the unseen, not an angel, and he follows only what is revealed.
- Knowledge of the unseen is limited to what Allah conveys, and the treasures are not in his hands.
- The claim to be a human messenger is not a downgrade, since the revelation itself is the honor.
- The blind and the seeing are not equal, and 13:19 says the same about the man who knows and the man who is blind.
- The three demands made of the Prophet ﷺ are answered by refusing the picture of prophethood behind them.

51.text:
"Warn with this ˹Quran˺ those who are awed by the prospect of being gathered before their Lord—when they will have no protector or intercessor besides Him—so perhaps they will be mindful ˹of Him˺." The verse tells the Prophet ﷺ where to take the message next, and it says what the message is for. The debate with the demanders has been answered, and what follows is not another round of it.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Warn with this ˹Quran˺"** means warn by means of the Qur'an, and it is also taken to mean warn by Allah. **"those who are awed by the prospect of being gathered before their Lord"** describes people who know this and are certain of it, and who live in awe, fearing their Lord and dreading the terrible reckoning (23:57, 13:21). The gathering is the Day of Resurrection, and the sinning believers are among those meant here. **"when they will have no protector or intercessor besides Him"** is what they fear. On that Day no relative, no patron and no intercessor will keep His torment off them if He decides to punish. The clause states the circumstance of the gathering rather than a separate hope. **"so perhaps they will be mindful ˹of Him˺"** is the aim, and it is double: they will ward off transgression, and that will help them perform deeds of obedience. Warn of the day when there is no judge except Allah. Then people will work good deeds in this life, and their works will save them on the Day of Qiyāmah from His torment and earn them reward in more than one form. The men named in this verse as people who know and are certain are Salmān al-Fārīsī, Khabbāb ibn al-Aratt, ʿĀmir ibn Fuḥayrah, Mihjāʿ ibn Sāliḥ, ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir, Bilāl ibn Rabāḥ, Ṣuhayb ibn Sinān and Sālim the client of Abū Hudhayfah. These are the people the Qur'an benefits, and whoever believes in the messengers and does right has no fear of what is ahead.

### Why the demanded signs were not sent

Many signs had already appeared before the disbelievers of Makkah. The Prophet ﷺ came into the world an orphan, unschooled and untutored, and lived his whole life unlettered in a land where there was no scholar and no institution of learning near or far. For forty years he lived under the eyes of his people in that state. Then, all of a sudden, there poured from his speech a stream of words whose eloquence challenged the masters of Arab diction and silenced them. Its wisdom and meaning reached to pragmatic human needs right down to the Day of Qiyāmah. With it he brought a practical system for the nurture of the complete human being. No human ingenuity could produce that, and he demonstrated it and proved it workable. The crowd of his time, whose life was eating, drinking, sleeping and waking, was made to look up at the purpose it was created for. Every period of that life, and every great event in it, was a miracle in its place and a sign of Allah, and against that background no just and reasonable person had room left to demand a sign.

Still, the Quraysh demanded miracles of a kind of their own choosing, and some of them Allah showed them openly. They asked to see the moon split in two. The parting of the moon was witnessed not only by Quraysh but by a great number of people anywhere in the world at that time. Their answer to it was that this was magic of a continuing sort, magic that had always been there. They saw, they understood, and they went on asking for something new, as verse 37 records. In reply the Qur'an tells the Prophet ﷺ to say that Allah has everything in His power. He has already manifested signs without their asking, and He is quite able to produce the ones they want. But there is a settled way Allah follows here. Once a people are shown the miracle they asked for and then refuse to believe in it, a sudden punishment seizes them. It was therefore in their own interest that the signs of their choosing should not be made to appear, and many people still do not understand the wisdom in that and keep insisting.

### The treasures of Allah

Commentators have named many things as the treasures meant in the first sentence of verse 50, but the Qur'an itself settles the reach of the phrase: there is not a thing whose treasures are not with Us (15:21). So the treasures of Allah cover everything, and cannot be pinned to a set of particular items. The scholars who listed particular things were giving examples, and there is no contradiction between the two. Then comes the point the commentary draws from this, and it draws it hard. The treasures of Allah were not in the hands of the foremost of the prophets and messengers, Muḥammad al-Muṣṭafā ﷺ. So how can anyone suppose that a pious elder or a wali in this community can do as he likes and grant whatever he chooses to anyone? That is plain ignorance.

### Why the wording changes in the middle

The first denial and the third are both framed as a claim he does not make, while the middle one says something stronger. It does not say, I do not tell you that I know the unseen. It says, nor do I have the knowledge of the unseen. Abū al-Ḥayyān pointed out the subtlety in his Tafsīr al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ. Owning the divine treasures, and being or not being an angel, are matters of observation, and his addressees knew them well. They knew that the treasures of Allah were not in his hands, and that he was not an angel. Their demands were built on malice and hostility, so it would have been enough to say: I have never claimed to own the treasures of Allah, or to be an angel. The knowledge of the unseen was different. These people already believed their astrologers and soothsayers knew the unseen, so attributing that knowledge to the Messenger of Allah was not unlikely for them. They had also heard news of the unseen from his mouth and watched it come true. So a bare denial of the claim was not sufficient, and the thing denied was the fact itself. The wording also clears up a misunderstanding. A share of knowledge about unseen things, given to an angel, a messenger or a wali through revelation or inspiration, cannot be called ʿilm al-ghayb in the terminology of the Qur'an. Nor can its recipient be called the knower of the unseen.

From the same place comes the balance the commentary insists on. No Muslim can doubt that Allah gave the Prophet ﷺ knowledge of many things of the unseen, more than angels and human beings put together from the first to the last. That is the belief of the whole Ummah. Alongside it, on the strength of countless statements of the Qur'an and the Sunnah, all the early Imams and the later ones hold that all-encompassing knowledge of the whole universe, al-ʿilm al-muḥīṭ, is the exclusive attribute of Allah. An angel or a messenger is not His equal as Creator or as Provider, and is not equal to Him as the Absolutely Powerful, al-Qādir al-Muṭlaq. So no prophet or angel, however much of the unseen he is given, is the Knower of the unseen. On the excellence of the Prophet ﷺ the commentary permits itself a line from a Persian poet: after Allah, you are the great one, and that is the whole short story. His rank in knowledge is ahead of angels, prophets and messengers, and it is not the equal of Allah's knowledge, and claiming equality there is the path of excess that Christianity took.

### Who the warning is aimed at first

There are three kinds of people about the hereafter: those who believe in it as certain, those who doubt and waver, and those who reject it outright. The prophets were commanded to convey the call and the warning to all three, and the Qur'an says so in many places. But the call is likelier to work on the first two, so this verse singles them out. It tells the Prophet ﷺ to turn the focus of his warning to people who believe they will be brought out before Allah to give an account, whether they are believers already or people who are not deniers, even if their holding is only probable. It also instructs him, in the same move, to draw a line and stop the argument with the obstinate and get on with the work of conveying. At the end of verse 50 the blind man and the seeing man were pronounced unequal. The sense is that they should drop their selfish concerns, abandon obstinacy and hostility, and look at reality as it is, so that they stop being counted among the blind. Their need was to start seeing, and a little thought and a little care about what is right would have returned to them the sight they were missing.

### Why the reckless cannot be warned

Admonition only reaches those who live in fear of God, because only a person worried about danger can be warned of an approaching calamity. People who live recklessly are never serious about being admonished, and that is why they never heed advice. Recklessness comes from two things: worship of this world, and worship of ancestors. Whoever is lost in worldly things, or satisfied with worldly success, does not remember that he will have to appear before his Creator and Lord the day he dies. The hereafter carries no weight for him, and the remembrance of it finds no place in his thinking. There is a second kind of false security as well: people who treat recommendation as the key to Paradise. They assume that the great ones they have attached themselves to will stand up for them in the next world, and that no matter how bad the conditions, that will be enough to save them. They live in the fond hope that nothing can go wrong with them, since they hold the hands of holy personalities and belong to the group that is ostensibly loved and favored. That is the temper which refuses to be afraid of the hereafter and will not consider anything that might throw doubt on its position.

### In short

- The verse directs the warning to those already softened by the thought of being gathered before their Lord, and the gathering has no protector or intercessor in it.
- Mindfulness is the goal, and it works in both directions: holding back from transgression and doing works of obedience.
- Signs already stood in front of Makkah, and a demanded sign that is refused only hastens destruction, which is why they are withheld.
- The treasures of Allah cover everything, and 15:21 is the verse that proves it, so no claim can be built on controlling them.
- The middle denial is harsher in wording because the claim it denies was the one they were actually prone to believe.
- Three kinds of people exist about the hereafter, and the warning is aimed first at the certain and the wavering.

52.text:
"˹O Prophet!˺ Do not dismiss those ˹poor believers˺ who invoke their Lord morning and evening, seeking His pleasure." The verse is a prohibition addressed to the Prophet ﷺ, and it is also the answer to a proposal put to him by people who considered themselves doing him a favor.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Do not dismiss those"** means: do not turn away from you the people with these qualities, and keep them close as your companions. **"who invoke their Lord morning and evening"** describes those who worship Him and call on Him, and one reading ties the two times to the obligatory prayers, which is how Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib, Mujāhid, al-Ḥasan and Qatādah took it. By the usage of the language the phrase covers all the times of day and night, and the calling means worship in general. **"seeking His pleasure"** is the restriction attached to it. They are seeking the Most Generous Face of Allah and nothing else in the world, and they do it by being sincere in the acts of worship and obedience they perform. Worship without sincerity is not trustworthy, and the worshipper is not seeking the fleeting things of this world when he does it. **"You are not accountable for them whatsoever, nor are they accountable for you"** is read by Ibn ʿAtiyyah, al-Zamakhsharī and others as being about the chiefs who had insisted on the removal of the poor believers. Its sense is that you are not responsible for anything in their account, and they are not responsible for anything in yours. There is therefore no reason to buy their entry into faith at the price of driving these men out. **"So do not dismiss them, or you will be one of the wrongdoers"** closes the door on the arrangement. The same ruling is spelled out again in these words: "And keep yourself patiently with those who call on their Lord morning and evening, seeking His Face, and let not your eyes pass beyond them toward the pomp and glitter of this life, and obey not him whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance, who follows his own desires and whose affair has been lost" (18:28).

### The proposal

Some of the chiefs of the disbelievers of Quraysh came to the Prophet's uncle Abū Ṭālib: ʿUtbah ibn Rabīʿah, Shaybah, Muṭʿim ibn ʿAdiyy, Ḥārith ibn Nawfal and others with them. Their complaint, reported through Ibn Jarīr, was that a real obstacle stood in the way of listening to his nephew: the people who kept company with him. They were either freed slaves of theirs or people living at their mercy, and with such men in the sitting they could not attend it. Their proposal was that these should be asked to leave when it was time for the chiefs to come. The nobles also went to ʿUmar and asked him to request that one day be set aside for them and another for the weak believers. Allah rejected the arrangement and warned them against it. One report has the Prophet ﷺ sending ʿUmar to the poor men with the message that they should come less often for a few days, so that perhaps those others would believe. ʿUmar had not taken three steps when Gabriel came down with the verse. Do not drive them away, since He has not driven them away, and do not caress those whom He has not called. The Prophet ﷺ called ʿUmar back. When the unbelievers despaired of getting days divided between them, they offered a compromise. They would sit along with the poor men for a while, they said, if the Prophet ﷺ looked at them and not at them, and showed them respect. Then ʿUmar was sent again to the poor men, to gladden their hearts and to ask their approval for it. ʿUmar himself had first advised accepting the arrangement for a few days. These men loved the Prophet ﷺ, he pointed out, and were not stiff with formality, and they would move out of the sitting when the chiefs arrived. After the verse came down he apologized and admitted the advice had been wrong. The poor men in question were Bilāl al-Ḥabashī, Ṣuhayb ar-Rūmī, ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir, Sālim the client of Abī Hudhayfah, Ṣābiṭ the client of Usayd, ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd, Miqdād ibn ʿAmr, Masʿūd ibn al-Qārī and Dhū al-Shimātayn. Other companions of the same standing are named with them, and their claim to nobility was delivered from heaven. The reason behind the whole episode, in another wording, is what ʿUyaynah ibn Ḥisn al-Fazārī said. Drive these away from you, he told the Prophet ﷺ, so that the nobles of Makkah will come to you, listen to you and believe in you.

### What the eagerness was

The Prophet ﷺ wanted those men to come to faith, and that wish is what the episode is built on. The unbelievers came to Muṣṭafā and told him that they wanted to believe in him, Muḥammad, but that sitting with these beggars, and the smell of their shabby clothes, was beneath their dignity. Their desire came first, and the Prophet ﷺ was so eager for their belief that another verse addresses the wish directly: perhaps you will consume yourself with grief over their footsteps, turning away (18:6). One Sufi reading takes the exchange as a lesson about who decides the company of the chosen. Those accepted by the Presence are one thing, and those turned away by severance another. The poor men were the ones called by the verse in which Allah invites to the abode of peace (10:25). The estranged ones were the ones driven away by the verse that says: slink into it, and do not speak to Me (23:108). The instruction that came down with the prohibition was: be with them, since I am with them, and want them, since I want them.

### The four lessons drawn from the verse

First, nobody has the right to look down on a man in tattered clothes or in a broken-down condition. People who look like that may be among those honored and accepted by Allah, and a hadith says that many a dust-covered, broken-down person is held dear by Allah, so that if he swears by Allah about something, Allah lets what he swore come about. Second, taking material affluence as the measure of nobility and lowliness is an insult to humanity, and what it actually depends on is good morals and deeds. Third, a reformer needs a call that reaches everyone, believers and dissenters alike. But the first claim on him belongs to the people who already own his teaching, and pushing them behind others in order to carry the call to outsiders is not permitted. In the case of this community, the education of unaware Muslims is not to be put off in favor of the call to non-Muslims. Fourth, the rewards and blessings of Allah rise in proportion to gratitude. Anyone who wants an increase in them must make gratitude, in word and in deed, a permanent part of his character.

### In short

- The verse forbids dismissing the people whose worship is sincere and whose only aim is the countenance of Allah.
- The proposal to trade their removal for the chiefs' attendance was rejected outright, and 18:28 repeats the ruling.
- Accountability runs each way on its own account, which is what makes the bargain unnecessary and unjust.
- The occasion names the men involved on both sides, from ʿUyaynah ibn Ḥisn al-Fazārī down to Bilāl and Ṣuhayb.
- The four lessons concern looking down on people, the real measure of nobility, the preacher's priorities and gratitude.

53.text:
"In this way We have tested some by means of others, so those ˹disbelievers˺ may say, 'Has Allah favoured these ˹poor believers˺ out of all of us?'" The verse explains why the arrangement of the community was left as it was, with the weak in front. The testing is not an accident of history.

### Phrase by phrase

**"In this way We have tested some by means of others"** means that He tried them against one another and checked them with each other. The noble was tested by the common man, the Arab by the client, and the rich man by the poor man. The preference was given to the last of these, by bringing him forward into faith first. **"so those ˹disbelievers˺ may say"** introduces what the test is meant to produce out of them, and their saying is: has Allah favoured these poor men, whom we look down on, with guidance from among the rest of us? They were tested by the clients. The men named here are Umayyah ibn Khalaf al-Jumahī, al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah al-Makhzumī, Suhayl ibn ʿAmr, Abū Jahl ibn Hishām, ʿUyaynah ibn Ḥisn al-Fazārī, ʿUtbah and Shaybah the sons of Rabīʿah, and their lot among the leaders of Quraysh. **"Does Allah not best recognize the grateful"** is the answer.
