Is not Allah more knowledgeable about the people who thank and appreciate Him, in what they say, in what they do and in their hearts, and is He not the one who guides them? He directs these believers along the ways of peace, takes them out of darkness into light by His leave, and brings them to the path that is straight.

### The logic of their objection

At first most of the people who followed the Messenger of Allah ﷺ were the weak: men and women with no standing, and slaves. Only a few chiefs or noted men followed him. Quraysh used to mock the weak among them who believed, and some of them they tortured. Their argument was that Allah would not guide these people to good instead of them, if the thing they had embraced were good at all. The Qur'an reports the same reasoning from other disbelievers: had it been a good thing, they would not have preceded us to it (46:11). And: when Our clear verses are recited to them, the disbelievers say to the believers, which of the two groups is better in position and station (19:73). The reply to that claim comes with the next verse: how many a generation before them have We destroyed that was better in wealth, goods and outward appearance (19:74). The saying in this verse is thus the outcome of a test they were given through poor and weak believers, and they failed it. Instead of looking at the demonstration of Allah's absolute power, and concluding that nobility turns on morals and deeds rather than on wealth or standing, they took it as a grievance against Allah. They spoke as though the honor had been taken from them and given where it was not due.

### Nūḥ's answer, and a question in a foreign court

The same objection had been put to Nūḥ by his people: "Shall we believe in you when the meekest of the people follow you" (26:111), and they followed you without thinking, without a moment's consideration (11:27). His answer is the answer this verse follows: "And what knowledge have I of what they used to do? Their account is only with my Lord, if you could but know" (26:112-113). Their account is not mine, just as my account is not theirs. Nūḥ did not answer by saying that these poor men were nobler than them by the standard of deeds and morals. His method of correction did not allow a reply that would only provoke his hearers further. It was enough for him to say that lowliness is a matter of deeds, and since their deeds were not fully known to him, he could not settle who was noble and who was not. This became a known test for later scholars of communities as well. The early followers of a prophet are the poor of his people, and that fact counts as evidence for the truth of his prophethood. When the letter of the Prophet ﷺ reached Heracles, the Byzantine ruler, inviting him to Islam, he wanted to investigate the claim, so he put questions to people who knew him. One of them was whether the noblemen or the weak followed him, and he was told that they were the weak. Such, he said, is the case with the followers of messengers. Another account of the same exchange has Heraclius ask Abū Sufyān the question, and Abū Sufyān answer that it is the weak among them who follow him.

### What the answer turns on

The answer to their complaint is about gratitude, not about birth. A noble and honorable person, in the real sense, is the one who recognizes the right of the Benefactor over him and is grateful. He is the one who deserves honor and reward. It is not the man who spends his days soaked in the blessings of his Provider and goes on disobeying Him. Those who have reached wealth and popularity prefer the weight of their worldly interests to supporting a call of truth stripped of every advantage. Supporting it would pull their whole structure of vested interest down. And when they see the truth being upheld by people of ordinary status, their way of thinking is only confirmed, since they feel that association with it would lower them. Instead of testing the truth by the standard of truth, they judge it by a private touchstone of their own, and when it does not measure up to that, they set it aside. Allah does not look at shapes or colors. He looks at hearts and deeds, and that is the criterion this verse is arguing for. Whoever strives, the verse says elsewhere, will be guided, and Allah is with the doers of good (29:69).

### In short

- The arrangement of who comes first is itself the test, and it runs both ways through the community.
- Their question, whether Allah favoured these poor men out of all of them, is answered by 19:74, where better-off nations were destroyed.
- Nūḥ's reply to the same arrogance, in 26:111-113, is the pattern this verse follows.
- Heracles used the same test, that a prophet's followers are the poor, as evidence for the truth of prophethood.
- Gratitude, not lineage, is what Allah recognizes, and He looks at hearts and deeds rather than at shapes and colors.

54.text:
When the believers in Our revelations come to you, say, “Peace be upon you! Your Lord has taken upon Himself to be Merciful. Whoever among you commits evil ignorantly ˹or recklessly˺ then repents afterwards and mends their ways, then Allah is truly All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.”

The verse comes straight after a passage in which certain men were asked to be moved out of the Prophet's circle to make room for their masters. It answers that with a greeting nobody had thought to offer them.

### Phrase by phrase

**"When the believers in Our revelations come to you"** The revelations here carry both meanings the word can bear: the verses of the Qur'an, and the wide signs of Allah's power set out in creation. Belief in either kind brings a person into the same room.

**"say, 'Peace be upon you'"** Two senses are given for this address. It can mean: pass on to them the greeting of peace from your Lord, which is the highest honour such a person can be given. Or it can mean: give them the good news that they are safe. Anything they fell short in stands forgiven, and no calamity will catch them. The verb matters. Allah does not tell the Prophet to excuse these people, or to defend their poverty, or to put up with them. He tells him to greet them.

**"Your Lord has taken upon Himself to be Merciful"** The word "Lord" is itself the proof offered to the hearer. A Lord is a nurturer and sustainer, and a nurturer does not let what he nurtures go to waste. Then the promise is made heavier and kinder at the same time: he has prescribed this mercy on himself. A promise is one thing. A mercy written down as an obligation he chose to take on, out of generosity and compassion, is another. An ordinary good person would not go back on his word.

**"Whoever among you commits evil ignorantly"** The wording is not that the sinner did not know the ruling. It is that he acted the way an unaware person acts, without reckoning what the act leads to. On that reading no one is excluded, because every act of disobedience has some of that blindness in it.

**"then repents afterwards and mends their ways"** Repentance is being ashamed of what was done. Mending is making the deed sound again, and that takes work of a specific kind, taken up below.

**"then Allah is truly All-Forgiving, Most Merciful"** Forgiveness is not the end of the sentence. A person who is only forgiven has been spared. This pair of names promises being spared and then given something besides.

### Which event does this verse answer

Leading authorities differ, and the difference turns out to be harmless. Most of them relate the verse to what came just before it: the demand that the chiefs of Quraysh put to the Prophet through his uncle Abu Talib, that he first remove the poor people he sat with, since they could not bear to sit beside them, and that then they would come and listen. It was Umar ibn al-Khattab who advised that this would be no great matter. If the chiefs asked, the poor could step aside for a sitting, hear the word of Allah, and perhaps believe. The revelation in the previous verses refused that advice outright, and called it cruelty and injustice. Umar then understood how serious his suggestion had been, and came to apologise for it. These verses were sent down to comfort him. In their gist, the Prophet is told to assure such people that there is no retribution for a mistake, that they will be blessed besides, and that a Muslim who does evil in ignorance, then is alerted, repents and watches himself afterwards, is forgiven what went before and is not deprived of blessing in this world or the next.

Some commentators take the verse differently, as a free-standing rule for anyone who sins, then feels shame, then repents and corrects himself. A little thought shows the two readings do not fight. It is agreed that an injunction of the Qur'an revealed against the background of one particular event, but whose words and subject are general, is not chained to that event. It keeps the force of a general rule. So even if the verse came about this episode, it stands open for every sinner who wakes up after the fact.

### How wide the word "ignorantly" reaches

One might hear the promise as narrow: it covers a person who did not know, and leaves out the man who sinned with his eyes open. The wording resists that. The Arabic noun used here is not the plain opposite of knowledge. It is used in opposition to forbearance and dignity, for ignorance shown in conduct, the behaviour of someone who has not thought about the end of the act. That is exactly what a sin is whenever anyone commits one. Hence the saying of certain pious elders that whoever acts against a command given by Allah and his Messenger is ignorant, in this practical sense, whether or not he was informed. And countless clear statements of the Qur'an and sound reports establish that every sin can be covered by repentance, done in heedlessness or in knowledge, deliberately, out of self-wickedness, or following one's own desire.

### What repentance and mending require

The promise in this verse is conditioned on two things: repentance, and the correction of the deed. Repentance is remorse. There is a hadith to that effect: repentance is another name for being ashamed of what was done. As for the correction of the deed, it means that what happened will not be repeated. That takes a firm resolve to stay away from the sin, and a habit of auditing one's conduct, and it also takes settling what the sin left unsettled.

So the way is prepared for those who fear the gathering, and they are the people of taqwa, and those who live in awe of their Lord, and who dread the terrible day of reckoning (13:21, 23:57). They are the ones described in the verse of the cave, who call on their Lord morning and evening, and the same Lord who has said: "Call on Me, I will respond to your invocation" (40:60). That is what supplication is worth here. The answer to these chiefs is the answer of Nuh to his people, who said: "Shall we believe in you, when the meekest of the people follow you?" (26:111). He said their account was for Allah and not for him.

The practical side of mending is spelled out at some length. Obligations that belong to Allah and were left undone through heedlessness have to be made up. Prayers, that is, the salah, and fasts, the sawm, missed out of laziness are replaced by making them up. Zakah unpaid is paid now. If there was a shortcoming in the sacrifice, the qurbani, or in the charity at the breaking of Ramadan, that is settled. A hajj that was fard on the person and never performed is performed now, and if he cannot do it in person, he arranges for it to be done on his behalf, and if he has neither the means to arrange a proxy nor the time to make up what he owes while he lives, then he leaves a will, so that his heirs pay the ransom of what he owed or arrange the pilgrimage for him.

The rights of Allah's servants go the same way. Property taken unlawfully is returned to its owner, or he is asked to forgive it. Pain caused by word or hand is answered by asking the person who was hurt to pardon. If that is no longer possible, because he has died or gone somewhere unknown, then the way out is to keep praying for his forgiveness before Allah steadily. It may be hoped that the holder of the right will be satisfied, and that the debt will be lifted from the one who could not reach him in his lifetime.

### The mercy that was written down

The scale of this is given in a report narrated by Abu Hurayrah, that the Messenger of Allah said: when Allah finished the creation, he wrote, in a Book that is with him above the Throne, his Arsh: "My mercy prevails over my anger." It is recorded by al-Bukhari and Muslim, and in the collection of Ahmad, and it is in the two sahihs besides. Salman said that he found it written in the Torah, that when Allah created the heavens and the earth and what is in them, he divided his mercy into a hundred parts. One part he spread over the whole creation. Every trace of tenderness you meet among people, animals and other created things comes from that one part: the love between parent and child, between brothers and sisters, between husbands and wives, between relatives, neighbours and friends. The ninety-nine parts he kept for himself. Other reports give the same content as a hadith of the Prophet, which shows how far this mercy was meant to reach.

Set against that, no act of worship or obedience is good enough to be presented to Allah as it stands, by an angel or by a human. Deeds looked at on their own do not bear inspection. Looked at in relation to the highest of the high, what we managed was not much better than bad. Still, a person should be thankful for what he was able to do, because nobody is free of real fault unless Allah protects him. Justice would then leave nobody safe from a general punishment. What actually happens is that every human being is showered with blessings all the time, and that is the direct outcome of the mercy which the Lord and nurturer of the universe wrote down as his own responsibility.

### The inner reading

One Sufi treatment of this verse draws a line between two kinds of people. The faithful look first at the artifacts and the signs, and reach Allah through them. The recognizers reach him first, and then return from him to the signs. The address is put on the lips of Allah: "O Muhammad", and he is told to convey the greeting of peace to those who believe by way of the signs, while those who find Allah without intermediary and without the artifacts receive it without one. That last kind is what is meant by the word: "Peace, a word from an ever-merciful Lord" (36:58). The Pir of the Tariqah said, in effect, that whoever recognises Allah through artifacts leans on secondary causes, whoever recognises him through the attributes is confined by what is reported, whoever recognises him by allusion is still looking for company, and whoever is taken hold of by him is protected from himself. Al-Wasiti said that they reached worship through his mercy, and not the other way round, and that whatever they attained with him came to them through mercy rather than through their own acts. For the Prophet said: "Not even I, unless Allah envelops me with his mercy."

It has come in a report, in the first person, that Allah says: you called on me and I answered you, you asked me and I gave you, you turned your back on me and I let you be, you ran off and I kept watch over you, you disobeyed me and I veiled you, come back to me and I welcome you. This is what the greeting of peace in the verse rests on.

The passage as a whole keeps its ear open for those who call on their Lord morning and evening, in the sense given by Said bin al-Musayyib, al-Hasan and Qatadah, that the wording refers to the obligatory prayers, sought with sincerity in acts of worship and obedience, seeking the generous face of Allah. They are occupied with remembrance, and their rank in this life is not the question. When the idolators of Quraysh said: is it these that Allah has favoured from among us, they were repeating the objection of the people of Nuh, and the same answer closes. Heraclius, emperor of Rome, asked Abu Sufyan whether the nobles of his people or the weak followed Muhammad, and Abu Sufyan said: rather the weak. Heraclius said: such is the case with the followers of the messengers.

### In short

- The poor believers who were to be cleared out of the sitting are the first addressees of a divine greeting of peace, and that is the answer to the chiefs' demand.
- "Your Lord has written mercy on himself" is a promise backed by the name Lord, and preserved in writing, so it is not a favour that can be withdrawn on a mood.
- Sin is called acting ignorantly in conduct, not in information, so the door of repentance is open to the deliberate sinner as much as to the heedless one.
- Repentance needs remorse, and mending needs restitution: missed acts of worship made up, zakah, hajj and sacrifice settled, and the rights of people returned or pardoned.
- The reports about the hundred parts of mercy, and the writing above the Throne, are the background that makes "All-Forgiving, Most Merciful" a large promise rather than a polite one.

55.text:
This is how We make Our signs clear, so the way of the wicked may become distinct

This verse is the hinge at the end of the passage. It steps back and names what has just been done.

### Phrase by phrase

**"This is how We make Our signs clear"** In the same way that the earlier rulings, arguments and stories were set out, the Qur'an is expounded in detail: commands, prohibitions, and what follows each of them. Whatever a responsible person needs explained, in the affairs of this life and of religion, is explained.

**"so the way of the wicked may become distinct"** The path of those who defy the prophets is made apparent and clear, so that it can be seen for what it is and avoided. Truth becomes manifest so that it can be worked out in deeds. A variant reading takes the verb as addressed to the Prophet himself, so that the sense is: so that you may discern the way of the wicked. On either reading, the exposition of the signs sorts the roads rather than forcing the traveller.

The concrete case named here is the way of the idolaters, and the folk of Uyaynah, and the question being asked about them is why they do not believe once the road is that visible.

### Why distinctness, and not compulsion

There is a deliberate design in the way guidance is offered in this world. Some people demanded miracles before they would accept the Prophet. Others believed on hearing the verses recited. That test goes on in every era. Allah does not appear in physical form now. He advances his arguments through the bearer of the truth, cast in words, so that they can be put before people. A nature that is still alive sees the glow of his Lord in those arguments and bows to it. A nature wrapped in artificial veils cannot find Allah through his words, cannot see him through reasoning, and so wants him to appear bodily, in an observable shape. That is not possible in a world of trial. Only the person who can recognise him while he is still invisible finds him, and the one who insists on seeing him here faces spiritual destitution of the most extreme kind.

That explains a habit worth noticing. People who carefully avoid the truth accuse those who accept it of every kind of wrongdoing, to prove that they themselves are better. They cannot see their own transgressions, but if a truthful person slips, the slip is magnified to show that everyone rallying to the quest for truth is unreliable. The reality is the reverse. Believers who have given up untruth and taken the truth tread the path of faith and righteousness, and in accordance with the will of Allah they become entitled to inspiration for the betterment of their present position, and share in his bounties. Those who keep clear of the truth only prove by their actions that they have no interest in that path. Even when they are deprived of guidance their bravado does not end, and that effrontery is the greatest crime in this world. Allah speaks in the language of symbols, and a symbol is useful only to somebody who wants to read it. Guidance is available only to somebody who is eager for it.

### What is not in the Prophet's hand

The same exposition is what makes the demand for punishment look absurd. Say: I have been forbidden to worship those you call on besides Allah, and I will not chase your desires the way you want me to. If I did that, I would be misguided, and not one of those who are rightly guided. Say: I am on clear proof from my Lord, and you deny it. I do not have what you are hurrying to get, and the decision belongs to Allah alone, who declares the truth and is the best of judges. If the torment they ask for were in his hand, the matter would have been settled between them at once.

A question is worth asking here, because a famous hadith seems at first to pull the other way. Aishah asked the Messenger of Allah whether he had met a day harder than the day of Uhud. He told her that his people had troubled him greatly, and that the worst of it was the day at al-Aqabah, when he had gone to Ibn Abd Yalil bin Abd Kulal and received no answer. He left in heavy sorrow and did not relax until he found himself at Qarn ath-Thaalib, where he raised his head and saw a cloud shading him unexpectedly. He looked up and saw Jibril in it, who called out that Allah had heard what his people had said to him and how they had answered him, and had sent the Angel of the Mountains, so that he could order him to do whatever he wished with them. The angel greeted him and offered the same choice: if he wished, al-Akhshabayn, the two mountains to the north and south of Makkah, would be let fall on them. The Prophet said: no. He hoped that Allah would raise from among them descendants who worship Allah alone and associate nothing with him. That is the wording of Muslim, and the hadith is in the two sahihs.

So how does the hadith sit with the verse? The answer given is that the verse says only this: if the punishment they were asking for were in the Prophet's hand at that time, he would have brought it down on them as they asked. In the hadith, the disbelievers had not asked him to bring a torment down at all. An angel with charge of the mountains came and offered him the choice, and he declined it and asked for respite, out of compassion. The two reports are about different moments and different people, and neither puts the reckoning in anyone's hand but Allah's.

### The knowledge that makes every road visible

The passage closes by handing back what the demand for a sign had assumed. The treasuries and the unseen were refused to anyone but Allah at the start of this passage, and they are refused again here: with him are the keys of the ghayb, which none knows but he. Al-Bukhari recorded a hadith in which Salim bin Abdullah reports from his father that the Prophet counted the keys of the unseen as five, and said that no one but Allah knows them. Then he recited the verse: "Verily, Allah! With him alone is the knowledge of the hour, he sends down the rain, and he knows what is in the wombs. No person knows what he will earn tomorrow, and no person knows in what land he will die. Verily, Allah is All-Knower, All-Aware" (31:34).

His knowledge covers whatever is on the land and in the sea, so that not even the weight of an atom escapes him, and not a leaf falls without his knowing its movements, which leaves the living, and leaves us. "Allah knows the fraud of the eyes, and all that the breasts conceal" (40:19). A way of conduct is not hidden from that knowledge while it is being chosen, and it will not be hidden when it is finished. That is how the signs are made clear, and that is how the way of the wicked becomes distinct.

### In short

- The verse states the purpose of the whole passage: the signs are expounded so that roads become visible, not so that anyone is driven.
- Two readings of the clause are kept side by side: that the way of the sinners be clear and avoided, and that the Prophet discern it.
- In a world of trial Allah gives arguments in words, and only the person who wants to read them reads them.
- The torment the chiefs demanded was never in the Prophet's hand, and the offer of the two mountains at Qarn ath-Thaalib shows him refusing what was given to him, so the verse and the hadith agree.
- The keys of the unseen stay with Allah, and the same knowledge that hides the hour sees the trick of the eyes, which is what makes every path distinct.

56.text:
Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “I have been forbidden to worship those you invoke besides Allah.” Say, “I will not follow your desires, for I then would certainly be astray and not one of those ˹rightly˺ guided.”

Two sentences of refusal, put in the mouth of the Prophet, and both begin with the same command: say.

### Phrase by phrase

**"I have been forbidden"** The prohibition is located in the Qur'an. Nothing is being invented here for the sake of argument. The one who refuses has been told to refuse, and he says so out loud.

**"to worship those you invoke besides Allah"** The ones addressed are worshipped by being called on, and the word for worship covers the calling, the hoping and the relying that go with it. The idols of the Arabs are the plain case, and the sentence does not stop with them.

**"I will not follow your desires"** The desires named are the wish that he stop preaching Allah's oneness, the wish that the idols be honoured, and the wish that a man like Salman and his fellow believers be pushed away from his sitting so that the chiefs can be pleased. To grant any of that would be following them, not leading them.

**"for I then would certainly be astray and not one of those guided"** The order of the two halves is worth keeping. Going astray comes first. Losing guidance is the description of the state he has entered, and not a separate punishment added afterwards. The sense is that he is astray from the path of truth, and so is not guided to it at all. Whoever follows his desires without proof from Allah is in that condition, whoever he is.

### What the refusal is worth

This is the answer to the demand made at the start of the passage. The chiefs would accept the message only if the Prophet moved the poor believers out and produced the sign they asked for. Both requests are answered with a single principle: there is a line he will not cross, and it is not his line to move. What he worships is settled by revelation, and what he wants is settled by the same revelation. A prophet who negotiates with his own desires would be indistinguishable from the people he is warning.

One commentator notes that the address here is aimed at ʿUyaynah and his folk, that is, at the men who were making the demands. The point of the verse is wider than the occasion, since it states the standing condition of anyone who claims to be guided while he chases what he likes.

### The wishful thinking that becomes worship

There is a slower kind of idolatry than bowing to a stone, and it is worth naming here because the verse cuts it off at the root. What a man wants to be true, and takes to be real, is far too often promoted into something he worships. Sometimes, to dodge the consequences of having neglected his duties, he takes somebody as a favourite of Allah and expects that man to stand up for him before his Lord and to put in a word for him. Sometimes he imagines that this man has a charismatic or supernatural greatness of his own, and that attaching himself to the man will make up for what he has failed to do. Sometimes, out of sheer easy-goingness, he invents a god who is easy of access and can be pleased with small things. All of that is supposition, and a supposition can never lead anybody to reality.

What makes the position worse is that such people then challenge those who have rallied to the real Lord of the Universe. They dare to put it to the believers in this form: if all this greatness and majesty belong to the one Allah you represent, then make his retribution come down on us, and we should like to see it. They talk like that because they see themselves surrounded by worldly glory, while the people who call others to Allah's oneness own almost nothing. They forget that their comforts are the fruit of their devotion to this world, and that the missionaries of Allah are empty-handed precisely because their yearning for the Hereafter has kept them from stooping to the level of that devotion.

### In short

- The Prophet's refusal is not a bargaining position but a report of what he has been forbidden.
- Following desires is named as the alternative to following revelation, and going astray is described as the shape of that alternative.
- Pushing weak believers out of the sitting would have been one of those desires, and it is refused in the same breath as idolatry.
- Wishful thinking about holy men, intercession and an easy god is treated here as a kind of worship, and it is refused on the same grounds.

57.text:
Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Indeed, I stand on a clear proof from my Lord—yet you have denied it. That ˹torment˺ you seek to hasten is not within my power. It is only Allah Who decides ˹its time˺. He declares the truth. And He is the Best of Judges.”

The claim made here is not that he is certain and they are wrong. It is that he is standing on something, and that something is not himself.

### Phrase by phrase

**"I stand on a clear proof from my Lord"** A clear proof is a clear statement, something visible in what has been revealed, and the phrase is read as: I have full insight into my matter and my religion. It is the opposite of the desires named in the previous verse. He is not relying on what suits him, and he is not relying on them.

**"yet you have denied it"** The denial is aimed at the Qur'an and at Allah's oneness. The proof has been put in front of them, and they have passed it by.

**"That torment you seek to hasten is not within my power"** They were asking for the punishment to arrive now, as a test of the claim. The answer is that it was never in his hand to hand out. He is a warner, not an executioner.

**"It is only Allah Who decides"** The ruling on whether to punish at once or to respite belongs to him alone. If he wills, he punishes in response to their demand, and if he wills, he gives them time, out of his great wisdom.

**"He declares the truth. And He is the Best of Judges"** One reading takes the verb as: he relates the truth, so that the sentence means that the report he gives is true and his judgement is just, and that he commands only what is right. On either reading the superlative closes the argument: in the reckoning between his servants there is nobody better, and nobody to appeal past.

### Who was asking, and why

According to al-Kalbi, the ones this verse came about are al-Nadr ibn al-Harith and the chiefs of Quraysh. They used to joke with the Prophet and ask him to bring the chastisement on them, the one he had promised. That mocking request is what the verse takes apart. It assumes that the proof offered by a messenger and the power to enforce it belong in the same hand, and they do not. The same assumption produced the demand in the previous verse, that the poor believers be cleared away, since wealth and rank were taken as evidence that Allah was pleased.

What the chiefs had hold of was the ordinary glamour of this world, and the messengers of Allah had nothing of it. Their standing did not come from what they had, and the reckoning of the two did not depend on their permission.

### In short

- A clear proof from Allah is set against desires, and the difference between the two is the whole content of the verse.
- The torment they demanded is not in the Prophet's hand, and the decision about its timing is not negotiable.
- A variant reading makes the verse say that Allah relates the truth, so that his report and his judgement are both in question.
- The mockery of al-Nadr ibn al-Harith and his folk shows what the verse is answering: a demand that proof and punishment arrive on the challengers' schedule.

58.text:
Say ˹also˺, “If what you seek to hasten were within my power, the matter between us would have already been settled. But Allah knows the wrongdoers best.”

The verse finishes the thought of the one before it and then hands the case over.

### Phrase by phrase

**"If what you seek to hasten were within my power"** The supposition is that the punishment were in his possession, which it is not. On that reading the clause is not a boast but a reductio: the thing they keep asking for belongs to somebody else.

**"the matter between us would have already been settled"** If it were his, he would have brought it down at once and been rid of the trouble, and they would have been destroyed. One reading adds the motive: he would have hastened it so that he might find rest.

**"But Allah knows the wrongdoers best"** He knows them, and he knows best how long the respite should run for each of them and when to punish. Settling the matter is not delayed because it is uncertain.

### What the linkage does

The verses before this one answered the demand for punishment with the words "the best of judges", and this verse repeats the point with "Allah knows the unjust best". Immediately after that, the description of Allah's knowledge and power takes over, and the passage turns to what is actually in his hand. The movement of the wording is the argument: the case is removed from the Prophet's shoulders and placed where it belongs, and then the verse states who is qualified to hold it.

One report records that the punishment al-Nadr ibn al-Harith asked for did come, and that he was killed after being taken captive on the day of Badr. That is not offered here as proof that every demand gets an answer on the spot. The point of the verse is that timing was never in the Prophet's control, and one man's death at Badr does not make a schedule for anybody else.

### In short

- The hypothetical is the whole argument: if the torment were his to give, the case would have been closed already.
- The delay is attributed to knowledge, not to inability, and the respite has a measured end that only Allah knows.
- The verse closes the sequence about the demanded sign and hands the decision to the one who judges.
- Badr is named in the reports as the day the asked-for punishment overtook one of those who demanded it.

59.text:
"With Him are the keys of the unseen—no one knows them except Him. And He knows what is in the land and sea."

That is where the verse begins. It goes on to name a leaf falling, a grain in the darkness of the earth, and everything green or dry, and it closes by saying that all of it is written in a perfect Record. After three verses in which the Prophet hands the decision over, this verse states what the one who holds the decision actually knows. It is the widest claim about Allah in this passage, and it is made in four images.

### Phrase by phrase

**"With Him are the keys of the unseen"** The word translated as keys is plural, and its singular can be read two ways. Maftah, with an a, means a treasury, and miftah, with an i, means a key. Both senses are carried by the plural, so some translators write treasures and some write keys, and the outcome is the same, since owning the keys to a treasury is owning the treasury. The phrase "with him" means that they are possessed and held by him alone. He has the exclusive power to bring what they open into existence, and to make it manifest when he decides. Placing "with him" before the rest of the sentence marks that restriction. The next clause then states it outright.

**"no one knows them except him"** The hint becomes a plain statement, driven home so that there is no room for an exemption. The unseen here has a defined sense, which the next section takes up, and most of the doubts raised against the verse are doubts about something else.

**"And He knows what is in the land and sea"** The creatures in the sea and on the land are included, and so is whatever he destroys in them. Naming the two of them is a way of naming the whole universe with everything in it. It is like saying morning and evening for all the time, or east and west for the whole world. Animals, plants and inanimate things are all inside that knowledge.

**"Not even a leaf falls without His knowledge"** He knows the movement of things that have no life at all. What then of the living, and above all of those on whom the divine laws have been laid, human beings and jinn? Every part of the leaf's history is within his knowledge: before it falls, when it falls, and after it falls. He knows how many times it swings and spins in the air, where it lands, and through what circumstances it passes. That a leaf's fall is picked out is also fitting. The fall is the end of its growth and its botanical life, and its last condition stands as a mirror for all the rest.

**"nor a grain in the darkness of the earth"** A grain sown in a field, or buried in the deep dark belly of the earth under a rock, is not outside that knowledge. The order is deliberate. First comes the thing that falls where anybody can see it. Then comes the thing hidden underground.

**"or anything green or dry"** Wet and dry cover every state a thing can be in, and nothing of that kind is left out. In the Arabic, the negation is carried onto the grain clause and onto the wet and the dry by wa-la, and not. The closing exceptive, illa fi kitabin mubin, is read as standing inside the earlier illa ya'lamuha, but he knows it. One affirmation therefore runs through several images.

**"but is written in a perfect Record"** A written book is a manifest book, and what is written stays preserved, leaving nothing to chance, to mistake or to forgetting. Some take the Record to be al-Lawh al-Mahfuz, the Preserved Tablet, where the precise measure and the time of each thing are noted. Some take it to be the divine knowledge itself. The comparison holds either way, because that knowledge is not built on conjecture.

### The five keys

The clause about the keys is read through a hadith that al-Bukhari recorded. In it the Prophet counted the keys of the unseen as five, and said that nobody but Allah knows them. They are the knowledge of the Hour, the descent of the rain, what is in the wombs, what a person will earn tomorrow, and the land in which he will die. The same five are recited in a verse of the surah of Luqman, where all of them are named as Allah's alone (31:34). One reading takes the keys to be the stores of the unseen themselves: rain, vegetation and fruit, and the descent of the punishment they kept asking for, which overtook one of its demanders on the day of Badr. The same knowledge that holds the stores is what makes a leaf and a grain reportable.

### What is not the unseen

Much of the unease around this verse comes from taking al-Ghayb in a loose sense. On that reading it means whatever is simply absent from my knowledge, whether or not somebody else has means of getting at it. Once the word means that, all sorts of practices look like counter-examples. There is astrology, the mathematical divination of fortunes, divination by figures and lines drawn in the sand, and palmistry, all of them harnessed to guess at future events. There is the person who seems to learn things about the future through illumination or inspiration. Then there are the weather forecasters. They examine the drift, power and velocity of the monsoons and announce rain and storms weeks ahead, and are then treated as though they had stepped into the territory of the unseen. Common people reach for these cases and start to doubt the verse, since observation appears to show that others acquire this knowledge too.

The answer given is that the Qur'an's usage is narrower, and the doubts evaporate once it is respected. Knowledge that has to be acquired through means and instruments is not knowledge of the unseen. The forecaster got his information only when the substance of the event had already come into existence and was available to be read. The only difference between him and an ordinary observer is that the sign is not open yet to everybody, and reveals itself to experts through instruments. When it grows stronger it becomes common observation too. That is why a forecaster cannot announce rain two months ahead. The solid evidence of that rain has not presented itself yet. It is also why no physician can tell from a pulse what a patient swallowed a year ago, or will swallow a year hence, because that does not habitually leave a mark. These are things whose existence is foretold by examining traces. Once the traces exist, the matter is observation and not the unseen, however refined the equipment is.

The same holds for the claim that a hidden event can be computed. A man works from existing data and announces that sunrise will be at five forty-one, or that an eclipse will fall on such and such a date. That is something like reading out the arrival board for trains and planes. Determining a time from the speed of something already perceptible is not knowing the unseen. As for astrology and its relatives, the claim to know by that route is deception. One true guess in a hundred false ones is not knowledge.

There is a further refinement. Awareness of this kind stays in the class of estimation and calculation, and the real word for knowledge is reserved for certitude, which none of these methods produce. That is why the records of such predictions are full of errors, and why an honest audit of the whole lot of them comes out badly.

And when part of what belongs to the unseen is given to a prophet through revelation, or to a righteous servant through illumination or inspiration, it has stopped being unseen in the language of the Qur'an. Such material is called news of the unseen, or reports of the unseen, and not the unseen itself. That is the wording of the verse: "That is some of the reports of the unseen which We reveal to you" (11:49). So when this verse states that no one knows the keys except Allah, there is no exception to be carved out of it.

Medicine is put to the test here in a concrete way. When the X-ray was invented it was hoped that the sex of a fetus could be settled, and it did not serve the purpose, and it carried its own harms. Specialists who study the fetus in section view, or who float it in water to read it digitally, are still helpless in the first stretch of pregnancy, when nothing can be known. Even the genetic tests cannot work before a certain stage, and that stage is a matter of observation. Later, predictions are made which are technical approximations at best, sometimes right, sometimes misread, and this is not the certitude the verse is talking about.

### Two attributes no creature shares

The distinctive feature of Islam among the religions is belief in Allah's oneness, and that oneness is not limited to counting him as one. It is believing in him as unique and without equal in all his attributes of perfection, and refusing to take any created being as a sharer in them. Life, knowledge, power, hearing, seeing, will, creation and sustenance belong to that list, and two of them stand out: knowledge and power. His knowledge embraces every existent and every non-existent, open and secret, large and small, atoms and particles, and his power surrounds and controls everything fully and conclusively. The verse before this one and the one after it are both about these two attributes. The tradition names them al-Ilm al-Muhit, the knowledge that encompasses everything, and the knowledge of the unseen besides.

Put the other way round, the claim that an angel's or a messenger's knowledge is all-encompassing hands that creature the status of Allah. In Qur'anic terms that is shirk, and it is the aspect of associating partners that surah Al-Shuʿara puts on the lips of the idolaters on the day of Qiyamah: "By Allah, we were in manifest error when we held you as equals with the Lord of the Worlds" (6:97), and the verse after it belongs to the same confession. That is why the clause about the keys is placed exactly where it is. It is not decoration. It is the line that keeps oneness intact.

The practical conclusion drawn from these two attributes is striking. If a person were to believe in them strongly and completely, and start to imagine them as present before him, then he could not even think of committing a crime. Here is somebody who, in every state, in word and deed, in rest and in movement, is conscious that an All-Knowing, All-Aware, All-Powerful one is watching over him. He knows him outside in and inside out, and he is aware of what the heart intends and what the mind lets pass through it. On that assumption, how could he take even a tiny step towards disobeying his All-Powerful Master? In religious terminology this is known as istihdar, and it has been called the philosopher's stone of the moral life. The verse has been called a sovereign prescription. It is the kind of belief that makes a person a model human being and keeps him one. Its effect is not a theory about the universe. It is a discipline, and a person may say that a discipline is all religion ever asked of him.

### The knowledge that leaves nothing out

Other verses confirm that this all-encompassing knowledge, from which neither a particle nor its condition is excluded, belongs to Allah alone. In the surah of Luqman it is said that Allah will bring forth a thing the weight of a mustard seed, though it be inside a rock or anywhere in the heavens or the earth. The reason given is that Allah is subtle and aware (31:16). In Ayat al-Kursi, the verse of the Throne in surah al-Baqarah, it is said: "They encompass nothing of his knowledge except what he wills" (2:255). In surah Yunus nothing the weight of an atom in the earth or in heaven is said to be hidden from your Lord (10:61). And in surah At-Talaq it is said that Allah encompasses all things in knowledge (65:12). The same point is made about the treasures: "We have treasures of everything, but We send them down in a particular measure" (15:21).

Two sentences in this verse therefore do two different jobs, and they are ordered with a system. The first states the knowledge of the unseen, which nothing else shares. The rest describe ilm al-shahadah, the knowledge of what is present and existing, in a way that lets no particle stand outside it. That is the shape of the claim: a knowledge that nothing fresh or dry escapes, and a power that owns the keys.

### In short

- The keys of the unseen are both the treasuries and the means of access to them, and both senses belong in the wording.
- The verse is read through the hadith of the five keys, and the five are what no creature can get at.
- Forecasts, instruments and computations are not counter-examples, because they read traces that already exist, and what Allah discloses to a prophet stops being unseen.
- Allah's knowledge of the leaf, the grain and everything wet or dry is a claim about the whole universe, recorded in a Preserved Tablet rather than left to chance.
- The verse is a prescription as much as a description. The discipline it aims at is simple, and whoever really holds these two attributes before him cannot bring himself to sin.

60.text:
"He is the One Who calls back your souls by night and knows what you do by day, then revives you daily to complete your appointed term."

The rest of the verse says that to him everyone returns at the last, and that he will then tell them what they used to do. The verse that follows the keys of the unseen does not argue about what Allah knows. It points at something everybody does twice a day, and draws the conclusion from it.

### Phrase by phrase

**"He is the One Who calls back your souls by night"** Sleep is a taking away, and the same verb covers death itself. He brings death to his servants during the sleep of the night, since sleep is a minor death. The same verb covers death itself, and another verse spells out the distinction: it is Allah who takes the souls at the time of their death, and those that do not die during their sleep, and he keeps the souls for which he has ordained death, and sends the rest on for a term appointed (39:42). Both kinds of taking are named together, and that is the point of the wording here. The verse about Isa uses the same idea, where Allah says: "O Isa, I will take you and raise you to Myself" (3:55).

**"and knows what you do by day"** The deeds and actions performed in the day are not outside the knowledge claimed in the previous verse. The verse covers movements and idleness, day and night. It is the same to him whether a person conceals his speech or declares it openly, whether he hides by night or goes about freely by day (13:10).

**"then revives you daily to complete your appointed term"** He raises you again, that is, wakes you up in the day, on the reading of Mujahid, Qatadah and As-Suddi. The appointed term is the life span of each person. One gloss adds the reason for the return, namely that you carry out your tasks until the fixed period is over. Another reading takes the term to be the point at which both your lifespan and your provision are finished.

**"To Him is your ultimate return"** On the Day of Qiyamah, after death.

**"then He will inform you of what you used to do"** This is not raw information. He will reward you, good for good and evil for evil, and the telling and the settling of the account come in the same breath.

### Sleep as a daily rehearsal

The example is chosen because nobody has to be told that it works. Every night and every morning a person witnesses his own rising from a simulated death, and the verse argues from that to the collective death and the collective rising after it. The Supreme Being who can do the first can do the second. With his most perfect power, this is how it shall be, and so the verse ends with the return, the reckoning of deeds, and then the rewards and the punishments.

A related note adds that sleep suspends the body in the way death would, and that this is stated in a hadith as well as in the verse. The world, on this reading, has been built to supply practical examples of the very things people are being asked to believe. A person who does not close his eyes and screen off his mind with false veils will find demonstrations of them across the universe. Branches emerge from a trunk and leaves sprout from the branches, but their joints are different, because the Creator knows that the branches have to stay attached while the leaves have to detach and fall. If it were otherwise, the leaves would never separate, and the whole system of bringing new life to the tree each year would be upset. A seed, once sown, finds in the soil around it all the ingredients from which it will grow into a full tree. So if he attends to the state of a leaf and of a seed, the claim that he is inattentive to the state of a human being makes no sense.

### Why night and day are a mercy

The same pairing appears elsewhere in the Qur'an as an argument from design. It is out of his mercy that he made the night and the day, so that people may rest in one of them and seek his bounty in the other (28:73). And the night was made as a covering, and the day as a means of livelihood (78:10-11). Read next to this verse, the arrangement is not merely kind. It is legible. The hours that take a person away and give him back to himself are the same hours in which his deeds are being noted.

### What the messengers' knowledge does not prove

The discussion of the unseen in the previous verse needs one guard rail here. Allah had given his messengers, and the last of them above all, knowledge of many unseen things that surpassed what all the angels and the other prophets were given. That does not narrow the gap at all. The knowledge of no one can be equal to Allah's, and it never can be. Otherwise this would be the same excess the Christians committed in their reverence for their prophet, when they began to equate him with Allah. In the language of the Qur'an that is shirk, and the verses about the keys and about sleep are both there to close that door.

### In short

- Sleep is a taking of the soul that stops short of death, and the verse uses it because everybody experiences the return.
- The knowledge claimed for the day and the night is the same knowledge stated in the verse about the keys, now applied to the person himself.
- The appointed term is the end of a lifespan, and the return after it is followed by being told what one used to do, which means being repaid.
- Honouring a prophet past the point of creatureliness is named here as the excess that turns into shirk.

61.text:
He reigns supreme over all of His creation, and sends recording-angels, watching over you. When death comes to any of you, Our angels take their soul, never neglecting this duty

One sentence covers the whole of a life: who is above whom, who is written down, and who does the collecting.

### Phrase by phrase

**"He reigns supreme over all of his creation"** The divine name here is the Vanquisher, the one who controls everything, so that all things are subservient to his grace, greatness and majesty. He is described as dominant and irresistible, to whom everything is subjugated, and as above his servants in a manner that befits his majesty. That last phrase is doing real work: the being above them is not a place or a posture.

**"and sends recording-angels, watching over you"** These are guardians over mankind. For every person there are angels in succession, before and behind him, guarding him by the command of Allah (13:11), and watching his deeds and recording them (82:10). Two receivers take what a person says, one sitting on the right and one on the left, and not a word does he utter but there is a watcher ready by him (50:17-18). One account has it that there are two angels in the day and two in the night, and that what they record is both the good and the bad.

**"When death comes to any of you, Our angels take their soul"** The appointed hour is when a person's lifespan ends and he is dying, and the angels in charge of that job are called "our messengers", which makes the taking of a soul an errand rather than a seizure. Ibn Abbas and several others held that the Angel of Death is helped by angels who pull the soul from the body. Once it reaches the throat, he captures it. A variant reading of the verb lets the sentence say that they take him fully, or that they cause him to die, and both senses point at the same act.

**"never neglecting this duty"** They do not fall short of what they have been commanded, and they do not delay the time of death by a fraction. They guard the soul of the dead person and carry it wherever Allah wills. If he was among the righteous it goes up to Illiyyin, and if he was among the wicked and the sinners it goes down to Sijjin.

### What the angels say at the bedside

A hadith recorded by Ahmad, transmitted from Abu Hurayrah, describes the same moment from the other side. The angels attend a dying person. If he was righteous, they say to his soul: O pure soul from a pure body, come out honoured, and take the good news of rest and contentment from a Lord who is not angry at you. They keep saying it until the soul leaves the body. Then they raise it toward heaven and ask that its door be opened. Something is asked at the door: who is this? The answer names the soul. The reply is a welcome, an entry with honour, and the same good news again. This goes on until the soul reaches the heaven above which there is nothing. If the dying person was evil, the angels say: O wicked soul from a wicked body, come out in disgrace. They tell it to expect boiling fluid, a fluid dark and murky and intensely cold, and other torments of the same kind, all together, matching what it did. This is repeated until the soul leaves. It is raised up, and the door is asked to open. The answer is no welcome and a return in disgrace, and the doors of heaven are not opened for it. Then it is thrown down until it comes back to the grave. There the righteous man is made to sit up, and is told as before. The evil man is made to sit up too, and is told the same kind of thing.

The detail worth noticing is the change of voice. In the verse the angels are "our messengers", and in the hadith they are the ones who speak, and in both cases the person dying is the one being addressed. Nothing in either text puts the honour or the disgrace of the soul in the hands of its family, its rank or its wealth.

### In short

- Allah's being above his servants is stated with a qualifier, so that supremacy is not imagined as a position.
- The recording angels are guardians in succession, and the record they keep is of words and deeds, good and bad.
- The taking of the soul is done by angels with assistants, on a description transmitted from Ibn Abbas, and it is never late by a fraction.
- The hadith of the pure soul and the wicked soul shows what is said at the moment of death, and that the doors of heaven open on the soul's character and not on its pedigree.

62.text:
"Then they are ˹all˺ returned to Allah—their True Master. Judgment is His ˹alone˺. And He is the Swiftest Reckoner."

Three clauses, and they close the whole passage about the unseen, the leaf, the sleep and the soul.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Then they are all returned to Allah"** This is read in two ways. It can be the return of each soul when its death comes, and it can be the return of the whole creation on the Day of Judgement, when they are presented to him and he subjects them to his just decision. The two are not in competition, since the verse is about where everything ends up.

**"their True Master"** He is their master and their possessor, the true one, the eternal one, the just. Another reading takes "their Lord, the Just" as a claim about who is entitled to be worshipped: he is their real master, whom they ought to have worshipped and did not worship as he ought to be worshipped. On that reading the sentence also says something about the alternatives, which is that objects of worship other than Allah are void.

**"Judgment is his alone"** The decree that will be carried out in their case belongs to him and to nobody else, which answers the demand made four verses back for a punishment delivered on the challengers' timetable. Say: those of the earlier times and the later ones will all be gathered together for an appointed day of a known time (56:49-50). They will be gathered so that not one of them is left behind (18:47), and the judgement will be made without any weight being lost, and then it is said: and your Lord wrongs no one (18:49).

**"And He is the Swiftest Reckoner"** He reckons with the whole of creation swiftly. One gloss, resting on a hadith to that effect, puts it as half a day of the days of this world, and another says he takes all of them to account in a single day. The two agree in what matters: nothing queues up in front of him, and no case waits while another is heard.

### The question the last clause answers

A reader could stop at "Judgment is his alone" and ask a practical question. How is it possible for one God to take the reckoning of age-long deeds of billions of human beings, and to remember each of them? The answer the wording gives is that the question itself is the error. Reasoning about what Allah does by analogy with what people do is ignorance, and he does it in no time. The clause is not there to reassure a nervous accountant. It is there to remove a comparison.

What is left, at the end of the passage, is a pair of descriptions that hold each other in place. He is the Just, so the reckoning will not be bent. He is the swift, so it will not be postponed, and the delay that made the mockers confident was never a reprieve that he was struggling to administer.

### The master who is also the guardian

The word translated as master carries more than ownership. Before this passage began, the same surah told the Prophet to greet the poor believers with peace, on the ground that his Lord had taken mercy upon himself. That is the shape of the sentence here too: he is the sovereign and the judge of judges, and something besides that. He is their master and guardian, and he comes to their help whenever they need him. The reckoning and the mercy were both written down, and the verse names the second before it names the first.

### In short

- The return is both the individual one at death and the collective one at the Judgement, and the verse is comfortable with both.
- Judgment belongs to Allah alone, which is the standing answer to those who wanted the torment scheduled to their convenience.
- Speed is asserted against a presumption of scale: billions of lives do not make a queue for the one who knows the leaf and the grain.
- "Their True Master" keeps guardianship inside the verdict, so that the passage about knowledge and power ends where the passage about mercy began.

63.text:
Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Who rescues you from the darkest times on land and at sea? He ˹alone˺ you call upon with humility, openly and secretly: “If You rescue us from this, we will be ever grateful.”"

The passage has just stated Allah's knowledge and his power in the abstract. Now it takes one case, the case of a person in genuine danger, and asks what he actually does.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Say"** The question is put to the disbelievers of Makkah, and it is a question whose answer the asker already knows. Their own behaviour supplies it.

**"Who rescues you from the darkest times on land and at sea"** The word translated here as the darkest times is the plural of darkness, and the plural is needed because English has no plural for the noun. Darkness comes in several kinds: the dark of night, the dark of a rain cloud, the dark of a dust storm, and the dark under the waves of the sea. All of them are included. Another way of putting the phrase is the hardships and tumults of travel by land and by sea.

**"He alone you call upon with humility, openly and secretly"** In that situation they forget their idols and call on nobody but Allah. At times the confession of helplessness comes out loud, and at times it stays in the heart of hearts, where no one else can hear it. One reading takes the pairing to mean that they call on him in public and in private, humbling themselves, and that the supplication is made with no partner mixed into it. In the surah of the Night Journey the whole scene is set out. He drives the ships through the sea so that people may seek his bounty, and when harm strikes them on the water the partners they called on vanish and only he is left, and when he brings them safely to land they turn away, since man is by nature ungrateful. Then comes the question: do they feel safe from his causing a side of the land to swallow them, or from his sending a storm of stones against them, or safe from his sending them back to sea a second time, sending a hurricane of wind and drowning them for their disbelief (17:66-69)? The same moment is put more briefly in the surah of the Ants (17:67).

**"If You rescue us from this, we will be ever grateful"** The promise is made in the middle of the danger: if he brings them out, they will be among the thankful, they will take him as the real rescuer, and they will not ascribe any partner to him. The verb in this clause is read two ways in the reports, so that the sentence can be taken as a direct address, rescue us, or as a report about them, if he rescues them. The surah of Jonas sets the whole scene out, the ship, the fair wind, the joy, then the stormy wind and the waves closing in from every side, and the moment when a man thinks he is surrounded, and then calls on Allah with faith made pure for him alone, saying: "If you deliver us from this, we shall truly be of the grateful" (10:22). And in the surah of the Ants the question is asked in its plainest form: is not he who guides you in the darknesses of the land and the sea, and who sends the winds ahead of his mercy, better than your gods? Is there any god with Allah? (27:63)

### Why the question works

The argument is not that the idolaters were honest in distress. It is that distress strips a person, and that what he then says is the truth he hides the rest of the time. No other living creature meets as much trouble as human beings do, and the reason is that a person is meant to be put through hard conditions so that the artificial and unreal thoughts are driven out of his mind and he can see his own nature. Whenever he confronts a major trouble he begins to call on Allah single-mindedly. All the man-made veils are swept away. He realises that in this world he is completely humble and helpless, and that power belongs to Allah alone. Then the trouble lifts. He goes back to his neglect and his recklessness, and he is the same man he was before it came.

The verse quotes them at the moment when they are most lucid, because that is the moment that will be brought into court later. Their own words at the mast, in the dark, are the evidence against them in the sunlight.

### The lesson runs the other way as well

A lesson with the rasp of a lash is in it for believers, and it is this: those people were prompt. They turned to Allah the instant they had nothing else to turn to, and we are not, despite claiming faith in his absolute power. Our attention is fixed on the material support we hope will get us out of trouble. We do not take idols, icons and images as our saviours, and yet the many support systems, logistics, mechanised rescue squads on land, at sea and in the air, and the backup of instruments close by and far away, have become no less than idols for us. We are so impressed with them and so taken up with them that we barely spare a thought for Allah and his perfect power.

The other verses about the same scene add what is missing from the idols' column. It is Allah who sends the winds as heralds of his mercy, and it is out of his mercy that night and day were made, and not one of the partners they call on has ever answered a prayer made in a storm.

### In short

- The verse asks a question about behaviour rather than belief, because the answer is visible in what the idolaters themselves do in danger.
- The darknesses are many, and the plural is deliberate: night, rain cloud, dust storm and the sea under the waves are all included.
- In distress a person is briefly a monotheist, and the verse quotes him at that moment to use his own words against his later shirk.
- The same passage carries a rebuke for believers, whose material supports have quietly taken the place of idols.

64.text:
Say, “˹Only˺ Allah rescues you from this and any other distress, yet you associate others with Him ˹in worship˺.”

One sentence takes back what the previous verse put on the table, and then names what they did with it.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Say, Allah rescues you from this"** Allah himself takes the initiative here, since the answer to the question was never going to be denied. Their own experience had already given it: nothing that they worshipped came up to help them in that hour, and only Allah did.

**"and any other distress"** The deliverance is not limited to the storm. Every distress, grief and turmoil of the same kind is in his hands, and so is the removal of hardships, troubles and anxieties generally. This is stated in other words in the surah of prostrating, where it is said that he will make them taste the lesser punishment before the greater one, so that they may return (32:21). And in surah Ash-Shura: "The hardship that reaches you is an outcome of your evil deeds, while many of them Allah forgives" (42:30).

**"yet you associate others with him"** The people of Makkah are the ones addressed. In times of comfort they go back to shirk and to the worship of false gods, which is the strange betrayal and the fatal ignorance the verse stands on. It is one thing to forget in ease. It is another to be shown an open sign, to be given relief after distress, and then to put the partners back where they were.

### The shapes that shirk takes

Shirk is, at bottom, reposing one's faith in some entity other than Allah, just as tawhid is directing a person's entire faith to him alone. The worship of deities and of other phenomena is one form of it. Another is ingratitude instead of gratitude, which is also called shirk in the wording here, since they promised thanks and did not pay it. The most common form is subtler: a man makes a deity of himself and comes to have faith only in his own efforts. When he is vain about what he has achieved, his trust is in his own work. When he thinks his earnings were generated by him, his faith is in his own talents. When he overlooks another person's right, he assumes that nobody can call him to account for it, and when he dares to oppress someone, he assumes that he has full power over that person and that nothing will stop him. All of this is vanity and pride, and pride, before Allah, is the worst kind of shirk, because indulging in it amounts to putting oneself in the position of God.

### What the hardships mean, and what they do not

The hardships and accidents that meet people here are mostly the result of their own evil deeds, and they are a mild sampling of the punishment of the Hereafter. Seen from that angle they are in a way a mercy, since through them heedless people are given a jolt, so that they may take the occasion to survey their evil deeds and think about how not to fall into them again, and so stay safe from the greater and harsher punishment hereafter. A saying of the Prophet puts the scale of it in a hard frame. He said, by the one in whose hand his life lies, that an ordinary scratch from a piece of wood, a faltering step, or an itching in a vein, are all after-effects of some sin, while the sins that Allah forgives are many. Al-Baydawi explains the difference this leaves: the diseases and calamities of criminals and sinners are traces of their sins, while those of people protected from sin exist to test their patience and fortitude and to raise them to higher ranks in Paradise. Everyone else is not free of sin either, so what people meet is a consequence in one form or another.

The conclusion is not that medicine, treatment and rescue work are useless. The point is that a person should believe in Allah as the prime mover and maker of things and happenings, and should use the means at the same time, taking them for nothing but his blessings, since every means and instrument is his creation, serving human beings under his command and will. Fire, air, water, dust and every force on the face of the earth are subservient to that command. Unless he wills it, fire cannot burn, water cannot extinguish, medicine cannot benefit, and food cannot hurt. What is being warned against is the attitude in which the means are trusted instead of the one who made them.

### In short

- Allah answers the question of the previous verse himself, and widens it from one storm to every distress.
- The Qur'an reads relief as evidence, so that going back to partners after being rescued is not a lapse of memory but a betrayal.
- Shirk includes ingratitude, and, in its commonest form, a person's faith in himself.
- Hardships are a lesser punishment and a summons to return, and the remedy is turning to Allah with repentance and a firm resolve, while still using every lawful means.

65.text:
Say, “He ˹alone˺ has the power to unleash upon you a torment from above or below you or split you into ˹conflicting˺ factions and make you taste the violence of one another.” See how We vary the signs, so perhaps they will comprehend

This is the widest of the three claims in the passage, and it is the one the Prophet himself reacted to out loud.

### Phrase by phrase

**"He alone has the power to unleash upon you a torment from above"** To punish a criminal Allah needs no police, no army and no helper of the kind a mortal ruler needs. The punishment from above is what comes down: stones, pebbles, wind, fire, flood, and, on one reading of the early commentators, cruel rulers and merciless officials set over a people.

**"or below you"** That is, from beneath your feet: the earth caving in and swallowing, water forcing up out of the ground, drowning, and, on the same reading, the dishonesty, idling and treachery of one's own subordinates and servants.

**"or split you into conflicting factions"** The third kind does not come from either direction. It spreads out from within, and it is the one the verse then glosses: confusion in party strife, a nation breaking up into parties and groups that confront each other. The word used for confusion comes from a root that means to hide or to cover up, and it is in that sense that clothing covers the body, and that a meaning can be hidden when what is said is not open and clear. The word for a faction is a plural form meaning adherence, following, being a partisan of somebody, as in the verse: and Ibrahim was of the company of Noah (37:83). In ordinary usage it means a group that gathers for a purpose and whose members help one another to get it, which is what a party or a faction is.

**"and make you taste the violence of one another"** Some of them will experience torture and murder at the hands of others, on the explanation given by Ibn Abbas and others. The fighting is itself named as a punishment, not as an accident that happened to fall out of the situation.

**"See how We vary the signs, so perhaps they will comprehend"** The signs are made clear, plain and duly explained, so that people understand them, and so that they realise that what they themselves follow is falsehood and what has been brought to them is the truth. The passage about the leaf, the grain and the soul ends here with an appeal to comprehension, because nothing in it is meant to stay abstract.

### Three punishments, and the warning inside the grammar

The three kinds are laid out as punishment from above, punishment from beneath, and punishment that spreads from within. The noun for punishment is left indefinite, and it is admitted by the rules of Arabic grammar that an indefinite noun in a warning of this sort signals that there can be sub-divisions and forms inside each kind. So the list is not closed. It gives directions, and the past supplies the samples.

From above: the flood on the people of Noah. The wind storm that overtook the people of Ad. The stones rained on the people of Lot. Blood and frogs sent upon the Israelites. And the birds that pelted the people of the Elephant with pebbles when they marched on Makkah, leaving them like chaff that has been chewed out.

From beneath: the water under the ground forcing its way up for the people of Noah, so that they were caught by two punishments at once. The drowning of Pharaoh's people. And Qarun, who sank down into the earth with his legendary treasures, as though the ground swallowed him.

### What the Prophet said when this verse was read out

Jabir bin Abdullah reported what happened when the words came down. At the phrase about a torment from above, the Messenger of Allah said: "I seek refuge with your face." At the phrase about a torment from beneath your feet he said the same again. At the phrase about being covered with confusion in party strife, and about tasting the violence of one another, he said: "This is easier, and this is lighter." Al-Bukhari recorded this hadith, and recorded it again in the book of divine oneness. An-Nasa'i recorded it in the book on interpretation. Another account reverses the order. It puts the first two terrors as the lighter ones, and places the flight to Allah's countenance at the last clause.

The same request and the same answer come in two longer reports. Sa'd bin Abi Waqqas said that they were with the Prophet and passed the mosque of Bani Mu'awiyah. He went in and offered two rak'ahs of prayer, and they prayed behind him, and then he supplicated to his Lord at length. When he finished he said that he had asked his Lord for three things. He asked that his community not be destroyed by drowning, and was given it. He asked that they not be destroyed by famine and hunger, and was given it. He asked that they not be made to taste violence from one another, and was not given it. Ahmad recorded it, and Muslim recorded it in the book on trials, though al-Bukhari did not.

A second report comes through Ahmad from Khabbab bin al-Aratt, who was at Badr with the Prophet. He met him one night while the Prophet was praying until dawn. When he finished, Khabbab told him that he had never seen him perform a prayer like that one before. He answered: "Yes, it was a prayer of eagerness and fear. I asked my Lord for three things, and he gave me two and refused me the third." Then he spelled them out. "I asked him not to destroy us with what he destroyed the nations before us, and he gave me that." "I asked him not to let our enemies prevail over us, and he gave me that." "I asked him not to cover us with confusion in party strife, and he refused." An-Nasa'i recorded it, and Ibn Hibban in his authentic collection, and At-Tirmidhi in the book on trials in his compendium. At-Tirmidhi graded it hasan sahih.

A third version, from Ibn Umar, names another of the three requests, that no enemy be set upon the ummah to destroy them. That one was answered. The request about infighting was the one he was stopped from making.

The reports prove a distinction. The kinds of punishment that came on earlier communities from above them and from beneath them, and wiped them out, will not come in that form on this community. One punishment will keep visiting it during its life in this world, and that is its infighting and the mutual confrontation of its factions and parties. This is why the Prophet forbade his community so emphatically from dividing into sects and parties and from challenging and fighting one another, and why, on every occasion he could, he put the fear of Allah in people by warning that if a punishment has to come on Muslims within this life it will come because of nothing else. A report drawn from Zayd ibn Aslam by Ibn Abi Hatim gives the words he used when this verse was revealed: "Do not, after me, become like disbelievers, striking at one another's necks."

### Rulers, servants, and the effect of sin

The reading of Abdullah ibn Abbas and Mujahid turns the two directions into something nearer home. Punishment from above means cruel rulers and merciless officials put over a people, and punishment from beneath means one's own subordinates and servants turning into traitors, idlers and thieves. Sayings of the Prophet confirm that reading. In the compendium Mishkat, citing the branches of faith recorded by al-Baihaqi, one is reported as: "As are your deeds, good or bad, so shall be your rulers and officials set upon you." The sense is that a good and obedient people get merciful and just rulers, and a people whose deeds are evil find merciless and unjust rulers set over them. A longer divine saying is quoted in the same compendium from a collection on the saints, in which Allah says: "I am Allah. There is no god worthy of worship but me. I am the master of kings, and I am the sovereign. The hearts of kings are in my hands." And then: "When my servants obey me, I pour mercy into the hearts of their kings and officials. When they disobey me, I harden their rulers against them, so that they taste every kind of evil punishment." The lesson drawn from it is practical: "Do not waste your energy speaking ill of rulers.
