Turn to Allah and correct your deeds, and I will put your affairs right." A report from A'ishah in Abu Dawud and An-Nasa'i runs the same way. When Allah wishes well for a ruler, he gives him a good minister and deputy, who reminds him if he forgets and helps him when he acts rightly. And when a ruler's ruin is willed, wicked men are put around him as his ministers.

So hardships suffered at the hands of those above are a punishment from above, and those inflicted through those below are a punishment from beneath. Neither is a stray accident. Both fall under a divine law about deeds. Sufyan Ath-Thawri said that when a sin is committed by him he sees its effect on his own servant, and even on the horse he rides and the donkey he uses for his things. He can feel the change in their temper, because they all start disobeying him. Rumi makes the same point in his Mathnawi. Allah puts a person under an apparent punishment, pain caused by cruel rulers or faithless subordinates in this world, in order to turn his attention towards himself. The hope is that he will be alerted, will start trying to make his deeds good, and will thereby be saved from the much greater punishment of the Hereafter. The remedy for both directions is therefore identical. Everyone looks back and examines what he has done, leaves the paths of error, and stops being disobedient, and then the conditions that remove the hardship are created. To try to remove such things by material means alone is self-deception, and it is an experience people keep having.

### Difference that punishes, and difference that is a mercy

Not every difference is the punishment the verse describes. The difference that is named as a deprivation of mercy is difference in the principles and articles of belief, or difference born of self-interest, wanton desires and fancies. What is not included is the difference of opinion that rests on ijtihad, exercised inside the light of the Qur'an and the sunnah. That is the difference which has continued in subsidiary questions among the jurists of this community since the time of the companions and the generation after them. Its frame of reference is restricted to the Qur'an, the sunnah and ijma, the consensus of scholars. Everyone involved intends to obey and to act on the injunctions in them. The disagreement arises because solutions have to be deduced from wording that is condensed or ambiguous. This kind of difference has been called rahmah, mercy, in a narration reported in the small compendium al-Jami al-Saghir, with references going back through al-Baihaqi and Imam al-Haramayn: "The difference of my community is a mercy." It is made particular to this community for a reason. Difference among scholars who uphold nothing but the truth, and among jurists who are unshakeably mindful of Allah, is governed by those principles. It is done with a true intention and for Allah's good pleasure, so it is never motivated by self-interest or by a wish for recognition, office or money. Al-Munawi, commenting on that compendium, gives the comparison: the different approaches of this community's jurists have the standing that the different law-systems of the blessed prophets in past ages had, since they were all, though they differed, nothing but the commands of Allah.

An illustration from an ordinary street is offered as the test case. A main road is marked out into lanes for the convenience of those who use it, with one lane for buses, another for cars and vans, and another for cyclists and pedestrians. Outwardly this is a division. But since everybody is headed in one direction, and each lane leads to the destination, the difference of routes is functionally useful rather than harmful, and it opens up space and mercy. So too with the approaches of the great imams of ijtihad: the approach one of them takes is weightier in his own sight, and he does not call the approach of another false. The leading imams and the jurists agree that an approach taken by any of them is not thereby false, and that it is not permissible for anyone to call the people who follow it sinners. Anyone who looks at the relationships between the jurists of the companions and the successors, and at the four leading imams, will find excellent working relations, full respect and recognition, despite real differences of technical, intellectual and juristic approach. A hadith from the Prophet, brought through various chains of narration, is quoted as the gloss on being covered with confusion in party strife: "This community will divide into seventy-three groups, all of them in the fire except one." Rancour, hostility and infighting were out of the question, and the same spirit continued among the followers of the main schools for as long as they held to sound knowledge and an honest attitude.

A common complaint is asked about here as well. When the scholars differ, where does one go? The answer is that the matter is as simple as it is in any other trade. A sick person whose case the physicians disagree about is not left hopeless. People find the doctor with the experience and the skill they trust and put the case in his hands, and nobody goes about speaking ill of the other doctors in the town. A client does the same when lawyers differ, and does not malign the rest of the profession. The rule should hold for the layperson too: when the rulings of the scholars differ, make the effort to find the one who is best in knowledge and in the fear of Allah, and act on his advice, and do not spend the time finding fault with the rest. Ibn al-Qaiyyim records this in his book on the signs of those who give rulings. He adds that once a person has chosen an expert and acted on the ruling of someone he considers the best in knowledge and honesty, he is free of blame in the sight of Allah. It is not his job to decide which of the scholars who give rulings has erred. If the one who gave the ruling did err, the responsibility is his own.

And not every agreement is praiseworthy either. If thieves, robbers and rebels joined hands and formed a union of their own, every reasonable person would call that union fatal for society, while police action against it, or public protest, would be called beneficial. So the problem is not difference, and it is not acting on one opinion rather than another. The problems start when others are suspected and slandered, which is the product of ignorance, dishonesty and an excess of self-serving desire. At that point the merciful difference turns into the punishing kind, and a community splits into parties, fights itself, and does the impossible thing of killing its own members, while insult is passed off as the defence of a religious position. Religion has nothing to do with that excess. In the reports collected by al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah it is cited as the cause of nations going astray, and it is what the two verses in the family of Imran were warning against: "Hold fast, all of you, to the cord of Allah, and be not divided" (3:103), and "do not be like those who became divided and fell into disputes" (3:105). The exception is stated in the surah of Hud: "They continue in their differences, except those whom Allah has blessed with mercy" (11:118). On that verse the whole discussion turns, since the point is that difference without mercy is the punishment, and the mercy is what keeps a difference from becoming one.

### The community's one bond, and how it was lost

The essence of all these verses and reports is that a difference which turns into confrontation is ill-fated and blameworthy, and that the root of most of what a community suffers lies in it. What is being described as a punishment is not merely the fighting itself but the loss of what held people together. The pivot of unity for this ummah was one sentence, the testimony that there is no god worthy of worship but Allah and that Muhammad is his messenger. Anyone who had faith in it, in any language, of any colour, of any lineage, was a brother or a sister to everyone else. Mountains and rivers were no handicap, and being Arab, Egyptian, Syrian, Turkish, Indian or Chinese did not matter, since such labels existed for the sake of identity and introduction and nothing more. In our day, intrigue backed by sustained effort has divided the people of that sentence again into racial, linguistic and regional nationalities, and each of those has gone on splitting itself into further factions. A people whose hallmark was that they forgave, forewent and sacrificed even for others now contains people ready to sacrifice the most precious rights for the cheapest and meanest of gains. That is the difference born of self-interest and fancies, and it is a cash punishment, paid here, not only deferred.

Within its bounds, difference is not a disease but an enlargement of a question. Honest minds cannot meet over a difficult problem without differing, and uniformity of opinion is conceivable only among people who have not understood it, or among those who will agree to anything to accommodate a pressure group, and who would sign an opinion against their own conscience. This is why the universe the verse points at is itself full of lawful difference: things differ in shape, form, colour, smell, property and benefit, countless living organisms differ, and human beings differ in temperament, occupation, skill and way of living, and those differences are the charm of living and the open avenue of countless benefits. The same Allah who varies the signs in this surah varies his creation, and asks for comprehension rather than uniformity.

### In short

- The three terrors named are the ones from above, the ones from beneath, and the confusion of faction, and the indefinite wording leaves room for many forms of each.
- The Prophet's own reaction is recorded at each clause, and the reports agree that the third was the one he was not granted protection from.
- On the reading of Ibn Abbas and Mujahid, unjust rulers and faithless subordinates are themselves the punishment, which is why the remedy offered is correction of deeds rather than complaint.
- Division into factions is a punishment because it replaces a bond that was one sentence, while difference of opinion inside the limits of the Qur'an, the sunnah and consensus is described as mercy.
- The layperson's duty when scholars differ is to find the one he trusts most in knowledge and mindfulness and follow him, and to leave the rest alone.

66.text:
Still your people ˹O Prophet˺ have rejected this ˹Quran˺, although it is the truth. Say, “I am not a keeper over you.”

The passage turns from what the people asked for to what the Prophet is not. He has not been made their keeper.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Still your people have rejected this"** The people named are Quraysh, and what they rejected is the Qur'an, brought to them with guidance and clear explanation. The charge is stated flatly, without the rhetorical question that preceded it.

**"although it is the truth"** There is no truth beyond this one. The verse does not argue the point, and it does not need to. It says that the denial came from a people who had been shown what is true, and that this is the whole of the case against them.

**"Say, 'I am not a keeper over you'"** I have not been appointed a guardian or a watcher over you, and I do not guarantee that I will bring you to Allah as believers. The gloss adds what the office is, in case the refusal leaves a vacuum: I am only a warner, and your affair is left to Allah. This was revealed before the command to fight the idolaters, when the Prophet's business was the message and nothing else.

The division of labour that follows from this disclaimer is spelled out in the commentary: my duty is to convey the message, and yours is to hear it and obey. Whoever follows him acquires happiness in this life and the Hereafter, and whoever defies him becomes miserable in both. The line is put in the same terms as the verse in the cave: "Say, the truth is from your Lord. Whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve" (18:29).

### Why the verse closes the door on pride

The human condition, taken seriously, leaves nobody room to be proud. A man is buffeted by winds that could turn into a cyclone at any moment and wreck his life. He stands on land that could be torn apart by an earthquake whenever it is willed. He lives among a people so full of hidden enmity that a single spark is enough to push the whole society into bloodshed. The ummah addressed here is not being told that the rejecters will be left alone. It is being told that the reckoning is not in anyone's hands but Allah's, and that a man who is not a keeper over others should not behave as though he were their judge.

### In short

- The rejection is attributed to Quraysh of Makkah, and the object of it is identified as the truth itself.
- The Prophet is told to disclaim the office of keeper, because the guidance of a person is not his to supply.
- The verse was revealed before the command to fight, and it sets the terms of the invitation in the period when argument, not the sword, was the method.
- Whoever hears the message and turns away has settled his own case, since every tiding has its appointed outcome.

67.text:
Every ˹destined˺ matter has a ˹set˺ time to transpire. And you will soon come to know

A short sentence that answers a question about timing, and then refuses to answer it.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Every destined matter has a set time to transpire"** For every tiding there is a reality, that is, a conclusion and a fixed time in which it takes place and is settled. Ibn Abbas and others took the sense to be that this news will come about, perhaps after a while. The phrase covers every announcement a person receives from Allah: commands, prohibitions, promises and threats, glad tidings of victory and warnings of punishment. Some of them fall in this world and some in the Hereafter, and the tidings about their punishment are included.

**"And you will soon come to know"** This is stated as a threat. You will come to know all of it, in this world or in the next. Another way of taking the clause is that every action and every speech of yours reflects a real meaning in your hearts, and that you will see what is done with you.

### The question behind the answer

Those who asked when the promised punishment would arrive were told that he had not been appointed to tell them. The point of time for everything is settled in the divine knowledge, and nothing can be pushed forward. It arrives when it arrives. They will see for themselves what that hour looks like, and nobody will be told in advance. Other verses say the same thing in other words: for each and every matter there is a decree (13:38), and "you will come to know the truth of it after a while" (38:88). A warning and a promise of this kind are certain to be met.

### In short

- The verse takes the question of timing away from the questioners and hands it to Allah.
- Every announcement has an outcome at a fixed time, and the punishment they mocked at is one of those announcements.
- "You will come to know" is a threat rather than a consolation, and it is left open as to when the knowing falls.
- The other verses cited here say the same thing, that a decree stands behind every matter.

68.text:
And when you come across those who ridicule Our revelations, do not sit with them unless they engage in a different topic. Should Satan make you forget, then once you remember, do not ˹continue to˺ sit with the wrongdoing people

This is a rule about sitting down, and it is stated as a rule about belief. A gathering is a place where a person's faith is either guarded or spent.

### Phrase by phrase

**"And when you come across those who ridicule Our revelations"** The wording in Arabic is built on a verb that means to enter into water and wade through it, and then comes to mean entering into activities that are vain, absurd or futile. The Qur'an usually uses it in that second sense. Two examples are enough: "we used to indulge in vain discourse with those who indulged" (74:45), and the talk of people who play with what they are busy with (6:91). The verb covers meddling with the verses of Allah for fun and ridicule, and fault-finding and disputing about them, and two scholars of the subcontinent, Shaykh al-Hind Mahmud al-Hasan and Ashraf Ali Thanavi, translated it in that latter sense. So the sense is: when you see these people meddling in the verses of Allah just for fun, or trying to find faults in them, turn away.

**"do not sit with them unless they engage in a different topic"** Stay away from them until they change the subject, until they talk about something other than the denial they were engaged in. Turning away can take several forms. A person can leave the gathering, or he can stay and busy himself with something else so that he pays no attention. The end of the verse makes clear which form is desirable. One should not keep sitting there. One should get up and leave.

**"Should Satan make you forget"** This covers a person who walked into their gathering unmindfully, whether he had forgotten the prohibition or had not recalled that these people speak against Allah and his Messenger in their meetings. In either case, once he remembers, he leaves at once. To keep sitting there after the reminder is a sin. The same subject appears in the women: "if you hear the verses of Allah being denied and mocked at, then do not sit with them until they engage in a talk other than that, for in that case you would be like them" (4:140). If you stay and sit with them, agreeing with what they say, you are one of them.

**"then once you remember, do not continue to sit with the wrongdoing people"** The remembrance is the turning point: the moment it arrives, the sitting has to end. The command includes every member of this ummah, and the address to the Prophet is there so that others hear it. Allah gave him this order in Makkah, and the companions found it hard to carry out, until the relief in the next verse let them sit with the idolaters in order to admonish and warn them. Nobody is to sit with people who deny the verses, distort them, and explain them wrongly. It is said that he never took part in such gatherings even in the days before his prophethood, so he needed no prohibition for himself.

### Who is exempt, and who is not

Imam al-Razi, in his great commentary, takes the real intent of the verse to be abstention from sinful gatherings and from their participants. The best course is to rise and depart. But if leaving would put a person's life, property or honour in danger, then for ordinary people it is permissible to turn away in another manner, by busying themselves with something else and paying no attention. The case of the people who are followed in religious matters is different. For them the only appropriate course is to get up and leave, because their sitting is read as approval.

Two further rulings are drawn from the wording. Imam al-Jassas, in a book on the legal rulings of the Qur'an, takes the verse to mean that Muslims should keep away from any gathering where things are being said against Allah, against his Messenger and against the law of Islam, in a case where it is not in their power to stop it or even to say what is right. Sitting in such a company with the intention of reforming it and carrying the truth to it does not fall under the prohibition. And al-Jassas goes on to say that sitting with people of this kind, unjust, irreligious and foul-mouthed, is a sin in itself, whether or not they happen to be saying anything impermissible at that moment. The reason is that the prohibition in the verse is unconditional. It does not make their behaving unjustly at that same hour a condition, because people of that character may break into their ridiculous rantings at any sudden moment. The same subject is put more explicitly in another verse: "do not incline towards the wrongdoers, lest the Fire should catch you" (11:113).

### Forgetting, and what it costs a prophet

The clause "should Satan make you forget" raises a question of its own. If the address is to Muslims at large, then forgetting is simply human, and there is no difficulty. If it is to the Prophet, someone may ask how the teaching of a man who can forget is to be trusted. The answer given is that a prophet may forget a thing under particular circumstances where divine wisdom decides that it should happen, in order to achieve a purpose. But Allah alerts him at once by a way that keeps the lapse from lasting, so that his teaching ends up free of any doubt left by forgetfulness.

The same clause carries a comfort for everyone else. If a person falls into an error inadvertently, that stands forgiven. There is a hadith to that effect, to the sense that error, forgetfulness and what a person is compelled to do have been removed from the account of this ummah. In other words, what is not chosen is not charged.

### A sin watched is a sin shared

The principle behind the rule is stated plainly: a sin is a sin whether you do it yourself or sit and watch others doing it. Muslims are being instructed, as a matter of principle, to keep out of the gatherings frequented by people who prefer to follow the false. The verse then goes on to details, and the details are the ones set out above, down to the last one: a man who cannot get out may cover his ears with his attention, but a man whose attention is looked up to has no such cover.

### In short

- The prohibition is about staying, not about being in the same city, and the remedy is to change the sitting or leave it.
- Wading into vain talk is the image the Arabic word carries, and the mockers and the fault-finders are covered by it alike.
- Sitting with people after you remember what they are doing is what the verse forbids, and the other cited verse says that whoever stays becomes like them.
- Danger to life, property or honour lets an ordinary person turn away in some other way, but not a scholar whose sitting is taken for endorsement.
- Forgetting is forgiven, in the general case and in the prophetic case, and the reminder obliges a person only from the moment it arrives.

69.text:
"Those mindful ˹of Allah˺ will not be accountable for those ˹who ridicule it˺ whatsoever—their duty is to advise, so perhaps the ridiculers will abstain"

The verse exists because the previous one was too much to bear.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Those mindful of Allah will not be accountable for those who ridicule it"** When this was revealed, the companions put a difficulty to the Prophet. If the absolute prohibition on going into those gatherings stayed in force, they would be shut out of the prayer and out of the circumambulation of the Sacred Mosque, since those people were always sitting there, before the hijrah and before Makkah was opened to the Muslims, busy with nothing but fault-finding and ill-speaking. The verse that answered them is this one. When people who observe restraint come to al-Masjid al-Haram for their own rightful purpose, they are not responsible for the evil deeds of the wicked people sitting there. One gloss notes that the Arabic particle which might suggest a share of responsibility is extra, so that the sense is simply that the mindful are not accountable for them in anything, if they sit with them.

**"their duty is to advise"** They remain under the obligation of telling such people what is right and true. That is the duty that survives the relief, and it is stated as a reminder: remind them, so that perhaps they will become mindful. The believers are clear of the mockers' sins, and they are not clear of the obligation to warn them.

**"so perhaps the ridiculers will abstain"** The purpose of the mild treatment is their restraint, not the believers' comfort. It was said: we told you to leave them, so that they notice what they are indulging in, give it up, and never go back to it.

### The shape of the exemption

Those who ward off disbelief, idolatry, indecency and mockery are not accountable for the sins, the unbelief and the ridicule of others. The relief is real, and it is bounded. It covers sitting in a place a Muslim has a right to be in, for a purpose he is entitled to pursue. It does not cover staying to enjoy what they are saying, and it does not cancel the duty of speaking the truth in front of them. A reminder given through the Qur'an is what the mindful owe, and the hope attached to it is small and honest: perhaps they will be wary of talking like that.

### In short

- The verse lifts a hardship the previous one had created, and does so without giving permission to sit and listen.
- Being free of another person's accountability is not the same as being free of concern for him.
- The duty left over is remembrance and advice, delivered by the Qur'an and aimed at their restraint.
- The companions' difficulty was about prayer and tawaf in the Sacred Mosque, and the answer let them keep both.

70.text:
And leave those who take this faith ˹of Islam˺ as mere play and amusement and are deluded by ˹their˹ worldly life. Yet remind them by this ˹Quran˺, so no one should be ruined for their misdeeds. They will have no protector or intercessor other than Allah. Even if they were to offer every ˹possible˺ ransom, none will be accepted from them. Those are the ones who will be ruined for their misdeeds. They will have a boiling drink and painful punishment for their disbelief

Two commands in one verse: leave them, and remind them. The verse then explains why the second one cannot be dropped.

### Phrase by phrase

**"And leave those who take this faith as mere play and amusement"** The word for leaving is built on a root meaning to be displeased with a thing and to abandon it, so the sentence can be read two ways, and the outcome is nearly the same. Either it means leaving people who have turned the true religion, sent for their own sake, into a plaything and a laughing stock, or it means leaving people who have abandoned their real faith and made fun and play their own religion and purpose in life. Those named in the reports are the Jews, the Christians, and the idolatrous Arabs who took the religion of their fathers as their own. The men specifically in mind are ʿUyaynah, al-Nadr ibn al-Harith and their folk. To take a faith as a joke is described as treating it as merriment and fiction. This too was revealed before the command to fight them, so the order to leave them alone stands.

**"and are deluded by their worldly life"** The comforts and bounties of this world deceived them. This is a true diagnosis of the problem. They are wicked and disobedient because they are bewitched by the glamour of their mortal life, and they have forgotten that another state of life is ahead. If they had believed in the Hereafter and in Qiyamah, they would never have acted so recklessly.

**"Yet remind them by this Quran, so no one should be ruined for their misdeeds"** Remind the people with the Qur'an, and warn them against Allah's revenge and his painful torment on the Day of Rising. The word translated as ruined is explained through several early readings. Ad-Dahhak, reporting from Ibn Abbas, and Mujahid, Ikrimah, al-Hasan and as-Suddi took it to mean being made submissive. Al-Walibi, also from Ibn Abbas, took it as being exposed to what one has earned. Qatadah said it means being prevented, and Ibn Zayd said it means being recompensed, while al-Kalbi said it means being reckoned. All of these are close. They come together in being exposed to destruction, being kept away from good, and being held back from getting what one wants. Every soul is held back by what it has earned, except the people of the right hand (74:38-39).

**"They will have no protector or intercessor other than Allah"** A person in trouble relies on three sources, and all three fail here. When it suits him he uses the power and influence of his party or his group to stay safe from the consequences of what he did. When he is helpless he seeks recommendations from influential people. When that fails too, he tries to buy his freedom with money. None of the three is left. No friend or relative saves Allah's criminal from punishment, no intercession succeeds without Allah's permission, and no wealth is accepted. If a person owned the wealth of the whole world and offered all of it as a ransom to be saved from punishment, that ransom would not be taken from him, as the verse in the family of Imran says about those who disbelieved and died in unbelief, from whom even the earth full of gold would not be accepted (3:91).

**"They will have a boiling drink and painful punishment for their disbelief"** They have been detained in the punishment of their own deeds, and this is stated twice in the verse, once as a warning and once as a verdict. Their drink in Jahannam will be boiling water, about which another verse says that it will shatter their entrails (47:15), and there will be painful punishments besides it, in return for their disbelief and denial. The Qur'an describes their hearts by one word for rust and stain: what they have earned has covered their hearts with a layer that stops good getting in (83:14). A report from the Prophet puts the process in order: when a man falls into a sin the first time, a dot shows up on his heart. It is like a black spot on a white garment, which everybody dislikes and is disturbed by, and he too feels the distaste. But when he goes on to a second sin and a third, without repenting of the first, black dots keep appearing one after another, until the bright tablet of the heart is black through and through. The outcome is that he loses the very ability to tell good from bad.

### The company is the danger

The verse also carries a warning that the company of people who are heedless of the Hereafter and content with this life is fatal for whoever sits with them. Its end is that whoever stays in their company becomes exposed to the same punishment they have been caught in. Many clear statements of the Qur'an and of the reports, and repeated observation, point to the same root of evils and crimes: the society and the environment a person grows up in. Once he is snared in it he slides into things against his own nature and his own conscience. Then he gets used to it, and the sense of evil dies away, until he takes evil as good and good as evil. Wrong environment and bad company hurt everybody and push people into an abyss, and the practical conclusion is drawn for the people who are responsible for raising children: keep them out of it.

### In short

- Leaving these people and reminding them are ordered in the same breath, so neither command cancels the other.
- "Taking the faith as play" is described as a religion of amusement, and the same phrase also fits people who left faith and adopted amusement.
- Being ruined is explained by early glosses that cluster around exposure, debasement and being held back from good.
- Party, connections and money are the three refuges a sinner reaches for, and the verse removes all three.
- The black dots on the heart are the mechanism by which a taken habit of sin ends in the loss of the ability to tell good from bad.

71.text:
Ask ˹them, O Prophet˺, “Should we invoke, other than Allah, those ˹idols˺ which cannot benefit or harm us, and turn back to disbelief after Allah has guided us? ˹If we do so, we will be˺ like those disoriented by devils in the wilderness, while their companions call them to guidance, ˹saying˺, ‘Come to us!’ Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Allah’s guidance is the ˹only˺ true guidance. And we are commanded to submit to the Lord of all worlds”

The answer to the offer of a bargain is a question, and the question comes with a picture attached.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Should we invoke, other than Allah, those which cannot benefit or harm us"** The interrogative is a disavowal, not a request for information. These three verses exist to refute shirk and to affirm Allah's oneness and the Hereafter, and the question is the refutation in the act. Worshiping an idol would bring no benefit in this life, in provision or livelihood, and no benefit in the Hereafter, and neglecting it brings no harm in either. The same answer is put to ʿUyaynah and his folk, and to the demand that preceded it.

**"and turn back to disbelief after Allah has guided us"** After he had honoured us with his religion. To go back after that is the thing the parable is about. As-Suddi reported that certain idolators pressed some Muslims to leave the religion of Muhammad and follow them instead, and that this verse came down about that exchange. Ibn Jarir recorded the report.

**"like those disoriented by devils in the wilderness"** The example, if a person reverts after believing, is that of a man who set out with some people on a road, lost his way, and was made to wander in confusion over the land by devils. He is bewildered, not knowing where to go. They call him by his name, and by his father's name and his grandfather's, and he follows the call, thinking it is a path of guidance. By morning he finds himself destroyed, and they may eat him, and the jinn leave him wandering in a wasteland where he dies of thirst. The word for the creatures who lead him is read as referring to ghouls. Meanwhile his companions on the road are calling him: come back to us, we are on the path. And he refuses.

**"while their companions call them to guidance"** The companions are the people on the road who want him to come back. The point of the parable is that the call is coming, and that the man who is destroying himself is being called out of it by people who are not lost. One account takes the verse to be about Abu Bakr and his son ʿAbd al-Rahman. Before he believed, ʿAbd al-Rahman used to call his parents to his own religion, while they called him to Islam and to repentance. On that reading the address tells the Prophet to put the question to his son in these terms: are you asking us to worship what neither benefits us in this world nor hurts us if we leave it, and to crawl back to what we were on before Allah led us into Muhammad's religion? If we did what you ask, we would be a man gone astray, lured off by devils.

**"Say, Allah's guidance is the only true guidance"** His guidance is Islam, and everything else is error. On one reading the sentence continues with a second identification: our qiblah is the Kaʿbah. The two are the same claim in different clothes, that the direction of the worship and the worship itself come from one source. Whoever Allah guides has nobody who can misguide him (39:37), and if you are eager for the guidance of those who refuse it, Allah does not guide those whom he lets go astray, and they will have no helpers (16:37).

**"And we are commanded to submit to the Lord of all worlds"** We are commanded to worship him with sincerity, without partners, and to make our worship and our confession of his oneness pure for him.

### What going astray looks like from the outside

When communities go astray, their religious acts change as well. People stop attending to the objective of an act and load everything onto its externals. Those who have reached the point of making religion a source of worldly fun, and who are oblivious to what it was for, show by their deeds that they are in earnest about nothing in it. Such people cannot have the point explained to them, because the explanation would go against their temperament. And what they own gives them the illusion that they own the truth as well. They see their needs met. They are the life and soul of every gathering, and nothing is missing from their lives. So they conclude that they will come out on top in the Hereafter as well. These are misapprehensions, and they will be undone by their own actions. Their arrogance will rebound on them, and there will be no easing of what they come to.

### In short

- The reply to the bargain offered is a question that puts the benefit and the harm of idols on the table, and finds neither.
- Reverting after guidance is illustrated as a man lured into the wasteland by voices that use his own name, while the people who could save him are calling.
- The call has not stopped. The companions on the road are calling, which is what makes the refusal indefensible.
- Allah's guidance is the true guidance, and the whole exchange is a claim about direction: the qiblah, the path, and the one who calls.
- Submission is stated as the command, with sincerity and oneness as its content.

72.text:
establish prayer, and be mindful of Him. To Him you will all be gathered together

Two obligations and one destination, in a fragment that depends on the verse before it.

### Phrase by phrase

**"establish prayer"** To submit to the Lord of the worlds takes shape in prayer, and the prayer meant here is the five daily prayers, established in a complete way rather than performed loosely. The same submission that refuses to worship idols is what stands up and prays.

**"and be mindful of Him"** Mindfulness of Allah, by fulfilling his instructions and staying away from what he has prohibited, is the second half of the command. The pairing matters. Prayer without mindfulness is the externals of an act, which is what the previous verse showed what happens to when a community goes astray.

**"To him you will all be gathered together"** He is the one to whom you will be gathered after death, and he will reward each person for what they did. The gathering is for the reckoning, on the Day of Rising. Whoever has been told that the call is still open, and that a path can be rejoined, is also being told that the gathering is not avoidable.

### In short

- Submission is given a body: prayer performed properly, and mindfulness in ordinary conduct.
- The two are addressed to the same people who were offered a bargain about idols, so the act of worship is itself the answer.
- The gathering to Allah is stated as the end of the road, and it is what makes seriousness about religion possible at all.

73.text:
"He is the One Who created the heavens and the earth in truth. On the Day ˹of Judgment˺ He will say, ‘Be!’ And there will be! His command is truth. All authority is His ˹alone˺ on the Day the Trumpet will be blown. He is the Knower of all—seen or unseen. And He is the All-Wise, All-Aware."

The passage about ridicule, company and return ends on the one who created all of it, and on the day when everything is handed to him.

### Phrase by phrase

**"He is the One Who created the heavens and the earth in truth"** In justice, as the one who made them and who owns them and governs their affairs and the affairs of everyone in them. Another sense is offered: he made them in order to make the truth manifest and falsehood exposed. And it is also said that the point is to show that they are ephemeral and evanescent. The three readings agree that creation has a purpose and is not a stage set.

**"On the Day of Judgment He will say, 'Be!' And there will be!"** This refers to the Day of Resurrection, when Allah says to the creatures: rise up, and they do. It will come faster than the blink of an eye. One reading takes the address in the Arabic as being made to a wall, so that the heavens become a wall that is blown into, the way a horn is blown, and the heaven is then changed into a different heaven. On either reading, the word that produces the event is the same word that produced the heavens the first time.

**"His command is truth"** His word about the resurrection is the truth that will doubtless come to pass.

**"All authority is His alone on the Day the Trumpet will be blown"** "The sovereignty on that day will be the true sovereignty, belonging to the Most Merciful, and it will be a hard day for the disbelievers" (25:26). Then a question is asked and answered in another verse: "Whose is the kingdom this day? It is Allah's, the One, the Irresistible" (40:16). There will be no kingdom for anybody else. The word for the Trumpet here is Sur, and it is the trumpet into which the angel Israfil will blow, on the second blast. A hadith recorded by Muslim states that Israfil has held the Sur in his mouth with his forehead lowered, waiting for the command to blow. In another report, recorded by Ahmad from Abdullah bin Amr, a bedouin man asked the Messenger of Allah what the Sur is, and the answer was short: a trumpet which will be blown.

**"He is the Knower of all, seen or unseen"** The unseen is what will happen in the future, and the seen is what has already happened. It is also said that the unseen means what is hidden from people while the seen means what Allah's servants see, and that his knowledge covers what is inwardly hidden and outwardly manifest, so that nothing is hidden from him. This is where the passage began, with the keys of the unseen and with a leaf that no one watches falling.

**"And He is the All-Wise, All-Aware"** Wise in his command and decree, and aware of his creatures and of what they do. The two names close the claim: creation was not done at random, and it will not be settled by guesswork.

### The two travellers

The last stretch of the passage is worth reading as a story about two men in the desert. One puts his entire trust in Allah. When he goes astray he begs Allah's assistance, and soon his feet are back on the path. The other has faith in entities other than Allah. When he loses his way he is hardly aware that he is wandering at all, and he ignores the calls of the faithful, who would gladly redirect him. The difference between them is the state of their minds. The first keeps his open, so he has no difficulty seeing which way is right, and if he strays he is willing to accept guidance in order to return. The second is lost before he sets out, since Satan has him under his influence, and his mind works in a perverse way. He may listen without hearing. He may look without seeing.

### In short

- Creation is stated as an act done in truth, and the day of judgement is stated as the same word at work a second time.
- "Be, and it is" is read as the moment the creatures are told to rise, and one early reading takes the heavens as a wall blown into and remade.
- The trumpet is named, and the reports about Israfil waiting with it in his mouth and about the bedouin's question give the verse its scenery.
- Sovereignty on that day belongs to Allah alone, which is the answer to every partner who was invoked in this life.
- The passage that began with the keys of the unseen ends by naming its owner as the Wise and the Aware, and leaves the reader to choose which of the two travellers he is.

74.text:
And ˹remember˺ when Abraham said to his father, Ȃzar, “Do you take idols as gods? It is clear to me that you and your people are entirely misguided.”

The passage about ridicule and company now gives an example, and the example is a son speaking to his father.

### Phrase by phrase

**"And when Abraham said to his father, Azar"** The address is respectful and the content is not. Azar is the name commonly given as his father's name, while most historians give the name as Tarikh and treat Azar as a title. Imam al-Razi and a group of early scholars hold instead that Tarikh was the father and that Azar was the name of his uncle, who became a polytheist after entering the service of Nimrud. Since calling an uncle father is ordinary in Arab usage, Azar is named here as his father. Al-Zarqani, in his Sharh al-Mawahib, collects several proofs for that reading.

**"Do you take idols as gods?"** Do you worship an idol in place of Allah? The question is a rebuke, not a request. The interrogation is meant to make him say out loud what he does: he takes, as objects of worship, things his own hands have made, many of them, small and large, male and female.

**"It is clear to me that you and your people are entirely misguided"** You who follow your way, and the people who go along with you, are confused about the path of truth, and you are in an error plain to anyone with sound reason, wandering in confusion and unaware of where to go. Ibrahim saw that the idols of earth were being made in the shape of heavenly angels, so that those angels would intercede for them with the Creator. His people thought they were too insignificant to worship Allah directly. That is why they turned to the worship of angels as a way of getting provision, victory and the satisfaction of their needs. Allah is the only being who deserves to be worshipped, and nothing else has any right to be worshipped besides him.

**"Your people"** The phrase does more work than it appears to. Ibrahim did not attach himself to his father's people here, and said "your people" instead of "my people". The choice was a sacrifice, since it cut the bond of blood brotherhood in the way of Allah, and it showed that the nationality of believers is founded on the bonds of Islam. Wherever nationality built on race or homeland clashes with that, the verse says by its wording, the first has to be left. The Qur'an raises the whole community to the same standard by pointing at him: it was said that certainly the best example, worthy of being followed and emulated, is the way and conduct of Ibrahim and of those with him, who told their brothers in blood, race and geography frankly that they were wary of them and of their false objects of worship, and that the wall between them stands until they believe and submit to none but Allah. On the journey of his last hajj, the Prophet met a caravan on the road and asked them which nationality they came from, and they answered: we are a nation of Muslims (al-Bukhari). In the old Arab way of naming themselves they gave no tribe and no family line, and by calling themselves Muslims they named the nationality that holds in every time, right through the trials of the Hereafter. At the place where he had to declare his principled disassociation, he did address them as his own, saying: "O my people, I am free of what you associate with Allah" (6:78). The hint runs: you are my people in race and homeland, and your disbelief has compelled me to give up your brotherhood.

### The same story in the surahs about the cave and Mary

The Qur'an tells this advice in other places at greater length. There he is a man of truth and a prophet, and he says: "O my father, why do you worship what does not hear, does not see, and cannot avail you in anything? O my father, there has come to me knowledge that has not come to you, so follow me, and I will guide you to a straight path. O my father, do not worship Satan, for Satan has been a rebel against the Most Merciful. O my father, I fear that a torment from the Most Merciful will overtake you, so that you become a companion of Satan in the Fire." The father answers: do you reject my gods, O Ibrahim? If you do not stop, I will stone you, so leave me in safety before I punish you. Ibrahim says: peace be upon you. I will ask my Lord's forgiveness for you, for he has been most gracious to me. And I will turn away from you and from those you call on besides Allah, and I will call on my Lord, and I hope I will not be unanswered in my supplication to him (19:41-48).

He kept asking forgiveness for his father as long as his father lived. When his father died an idolater and he learned it, he stopped, and he disassociated himself from him. That is the sense of the verse about his father's forgiveness: it came only from a promise Ibrahim had made the man, and when the man turned out to be an enemy of Allah, Ibrahim drew away from him. He was patient in supplication and forbearing (9:114).

A report in the authentic collection describes the meeting of the two on the Day of Rising. Ibrahim will meet his father Azar, and Azar will say to him: my son, I am not going to disobey you today. Ibrahim will say: Lord, you promised me you would not disgrace me on the day they are raised, and what could be more shameful than being disgraced by my father? Then Allah will tell him: look behind you, Ibrahim. He will look and see that his father has been turned into a male hyena covered in dung. The creature will be seized by the legs and thrown into the fire.

### Reform begins at home

The verses about Ibrahim are placed here to support the call of the Prophet, and the placement is not accidental. Arabia's people held Ibrahim as their patriarch, and the whole peninsula paid him homage, so the argument runs through the man they could not dismiss. He is being presented as the one who taught them what a true belief in Allah's oneness looks like.

The first thing the verse shows is where the call began: with a respectable elder of the family. This is the same command the Prophet received: "warn your near relatives of the punishment" (26:214), and he obeyed it by gathering his own family when he stood on the hill of Safa to deliver his call. Tafsir al-Bahr al-Muhit draws the lesson that inviting a respected elder of one's family to the right path is not a breach of reverence, and that wishing well for him is exactly what is happening. It adds that beginning the work of daʿwah, and of the reform that follows it, from one's home, family and immediate circle is a sunnah of the prophets. The ummah that came after him was given this as its order of battle: the call starts with the people who know you best.

### The two-fold error he argued against

Ibrahim and the people of his father were caught in a shirk with two faces, and he debated both of them. They worshipped idols, and they worshipped stars. Against idolatry he spoke plainly, because the error was in common sight, and he told his father flatly that he and his people had gone astray. Against star-worship he took a different method, stage by stage, and that debate is what the next verses set out. The reason for the difference is in the material itself: the falsehood of a statue you have carved is obvious, while the falsehood of a bright object in the sky is not.

And the universe itself testifies against both kinds. Heaven and earth, with the systems running through them, deny that any being has power except the one Supreme Being. A person who makes worldly glory his purpose, and tramples truth and justice to get it, is behaving as though this world were a showplace for selfish men. But the perfect order of the universe shows resplendent glimpses of a perfect Maker, and it cannot be imagined that such a being would set up a showplace with no meaning. What a person sees now is temporary. Allah may issue a new command at any moment and break the present system down, and then human freedom of action will end and his authority will run over people the way it already runs over everything else in creation. At that point only those who surrendered during the test will succeed, those who feared him before any pressure was put on them to bow.

### In short

- Ibrahim's first address is to a family elder, and the verse makes plain that daʿwah starts at home.
- The name in the verse is read either as his father's name or as his uncle's, and the entry gives both readings with their reasons.
- "Your people" and then "my people" marks a deliberate line: the bond of faith outranks the bond of race and homeland.
- His long prayer for his father, and his withdrawal after the man died an idolater, are the background of the rule that a promise does not outlive enmity to Allah.
- The error he argued against had two faces, idols and stars, and each needed a different method.

75.text:
We also showed Abraham the wonders of the heavens and the earth, so he would be sure in faith

A verse of one line, placed between the quarrel with his father and the argument with the star-worshippers, and it explains where the argument came from.

### Phrase by phrase

**"We also showed Abraham"** Just as Allah had shown him the misguidance of his father and his people, so he showed him what is in the heavens and the earth. The showing is described as a gift given before the debate. So the debate speaks from what he had been shown, and not from speculation.

**"the wonders of the heavens and the earth"** That is, the kingdom of both, and everything between them: the sun, the moon and the stars. The sense of the showing is that Ibrahim saw what Allah has created in a way that unravelled the reality of these created things, manifestly and one after another. He was then able to infer from them the truth of Allah's oneness, and that nothing besides him deserves worship.

**"so he would be sure in faith"** So he might be among those who know with certainty, and whose certainty is firm. They acknowledge that Allah is one, the maker of the heavens and the earth and of everything in them. The verse pairs with two invitations to look: "Say, behold all that is in the heavens and the earth" (10:101), and "do they not see what is before them and what is behind them of the heaven and the earth? If he wills, Allah may sink the earth with them, or cause a piece of the sky to fall upon them. In that is a sign for every servant who turns to him" (34:9).

### What the showing did for him

One account of the same moment has Ibrahim shown all this when he came out of the hole into which he had been thrown. Another has Allah showing it to him on the night he was made to ascend. He saw as far as the seventh heaven and the seventh earth, and his certainty became the certainty of inspiration rather than of report. In either account the sequence in the verse matters: the seeing comes first, and the argument afterwards. Allah describes him elsewhere by saying that he had already been given his portion of guidance, and that he was well acquainted with him, and that he said to his father and his people: "what are these images to which you are devoted?" (21:51-52).

Verse 75 is also a preface to a wondrous dialogue, and it is worth noticing that the Qur'an introduces the debate by naming the qualification of the debater. Stage by stage, what follows shows a quality of argument that survives even in translation.

### In short

- Certainty is given as the fruit of looking at creation, and it is placed before the argument rather than after it.
- The showing is a favour, and the verse's grammar ties it to the misguidance Ibrahim had already been shown.
- Two other verses are cited as the same invitation to observe, and they carry the same threat inside the invitation.
- The quarrel with the stars that follows is spoken from what he had been shown, which is why it is so short and so plain.

76.text:
When the night grew dark upon him, he saw a star and said, “This is my Lord!” But when it set, he said, “I do not love things that set.”

The argument begins in the way his people were already thinking, and ends by dismantling that way of thinking.

### Phrase by phrase

**"When the night grew dark upon him"** The night covered him with its darkness. His people were astrologers, and the heavens were where they looked for lordship.

**"he saw a star"** The star is named in the reports as the planet Venus, the brightest of the objects they honoured after the sun and the moon. He said: "this is my Lord", and the sense in which he said it is not a confession but a trap. As you think and believe, is this not my Lord and your Lord? In a little while, you will see how much that claim is worth. One reading takes the words as a question: could this be my Lord? Another takes them as spoken in mockery of his people, since they worshipped the sun, the moon and the stars, and his point is: can the like of these be a Lord? The sentence can also be filled out as: this is evidence of my Lord, for my Lord has no beginning and no end, and this has set.

**"But when it set, he said, 'I do not love things that set'"** The word for setting gives the whole point, since it comes from a root for vanishing and disappearing. Whatever sets, whatever changes colour and fades out of sight, cannot be given the status of an object of worship, because what is worshipped has to be most worthy of love and reverence. A true Lord cannot be transformed or moved from place to place, since those are the marks of created things. So the sentence means: I do not love a lord who does not last. Qatadah commented on this that Ibrahim knew his Lord to be eternal, never ceasing. The argument is drawn from observation, and it testifies to the belief he already held. The way he conducts it has a name in the books of dialectic, since he repeats the words of the addressee and then convinces him, and the same method appears elsewhere in the Qur'an, at verse 97 of the chapter numbered 20. The signs of creation spread through the universe are not only a source of increase in faith. They also provide strong arguments for the call to the truth.

### Why he chose the setting out of all the states a star has

A star could have been argued against at several moments. It could have been shown rising, and held to be untrustworthy while it climbed. Its middle stage, before it sets, could have been used, since it moves in a pre-specified orbit at another's command and swerves neither to the right nor to the left, and has no say at all in its own affairs. Ibrahim chose the moment of its setting, because a setting spells decline in the sight of ordinary people. That is the usual method of the prophets. They do not chase philosophical truisms. They address people at the level of common comprehension, and they prove the helplessness of what is worshipped with the fact that everyone can already see.

### In short

- The opening words are not a statement of belief but a device, and the entry records the three ways the sentence has been read.
- The star named is Venus, and its brightness is the reason it was chosen first for the argument.
- Setting, vanishing and changing place are treated as marks of a created thing, and therefore as disqualifications for lordship.
- The moment picked for the argument is the one the crowd can see, which is the point about the prophets' method.

77.text:
Then when he saw the moon rising, he said, “This one is my Lord!” But when it disappeared, he said, “If my Lord does not guide me, I will certainly be one of the misguided people.”

The second round of the argument uses the same move on a bigger object, and adds a sentence that is easy to miss.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Then when he saw the moon rising, he said, 'This one is my Lord'"** He followed the earlier method with the moon, on another night, with the moon glowing in front of him. According to your view, this is my Lord, and this is bigger than the first. Its reality you will find out in a little while. The purpose was to carry his people through the same steps and convince them by what they watched.

**"But when it disappeared, he said, 'If my Lord does not guide me, I will certainly be one of the misguided people'"** This is the sentence that is not about the moon. Unless my Lord establishes him within true guidance, he will be one of those who have strayed, like the rest of them, and the moon would have been what he took as his Lord and his object of worship. He is saying that guidance keeps a man out of the abyss, and that argument alone does not. It also tells them that Allah's oneness is not reached by cleverness but by being made firm on it. And there is a hint in the wording that the Lord of Ibrahim is a different order of being entirely, from whom guidance keeps arriving to him.

The sentence also tells the hearers something about the debater. A man who says "unless my Lord guides me" is not claiming to be immune. He is telling them that a person can be wrong without noticing, and that the only safety is being made firm. It is an intimation to his people that they are astray, delivered as a confession about himself, and it is recorded that, like the first round, this had no effect on them.

### In short

- The moon round repeats the star round's structure, and the escalation is the point: bigger does not mean greater.
- The words about being guided are Ibrahim speaking of himself, and they place certainty in Allah's hand rather than in the argument.
- The verse hints that the Lord who gives guidance is not of the same order as the objects being watched.
- Persistence in the argument produced no effect, which is why the next round is the last.

78.text:
"Then when he saw the sun shining, he said, “This must be my Lord—it is the greatest!” But again when it set, he declared, “O my people! I totally reject whatever you associate ˹with Allah in worship˺”"

The third round ends the argument, and the sentence that follows is not about the sun any more.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Then when he saw the sun shining, he said, 'This must be my Lord, it is the greatest'"** This is bigger than the first and the second, and more radiant. The people's reckoning was that the sun was the brightest and most honoured of the objects they worshipped, and Ibrahim worked through their list in the order of their reverence. The seven planets they named were the moon, Mercury, Venus, the sun, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn, and he began with Venus, then the moon, then the sun. When he had proved that these three were not gods, although they are the brightest objects an eye can see, the rest of the list went by the same argument.

**"But again when it set, he declared, 'O my people! I totally reject whatever you associate with Allah'"** Now the reality had become too obvious to be argued about, and the words change from "I do not love" to "I am free of". He is free of worshipping those objects and of taking them as protectors. If they are gods, as you claim, then bring your plot against me all of you, and give me no respite. One account of his life has him speak this at seventeen years old, when he emerged from the hole he had been thrown into, went to his people, looked at the sky and the earth, and said that his Lord is the one who created this. Then he came upon a group of them devoted to their idols, and said what the verse reports.

### The three tests the objects fail

The case Ibrahim builds against star-worship rests on three marks, and each of them is visible without instrumentation. A thing that is subject to change cannot be anyone's Lord. A thing that alternates in its conditions cannot be anyone's Lord. A thing that moves in obedience to another power cannot be anyone's Lord. Nothing in the sky is independent in its existence. The heavenly bodies are hemmed in on every side by the changes of rising and setting. So no created body, however bright, can be the Lord of life who nurtures, cherishes and sustains it.

### Two lessons for whoever carries the call

The method here gives preachers their guidance. First, in carrying the call to people and seeking reform among them, being universally rigid or universally lenient is not appropriate. Each has its occasion and its limit. Ibrahim used strong words about idolatry, because its error is in common sight, and he used a graduated method about the stars, because the helplessness of the planets is not obvious to the people who consult them. So when ordinary people are caught in an error of judgment or conduct that they do not recognise as such, the scholar or the preacher should avoid a hard, dogmatic line and find a better way to remove the doubt.

Second, the manner in which the truth is presented belongs to the argument. Ibrahim did not order his people to do what had to be done. He told them how matters stood for him: he could not declare as objects of worship things that are caught in a cycle of rising and setting, and that is why he had turned to the being who created, nurtured and cares for them. The purpose was to bring them round to the same place, and he avoided a direct command lest they refuse simply for the sake of refusing. The job of a reformer is not to state what is true in any manner that comes to hand. It is to say it in the way that will actually land.

### In short

- The sun is the largest and the last, and the argument stops where the people's reverence was strongest.
- "I do not love" becomes "I am free of", which is the move from a personal preference to a public break.
- Three tests are given for anything that claims to be a lord: change, alternation, and dependence on another's command.
- The graduated method against the stars and the plain method against idols are both kept as instruction for preachers, each with its occasion.

79.text:
"I have turned my face towards the One Who has originated the heavens and the earth—being upright—and I am not one of the polytheists.”"

The declaration that the three rounds were built to reach, and it is written as an about-turn.

### Phrase by phrase

**"I have turned my face towards the One Who has originated the heavens and the earth"** To turn one's face to someone is to direct one's religion and one's deeds to him sincerely. He originated them, made them without any precedent, and shaped them. Having shown that nothing in the sky can be a Lord, he names as his Lord the one who made the sky, the one who decrees and governs its affairs and holds it in obedience, in whose hand is the dominion of everything. He is the creator, the Lord, the king and the God of all that exists. The wording here matches the verse in the heights: "Your Lord is Allah, who created the heavens and the earth in six days and then rose over the Throne. He brings the night as a cover over the day, seeking it rapidly, and he made the sun, the moon and the stars subject to his command. Surely his is the creation and the command. Blessed is Allah, the Lord of the worlds" (7:54).

**"being upright"** The word translated as upright means one by nature upright, inclining to the straight religion, avoiding shirk and embracing tawhid. The upright person is not the one who has found a position and is defending it. He is the one whose orientation has been corrected.

**"and I am not one of the polytheists"** He states the exclusion as plainly as the commitment, and the word used is that he is not a mushrik, a disbeliever or a polytheist like them. The line is drawn as a permanent one, after a whole debate that never once asked them to admit they were wrong.

### The inner reading of the three rounds

A Sufi treatment of these verses takes the sequence as the movement of a heart rather than as a lesson in astronomy. First Allah showed Ibrahim the dominion of the heavens and the earth, so that he would come to know the maker by way of inference. He looked at the star and said "this is my Lord", meaning that it was evidence pointing to his Lord. His Lord has no beginning and no end, and this thing sets. At each piece of evidence he clung to it, until he passed beyond the degrees of evidence, and then the beauty of the real showed its face to him. By inference and proof he returned to witnessing and to face-to-face vision. He turned away from everything, and said, as another verse puts it on his lips: "Surely they are an enemy to me, and what you worship besides Allah will not benefit me" (26:77). One report has him say to Gabriel, when Gabriel came at that point: as for turning towards you, no. He was at first like one who knows, and then he became like one who recognises.

Al-Wasiti put the distinction in a sentence of his own: the creatures are going to Allah, and the recognizers are coming from him. And he said: if a man tells you that he came to know Allah through evidence, ask him how he came to know the evidence. The entry of evidence is unavoidable at the beginning, and this was the beginning of Ibrahim's path. When he reached each piece of evidence he said: this is my Lord. When he passed beyond all of it, he saw the beauty of tawhid with the eye of direct vision, and he said: "O my people, I am free of what you associate", that is, I am free of inferring the Creator from the creatures, since there is no evidence for him but himself. It is the same stand taken by a great name of this religion, who said that he came to know Allah through Allah, and came to know what is beneath Allah through Allah's light.

### In short

- The declaration is an orientation, not a creed recited from a distance, and the wording puts the face, not the mouth, into the sentence.
- The one he turns to is named as the originator of the heavens and the earth, which answers the sky-worshippers on their own ground.
- Being upright is defined as a turning away from shirk and a turning to tawhid at the same time.
- The inner reading treats the three rounds as a path from evidence to witnessing, in which the evidence is honoured and then left behind.

80.text:
"And his people argued with him. He responded, “Are you arguing with me about Allah, while He has guided me? I am not afraid of whatever ˹idols˺ you associate with Him—˹none can harm me,˺ unless my Lord so wills. My Lord encompasses everything in ˹His˺ knowledge. Will you not be mindful”"

The debate that began with a star now turns into a stand-off, and the verse records what Ibrahim says when he is threatened.

### Phrase by phrase

**"And his people argued with him"** The argument is about their gods, and it comes with a threat attached, and the threat is meant to push him out of the religion of Allah. The shape of the threat is specific: they feared that as a result of this insolence he would be punished by the deities he belittled. He would go blind, or go mad, or meet destruction. A people who suppose that a thing has a high status in the scheme of the universe naturally assume that pleasing it brings good fortune and displeasing it brings the reverse, and Ibrahim's words had removed the protection his gods were supposed to provide.

**"Are you arguing with me about Allah, while He has guided me?"** Do you dispute with me about Allah? There is no god worthy of worship besides him, and he has guided me to it and shown me what it is. The dispute is about Allah's oneness, and about tawhid as against the partners they keep attaching to him, and he has been given the certainty of it. The reciters of the Qur'ānic text read the verb in two ways, with the two letters nūn intact or with one of them dropped. Grammarians call the dropped one the nūn of modal independence, and the reciters call it the nūn of preservation. The meaning is unaffected, and the sentence is a question that has no answer in it: how could I weigh your doubts against what I have been shown?

**"I am not afraid of whatever idols you associate with Him, none can harm me, unless my Lord so wills"** Part of his proof is that these gods he is being warned about produce no effect at all. He does not fear them and does not take them into account. So if they can cause harm, use them against him now, and give him no respite. Except that only Allah brings about benefit or harm. One gloss takes "unless my Lord wills" as a further refinement: he is not afraid of them unless his Lord wills to take the knowledge out of his heart, so that he would fear as they fear. The meaning is that a man can lose what he has been given, and everything rests on being held.

**"My Lord encompasses everything in His knowledge"** Allah's knowledge surrounds all things, and nothing escapes his complete observation. He knows that you are not following the truth.

**"Will you not be mindful"** Will you not then remember what I have explained to you, see your idols for the false gods they are, and stop worshipping them? The question is the last courtesy in the argument. It is also the pivot of the verses that follow, since verse 76 opened with a star and ended in a demand for proof.

### The same answer from another prophet

Ibrahim's reasoning here belongs to a pattern. Hud answered his people, ʿAd, in almost the same terms when they told him that some of his gods had seized him with evil. He said: "I call Allah to witness, and bear me witness, that I am free of what you ascribe as partners to him, so plot against me, all of you, and give me no respite. I put my trust in Allah, my Lord and your Lord. There is no moving creature but he has a grasp of its forelock, and my Lord is on the straight path" (11:53-56). Whoever is on the straight path does not need the protection of things that cannot speak.

### In short

- The threat against Ibrahim is not abstract. He is told that his safety depends on the gods he has insulted, and he answers by taking that claim literally.
- His fearlessness is not bravado but a definition: only Allah brings benefit or harm, so nothing else is a candidate for fear.
- The reciters' two readings of one verb in the verse change nothing of the sense, and are recorded for that reason.
- The knowledge of Allah is the closing weight in the sentence: whatever they do is already encompassed.

81.text:
"And how should I fear your associate-gods, while you have no fear in associating ˹others˺ with Allah—a practice He has never authorized? Which side has more right to security? ˹Tell me˺ if you really know!”

One question, put twice, and then a third that decides the case.

### Phrase by phrase

**"And how should I fear your associate-gods"** How should I fear what you have set up beside him, when it can neither profit nor harm? The idols he is being threatened with are themselves set up, and set up wrongly. He asks them to notice the asymmetry: a thing that needs its worshippers in order to exist at all cannot be what keeps a man safe.

**"while you have no fear in associating others with Allah, a practice He has never authorized"** And you do not fear Allah in associating with him things that he created, for which he has sent down no warrant to you. The word for warrant here means proof and authority, as Ibn Abbas and others among the salaf explained it. Two other verses state the same standard. "Do they have partners who institute for them a religion that Allah has not permitted?" (42:21). "They are but names which you and your fathers have named, for which Allah has sent down no authority" (53:21). Worship, in other words, is not a matter of taste or inheritance. It needs a permission, and no permission has come.

**"Which side has more right to security? Tell me if you really know"** Which of the two parties is on the truth? Is it the one that worships him in whose hand are harm and benefit, or the one that worships what cannot bring harm or benefit without any authority to justify it? Which of the two is more deserving of safety from Allah's punishment on the Day of Rising? The question is put to them as an examination, and the wording of the gloss is blunt: if you have knowledge of which party is more deserving, then follow that party. The answer, in the sense of the verse, is the believers who are monotheists, and they are the ones without doubt.

### Why the question is left open

One reading takes the sentence as addressed to the two factions together, asking which of the adherents of the two religions has more right to be safe from the God he worships. The question is not asked for information, and it is not answered in the verse either. It is left open so that the hearers have to say it themselves, and the next verse then gives the answer out loud. The silence after a question like this is what makes the answer in verse 82 sound like a verdict rather than a claim.

### In short

- The verse turns the threat back on the people making it, by asking which side has a warrant for what it does.
- A sent-down authority is the missing item in idolatry, and two other verses are quoted to show that the standard is general.
- Security is measured against the God one worships, not against the crowd one belongs to.
- The question goes unanswered by his people, which is why the answer in the next verse is stated as a rule.

82.text:
It is ˹only˺ those who are faithful and do not tarnish their faith with falsehood who are guaranteed security and are ˹rightly˺ guided

The answer to the open question, and the sentence that frightened the companions when it was revealed.

### Phrase by phrase

**"It is those who are faithful"** When they did not answer what Ibrahim asked, the answer came as a statement about a class of people rather than about the argument. The verse does not say: you are all ruined. It says who is safe. Those who believe in Allah and follow his laws.

**"and do not tarnish their faith with falsehood"** The verb here is built on a root that means to wear, to cover, and to mix, so the sense is that they do not mix up their faith with injustice and do not pollute it with idolatry. The word for injustice is left indefinite in Arabic, which by the rules of grammar makes it general, and it therefore takes in every kind of shirk, not only the open prostration to a stone. One gloss adds that they are not hypocrites either, since a hypocrite is exactly a person who mixes something else into what he professes.

**"who are guaranteed security"** For them is safety from Allah, and safety from his punishment, and they are the guided ones in this life and in the Hereafter. They are guided to what is right, and it is also said that they are the people who have safety and are guided to the proof of faith, and their Lord has shown them the path of guidance.

### What the companions took from it

When the verse came down, saying "and do not tarnish their faith with injustice", it was hard on the people, and they said: messenger of Allah, who among us has not been unjust to himself? If the only way to be safe is to have done no injustice at all while believing, how can anybody be saved? The answer came back: "It is not what you understood from it. Did you not hear what the righteous servant said?" And that servant said to his son: "O my son, do not join others in worship with Allah. Verily joining others in worship with Allah is a great injustice indeed" (31:13). So the injustice in the verse is shirk. The report is in the two Sahīhs, that of al-Bukhari and that of Muslim, and Ahmad recorded it through Abdullah as well. Whoever enters into faith and then does not associate anyone with Allah in his being or in his attributes remains safe from the punishment, and is counted among the well guided.

### A wider definition of the same crime

The verse also settles a question that people tend to answer too narrowly. Shirk is not restricted to becoming an idolater in the customary sense. A person may recite the words of Islam, and still take some angel, messenger or saint as a sharer in attributes that belong to Allah alone. The warning in this verse is stern for anyone who treats the men of Allah and their resting places as able to answer a prayer or grant a need, and who behaves practically as though the divine powers had been delegated to them. The verse also decides that shirk is not confined to the man who becomes a mushrik in the usual sense. Those who worship idols, rocks, trees, rivers and stars do so out of a bland simplicity, taking them to be holders and wielders of power. Ibrahim gave such people the key to their problem when he told them to fear the Allah who knows everything they do and has power over whatever reaches them, rather than to fear things that have neither knowledge nor power. That fear is unreasonable, and whoever believes that it is unreasonable is out of danger.

### In short

- The guarantee of safety is attached to a combination, not to a label: faith plus the absence of any mixture in it.
- The verse's first readers understood "injustice" as ordinary sin and had to be corrected to shirk, which is how the range of the word got fixed.
- Mixing covers more than statues, since it covers borrowing attributes for a creature, and the entry says so as the material does.
- Guidance is named in the same breath as security, because the verse's promise is not only safety but direction.

83.text:
